stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Rain and weather small talk, being hungry or thirsty, feeling unwell and going to the doctor, getting dressed, taking the train, work, bathing, and how long or how much something takes.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Aches and colds, meals and taste, what you like and what you notice, photos, messages and phone calls, hats and glasses, and what people look like.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Making plans and friends, lights at home, finding your way, eating out, shops and cash, hobbies, masks and outfits, picking people up, and what people are like.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Joking and secrets, locks, chores and alarms, mood and stress, splitting the bill and saving, favours and thanks, exams, battery and signal, winning and losing, and getting caught outdoors.

categories.name: Weather & nature
categories.scope: Rain, snow, wind, thunder, sun, clouds, temperature, seasons: ame ga furu / yuki ga furu, ame ga yamu, ame ni furareru (get caught in the rain), kaze ga fuku, kaze ga tsuyoi, tsuyoi ame (heavy rain), kaminari ga naru, hi ga deru / taiyou ga deru, hi ga kureru (get dark), niji ga deru, kasa o sasu, kion ga agaru / sagaru, ase o kaku (if not in body), tenki ga ii.

blocks.label: Rain and snow
blocks.rationale: The basic rain-and-snow sentences: it's coming down, it has stopped, and the umbrella's own verb.
blocks.interference: ame ga furu and yuki ga furu share furu, so drill them in one frame (soto, ___ futteru yo); snow lying on the ground is yuki ga tsumoru. Keep ame ga yamu (rain stops by itself) apart from yameru (a person quits), and kasa o sasu (have it up) apart from kasa o motsu (carry it).

items.use: You hear ame futteru (it's raining) most, usually without ga. Plain ame furu points ahead, as in ashita ame furu kana (will it rain tomorrow?).
items.verbSense: fall from the sky (rain, snow, hail)
items.trap: Not ame ga ochiru: rain falls with furu. Once the topic is weather, furu alone means rain: futte kita (it's started raining), furisou da ne (looks like rain).

example.ja: 外、雨降ってるよ。
example.english: It's raining outside.

examplePolite.romaji: soto, ame ga futtemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 外、雨が降ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's raining outside.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 雨が降る is also listed as a set expression at #5450. Kana あめ also covers 飴 (candy), and ふる covers 振る (wave/dump), so the kanji ranks are used. Hail 雹 is #67652, hence 'rare' in partners.
items.notes: ame furisou = looks like rain; ame futte kita = it's started raining.

items.use: Same shape as ame ga furu: yuki futteru is 'it's snowing', and ashita yuki furu kamo is 'it might snow tomorrow'.
items.verbSense: fall from the sky (rain, snow, hail)
items.trap: Not yuki ga ochiru: snow takes the same furu as rain, so yuki futteru is 'it's snowing'.

example.ja: 外、雪降ってるよ！
example.english: It's snowing outside!

examplePolite.romaji: soto, yuki ga futtemasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 外、雪が降ってますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's snowing outside.

items.freqNote: Kana ゆき also covers place names and 行き, so the kanji rank is used.
items.notes: Snow lying on the ground is yuki ga tsumoru (yuki tsumotteru = the snow's settled / there's snow on the ground).

items.use: Mostly heard as ame yanda? (has it stopped?) or ame yamu made matou (let's wait till it stops). Ima wa yanderu means it has stopped for now, not 'it is stopping'.
items.verbSense: stop or die down by itself (rain, wind, noise)
items.trap: Not ame ga tomaru, and not yameru (a person quitting something): rain stops with intransitive yamu.

example.ja: もう雨やんだ？
example.english: Has the rain stopped yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ame, mou yamimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨、もうやみましたか？
examplePolite.english: Has the rain stopped yet?

items.freqNote: Rank is for kana やむ (#3517), the usual spelling of this verb; 病む (#9762) and やむを得ない (#17615) have their own rows, though the kana row may still hold a little kana-written 病む. The kanji 止む alone is #14280.
items.notes: ame ga agaru (the rain lifts) is a common alternative: ame agatta ne.

items.english: put up (open) an umbrella; have an umbrella up
items.use: Said about having an umbrella up over you: kasa sashite aruku (walk with an umbrella up), kasa sasanakute ii yo (no need to put it up). Kasa sashiteru means someone has one up. Taking one with you is kasa motte iku, not sasu: kasa motte itta hou ga ii yo (you'd better take an umbrella).
items.verbSense: hold something up over you (an umbrella, a parasol)
items.trap: Not kasa o akeru: an umbrella you hold up over you is sasu. Hiraku is only the moment of opening it, motsu is carrying it (kasa motteru? = got an umbrella?), and tsukau fits offering one (kasa tsukau? = want to use my umbrella?).

example.romaji: kasa sashita hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 傘さしたほうがいいよ。
example.english: You'd better put your umbrella up.

examplePolite.romaji: kasa o sashita hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 傘をさしたほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You'd better put your umbrella up.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 差す (#7696). 傘をさす is usually written in kana, and kana さす (#3059) also holds the causative and other kana-written senses (刺す #1780 and 指す #6552 have their own rows), so the umbrella sense ranks somewhere between the two.
items.notes: Closing it is kasa o tojiru, or kasa o tatamu (fold it up). A different sasu from the 'sting' in ka ni sasareru, though they sound the same.

blocks.label: Weather small talk
blocks.rationale: The remarks people trade about conditions outside: nice weather, strong wind, heavy rain, and how early it gets dark.
blocks.interference: kaze ga tsuyoi and ame ga tsuyoi both use tsuyoi where English says 'windy' and 'heavy', so learn them in one frame (kyou ___ tsuyoi ne); kaze (wind) sounds like kaze (a cold): kaze ga tsuyoi vs kaze o hiku. Keep hi ga kureru apart from kureru 'give'.

items.use: The default weather opener, usually as ii tenki da ne (nice weather, huh?); bad weather is tenki ga warui.
items.verbSense: good, fine
items.trap: English 'beautiful/lovely weather' pushes kirei na tenki, which sounds odd: nice weather is ii tenki, bad is tenki ga warui.

example.ja: 今日いい天気だね。
example.english: Nice weather today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ii otenki desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日はいいお天気ですね。
examplePolite.english: Nice weather today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: いい is #24 (the spelling 良い is #1474). Native judgement: the attributive ii tenki (da ne) is the more common spoken shape. The list has no phrase count.
items.notes: Polite speech usually says otenki. The past is yokatta, not iikatta: tenki yokatta ne. tenki ga kuzureru = the weather turns bad; tenki motsu kana = will the weather hold? Sunny and cloudy are single verbs: hareteru (it's clear), kumotteru (it's cloudy).

items.use: The normal way to say 'it's windy': kyou kaze tsuyoi ne. When it picks up, kaze tsuyoku natte kita.
items.verbSense: strong (wind, rain, sun, a person)
items.trap: There is no Japanese adjective for 'windy': say the wind is strong (kaze ga tsuyoi), or kaze ga aru for 'there's some wind'.

example.ja: 今日風強いね。
example.english: It's windy today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze ga tsuyoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風が強いですね。
examplePolite.english: It's windy today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 風 (kaze, wind) is #1532. The homophone 風邪 (kaze, a cold) is a separate entry at #2666. 強風 (strong wind) is #22617 but belongs to news register.
items.notes: kaze ga dete kita = the wind's picking up; ii kaze fuiteru = there's a nice breeze (kaze ga fuku = the wind blows, not to be confused with kaze o hiku, catch a cold). For no wind at all people say kaze ga nai.

items.use: Said as ame tsuyoi ne or ame tsuyoku natte kita (it's really coming down now). Tsuyoi ame is the same pairing before the noun. Just as often you hear ame sugoi ne or hidoi ame.
items.verbSense: strong (wind, rain, sun, a person)
items.trap: Not omoi ame: omoi is only weight, so heavy rain is strong rain; ame ga hidoi and ooame are also fine.

example.ja: 今日雨強いね。
example.english: The rain's heavy today, huh?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa ame ga tsuyoi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は雨が強いですね。
examplePolite.english: The rain's heavy today, isn't it?

items.freqNote: The attributive tsuyoi ame is the same pairing. The single nouns 大雨 (#11181) and 土砂降り/どしゃ降り (#30415–32931) are alternatives, not collocations.
items.notes: When it eases off: ame yowaku natta; a downpour is doshaburi.

items.use: Mostly heard in hi ga kureru mae ni (before it gets dark) and hi ga kureru no ga hayai (it gets dark early). In plain chat people also just say kuraku natte kita.
items.verbSense: (of a day or year) draw to a close; grow dark at dusk
items.trap: Nothing in English points to kureru, and it isn't kureru 'give me': the day 'closes'. Kuraku naru (get dark) is also natural.

example.romaji: hi ga kureru mae ni kaerou.
example.ja: 日が暮れる前に帰ろう。
example.english: Let's head home before it gets dark.

examplePolite.romaji: hi ga kureru mae ni kaerimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 日が暮れる前に帰りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's head home before it gets dark.

items.freqNote: The phrase 日が暮れる is listed as a set expression at #7770, which ranks higher than the bare verb 暮れる (#14744). 日 #209 mixes the 'day' and 'sun' senses. Kana くれる (#565) is mostly 'give'.
items.notes: Classic autumn remark: hi ga kureru no hayaku natta ne (it's getting dark earlier). Joking 'this'll take forever': sonna no yattetara hi ga kurechau yo. Days getting longer: hi ga nobita ne.

blocks.label: Caught outdoors
blocks.rationale: Three things the outdoors does to you, each with the cause marked by ni where English says 'get -ed'.
blocks.interference: ka ni sasareru and ame ni furareru are passives but hi ni yakeru is not (yaketa, not yakareta); ame ni furareta says it rained on you, ame ga futta just reports the rain.

items.use: Almost always past or -teru: hi ni yaketa (I got tanned or burnt), yoku yaketeru ne (you're nicely tanned). Often just yaketa, without hi ni.
items.verbSense: get grilled, roasted or burned (meat, toast, skin in the sun)
items.trap: English 'tan' or 'get sunburnt' gives no clue: the skin gets grilled by the sun (yakeru, the same verb as toast or meat), with the sun marked by ni. It's plain yaketa, not the passive yakareta; tanning on purpose is transitive hada o yaku.

example.romaji: kinou umi de hi ni yakechatta.
example.ja: 昨日海で日に焼けちゃった。
example.english: I got sunburnt at the beach yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou umi de hi ni yakemashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日海で日に焼けました。
examplePolite.english: I got sunburnt at the beach yesterday.

items.freqNote: The 日 row is listed under the reading hi but probably absorbs other uses of the character. The noun 日焼け (hiyake, a tan) is #11984; the transitive 焼く (yaku) is #1576.
items.notes: hiyake suru / hiyake shita (got a tan) is just as common. What tans takes ga: hada ga yaketa, kao dake yaketeru (only my face is tanned). Also for sun-fading: kaaten ga hi ni yaketa (the curtains faded in the sun).

items.use: Nearly always past, often with the spot first: ashi, ka ni sasareta (I got bitten on the leg). With the spot inside the sentence the body part takes o: ka ni ashi o sasareta (a mosquito got me on the leg). Kayui (itchy) usually follows.
items.verbSense: sasu = pierce, stab, sting (needles, insects); the passive sasareru means get stung or bitten
items.trap: English 'bite' leads to ka ni kamareru, but the standard verb is sasu (pierce); kamu is for teeth, as with dogs. Ka ni kamareru is heard in some regions, but sasareru is the safe default. Casual ka ni kuwareta ('got eaten') is also common among friends, though a bit rough.

example.romaji: kinou kouen de ka ni sasarechatta.
example.ja: 昨日公園で蚊に刺されちゃった。
example.english: I got bitten by mosquitoes in the park yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kouen de ka ni sasarechaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日公園で蚊に刺されちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I got bitten by mosquitoes in the park yesterday.

items.freqNote: verbRank is the dictionary form 刺す (sasu); the passive sasareru has no row of its own. Kana か is the question particle, so the kanji 蚊 rank is used.
items.notes: Same sasu as hachi ni sasareru (stung by a bee); unrelated to kasa o sasu.

items.use: Almost always past, usually with -chatta: ame ni furarechatta (I got rained on). Ame ga futta just reports the weather; furareta says it happened to you.
items.verbSense: furu = fall from the sky; the passive furareru means it fell on you, to your cost
items.trap: 'Get caught in the rain' points to tsukamaru, but Japanese says the rain fell on you, with furu's suffering passive: ame ni furareta. Ame ni au (run into rain: ame ni atchatta) is just as natural.

example.romaji: kinou kaeri ni ame ni furarechatta.
example.ja: 昨日帰りに雨に降られちゃった。
example.english: I got caught in the rain on the way home yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kaeri ni ame ni furarechaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日帰りに雨に降られちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I got caught in the rain on the way home yesterday.

items.freqNote: The passive 降られる is not a dictionary form, so it isn't in the list. The rank is for the base 降る. The alternative's verb 遭う (au, run into) is #2225.
items.notes: Getting soaked is nureru: ame ni nurechatta (I got wet in the rain). Ame ni au sounds like au 'meet' but is a different verb (遭う, run into).

changelog.change: Trap rewritten: dropped the misleading 'no verb to rain' claim, added that bare furu means rain in context (futte kita, furisou da ne). englishVerb fall -> rain. Partners: hyou marked rare (雹 #67652, noted in freqNote). Added I-te-kuru link for ame futte kita.

trapRisk 4 -> 3 and trap shortened to the furu point (same verb as rain, not ochiru); dropped the 'no verb to snow' claim for the same reason as rain. englishVerb fall -> snow to match ame-ga-furu. Partners: hyou marked rare. Notes gloss fixed ('the snow's settled / there's snow on the ground'). Added F-kamo link for yuki furu kamo.
Polite example made natural (ame, mou yamimashita ka?). verbRank 14280 -> 3517 (kana やむ, the usual spelling; 病む and やむを得ない checked and have their own rows); freqNote rewritten to match.

FATAL fixed: use no longer glosses kasa sashite iku as 'take an umbrella'; now kasa sashite aruku / sasanakute ii yo (no need to put it up), and 'take one with you' is given as kasa motte iku. Trap now leads with kasa o akeru; tsukau glossed as offering one, not borrowing. englishVerb open -> 'put up / open'; english -> 'put up (open) an umbrella; have an umbrella up'. freqNote corrected (刺す and 指す have their own rows; kana さす holds causative etc.). Notes: closing it is tojiru / tatamu. Left out the reviewer's '(not shimeru)' because I'm not sure that form is wrong.

Trap rewritten around 'beautiful weather' -> kirei na tenki; the yokatta/iikatta point moved to notes. Polite example now uses ii otenki desu ne. freqNote no longer claims frequency without data (now marked as native judgement). Notes add otenki, tenki ga kuzureru and tenki motsu kana. Past-tense sentence removed from use (now in notes).

Trap: kaze ga aru is now glossed 'there's some wind', not 'a light breeze'. Example English 'It's windy today, huh?' ('really' removed). Added I-te-kuru and H-aru links. Notes take over from the dropped kaze-ga-fuku: kaze ga dete kita, ii kaze fuiteru, and kaze ga fuku vs kaze o hiku.
Example English 'The rain's heavy today, huh?' ('really' removed). Use adds ame sugoi ne / hidoi ame. Added I-te-kuru link.
Added links D-hayai and H-kaeru-return (used in use and examples). Notes add the joking hi ga kurechau yo (romaji yattetara, joined per convention) and hi ga nobita ne.

Trap rewritten: dropped the false 'no verb to tan' claim; it now says English gives no clue to yakeru, adds the passive warning and transitive hada o yaku. Partners hada/kao removed (they are ga-subjects) and moved to notes as hada ga yaketa / kao dake yaketeru. Polite example now plain past (yakemashita). Added I-chau link. Notes add sun-fading (kaaten ga hi ni yaketa). freqNote adds 焼く #1576.

Use adds the in-sentence frame ka ni ashi o sasareta. Trap adds that ka ni kamareru is regional (sasareru is the safe default) and marks kuwareta as casual and a bit rough, written in the trap because the flags enum has no slot for an alternative's register. verb/verbJa -> sasareru/刺される to match the headword; verbSense explains sasu -> sasareru. Added I-chau link.

Trap adds ame ni au as an equally natural alternative (romaji atchatta, per the t-before-ch rule; reviewer wrote acchatta). Added H-au-meet link, and a note that it sounds like au 'meet' but is the verb 遭う (run into). verb/verbJa -> furareru/降られる to match the headword. englishVerb caught -> get caught. freqNote adds 遭う #2225.
Interference adds yuki ga tsumoru (snow lying on the ground) and the kasa o sasu vs kasa o motsu contrast.
Rationale and interference updated for the dropped kaze-ga-fuku: the kaze homophone warning now pairs kaze ga tsuyoi with kaze o hiku.

Not added, because the rules forbid adding items. Reviewers flagged these gaps for a later pass: kaminari ga naru (雷 #7324, 鳴る #2069), yuki ga tsumoru (積もる #9027, now in notes only), ame ni nureru (濡れる #6660, would fill out the 3-item 'Caught outdoors'), hi ga ataru, tenki ga kuzureru, niji ga deru, taifuu ga kuru, kion ga agaru/sagaru.

dropped.reason: Two reviewers want it out of this domain. The traps review cuts it as fully guessable ('the wind blows' maps straight onto fuku; the draft itself says 'no verb trap'; lowest score in the domain at 3/2/2). The nuance review says to move it beside kaze o hiku in the body domain, or cut it, and this weather pass can't place items in another domain. Its content moved into kaze-ga-tsuyoi's notes (ii kaze fuiteru, kaze ga dete kita, kaze ga fuku vs kaze o hiku). The body domain can bring it back as a contrast partner if it wants one.

reviewSummaries: natural: The pairings are all the ones natives actually use, and nearly every example sounds natural, with particles dropped where people drop them. All listLinks, ranks and alsoIn pointers check out. There is one real error: kasa-o-sasu glosses 'kasa sashite iku' as 'I'll take an umbrella', which is the motsu/sasu mix-up the item exists to prevent. The hi-ni-yakeru trap also wrongly says English has no verb 'to tan'. The rest is polish: extra 'really' in two glosses, one stiff polite example, an understated やむ rank, an unflagged rough kuwareta, and a few missing links. kaze-ga-fuku is the weakest item (trap 2, speakNeed 2), but it's worth keeping as the partner to kaze o hiku. Gaps: kaminari ga naru (雷 #7324 / 鳴る #2069, and English 'it thunders' gives no noun+verb hint), taifuu ga kuru (#8171), kion ga agaru/sagaru, and yuki ga tsumoru / ame ni nureru (now only in notes) are high-value weather collocations missing from this domain.

traps: The draft is solid overall: I checked every nounRank and verbRank against freq.py and they match, every listLinks id exists, and every alsoIn pointer resolves. Romaji, examples and transitive/intransitive labelling are clean. One fatal error: kasa-o-sasu glosses sashite iku as 'take an umbrella', which teaches the motsu mix-up its own trap warns against. Several traps miss either the learner's likeliest wrong form or a natural alternative: kasa o akeru, ame ni au, bare furu meaning rain, and hada o yaku. hi-ni-yakeru lists its subjects as partners. Two items are guessable and should be cut (yuki ga furu, kaze ga fuku); their slots should go to kaminari ga naru and yuki ga tsumoru.

nuance: The draft is strong overall. Glosses, traps and aspect notes are accurate (ame yanderu = has stopped, furareta vs futta, yakeru not passive), polite pairs are true desu/masu counterparts, and every listLink id and alsoIn pointer checks out against the source files. One fatal error: kasa-o-sasu glosses kasa sashite iku as 'take an umbrella', which teaches the sasu/motsu confusion the item warns against. The structural problems are the kaze-fuku-hiku contrast set split across domains (kaze ga fuku should move beside kaze o hiku, or be cut) and a 3-item 'Caught outdoors' block that should take ame ni nureru. The rest is polish: two freqNotes misread the kana rows, some examples add 'really', and a few listLinks and notes are missing.

form: The form and data are clean overall. I checked all 26 nounRank and verbRank values and every set-expression rank against freq.py, and all are exact. All 20 listLinks ids exist in the versatility list, and the alsoIn pointers (10-list-nouns #8, #88, #89, #90, #137; vocab-trainer weather-terms and accessories) are correct. Romaji, kana, polite forms and example ja/romaji pairs all match, there are no macrons, and the spacing follows the existing list's style (te kita and hou ga ii written separately). The one real error is the kasa-o-sasu use gloss: kasa sashite iku is glossed as 'take an umbrella', which teaches the motsu confusion the item exists to prevent, and its englishVerb 'open' points the same wrong way. The rest is polish: the ame-ga-yamu verb rank (#14280 for the rare kanji spelling instead of kana #3517), verb fields that don't match the two passive headwords, missing I-chau and I-te-kuru links, and two English example translations that add 'really'.

categories.name: Body & health
categories.scope: Illness, pain, symptoms, hunger and thirst, injury, medicine, the doctor: kaze o hiku, netsu ga aru / netsu ga deru, takai netsu, seki ga deru, hanamizu ga deru, nodo ga itai, atama ga itai, onaka ga itai, onaka ga suku, onaka ga ippai, nodo ga kawaku, kusuri o nomu, kega o suru, chi ga deru, ase o kaku, guai ga warui, memai ga suru / samuke ga suru, chuusha o utsu, ashi o kujiku, me ga tsukareru, toshi o toru.

blocks.label: Hunger, thirst, sweat
blocks.rationale: Everyday body signals around meals, heat and exercise, none of them illness.
blocks.interference: onaka ga suku and nodo ga kawaku put a feeling you have now in the past (suita, kawaita), while onaka ippai has no verb of its own (ni natta is added for the past); ase o kaku pairs sweat with kaku, and ase ga deru (sweat comes out) is also natural, but ase suru is never said.

items.use: Said in the past for hunger you feel now: onaka suita (I'm hungry), ga usually dropped. Onaka suiteru? asks if someone is hungry, and onaka suitenai is 'I'm not hungry'.
items.verbSense: become empty, thin out (densha ga suiteru = the train isn't crowded)
items.trap: No everyday 'hungry' adjective (himojii is old-fashioned): the stomach empties, onaka suita, in the past tense for hunger you feel now.

example.ja: ああ、お腹すいた。なんか食べよう。
example.english: I'm so hungry. Let's get something to eat.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, onaka ga sukimashita ne. nanika tabemashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、お腹がすきましたね。何か食べましょうか。
examplePolite.english: I'm hungry, aren't you? Shall we get something to eat?

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758). Verb rank is kana すく #2947. 好く 'like' (#1880, mostly 好かれる / 好かない) is a separate word and is not counted, though the tokenizer may file some kana すいた under it, so #2947 may undercount this sense. Kanji 空く read すく is #47898 (read あく it is #1498). Phrase entries: お腹が空く #22626, お腹がすく #27605. The rough 腹が減る is #6497 and 腹減った #4970.
items.notes: Hara hetta (hara ga heru) is the rough, mostly male version. Onaka pekopeko (I'm starving) is childish or cute.

items.use: Said at the end of a meal and to turn down more food, usually without ga: mou onaka ippai (I'm full). It has no verb of its own: add desu to be polite, and ni natta for the past, as in onaka ippai ni natta? (are you full?).
items.verbSense: full, filled up; also 'a lot' (ippai aru = there's lots)
items.trap: English 'I'm full' names no body part; Japanese says the stomach is full, onaka ippai. Keep onaka in: ippai alone mostly means 'a lot', and mou ippai can be heard as 'one more (drink)'.

example.ja: ああ、お腹いっぱい。もう食べられない。
example.english: I'm so full. I can't eat another bite.

examplePolite.romaji: mou onaka ippai desu. gochisousama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: もうお腹いっぱいです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: I'm full. Thank you for the meal.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); いっぱい #512 counts every sense ('a lot', 'full'); 一杯 #2892 and １杯 #2744 are mostly 'one cup'. Ippai is a noun or adverb, not a verb or adjective; it goes in the partner slot. Phrase entry お腹いっぱい #14252 (particle dropped); 満腹 #18617.
items.notes: Hara ippai is the rougher, mostly male version; hara ippai taberu = eat your fill. Mou onaka ippai can also mean 'I've had enough of that'.

items.use: Said in the past for thirst you feel now: nodo kawaita (I'm thirsty), ga usually dropped. Nodo kawaiteru? asks if someone is thirsty.
items.verbSense: become dry (of the throat); the same-sounding kawaku is also used for laundry or paint drying
items.trap: No 'thirsty' adjective: the throat dries, nodo kawaita, in the past tense for thirst you feel now.

example.ja: 喉渇いた。水ある？
example.english: I'm thirsty. Is there any water?

examplePolite.romaji: nodo ga kawakimashita. omizu o moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 喉が渇きました。お水をもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: I'm thirsty. Could I have some water?

items.freqNote: 喉 #3552 (kana のど #7553); 渇く #6159 (its homophone 乾く 'dry' is #6556); phrase entry 喉が渇く #14507.
items.notes: The same nodo is the throat in nodo ga itai (sore throat).

items.use: Mostly heard in the past, ase kaita or ase kaichatta (I got all sweaty), after heat or exercise. For dripping with sweat natives say asedaku: asedaku ni natta.
items.verbSense: scratch; with sweat or snoring it means to give something off from the body
items.trap: 'Sweat' is a verb in English, but Japanese uses the noun with kaku: ase o kaku, not ase suru (ase ga deru, 'sweat comes out', is also fine). This kaku is not kaku 'write'.

example.ja: 汗かいたから、シャワー浴びたい。
example.english: I'm all sweaty, I want a shower.

examplePolite.romaji: ase o kaita node, shawaa o abite kite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 汗をかいたので、シャワーを浴びてきてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I got all sweaty. Would it be OK if I had a shower?

items.freqNote: 汗 #2650. Verb rank is kana かく #11889, the spelling used here, which mixes 掻く with kana-written 書く/描く. Kanji 掻く is #51963. Phrase entry 汗をかく #13368.
items.notes: The same kaku goes with embarrassment: haji kaita (I embarrassed myself).

blocks.label: Feeling unwell
blocks.rationale: What you say when you're unwell and what you do about it.
blocks.interference: guai ga warui is feeling unwell in general (kibun ga warui is feeling sick right now); yoko ni naru is lying down to rest, neru is sleeping; kusuri o nomu and byouin ni iku replace an English 'take' and 'see' that pull toward toru and miru or au.

items.use: The general 'I'm not feeling well', usually softened to chotto guai warui; others ask guai warui no? or guai dou? (how are you feeling?).
items.verbSense: bad
items.trap: 'I'm sick' as byouki desu sounds like a real illness; for just feeling unwell, the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
partners: kibun (feeling; kibun ga warui = feel sick, also 'be put off')

example.romaji: chotto guai warui kara, saki ni kaeru ne.
example.ja: ちょっと具合悪いから、先に帰るね。
example.english: I'm not feeling great, so I'll head home early.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto guai ga warui node, kyou wa saki ni kaette mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと具合が悪いので、今日は先に帰ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I'm not feeling well. Would it be all right if I went home early today?

items.freqNote: 具合 #1423; 悪い #139; phrase entry 具合が悪い #5837, high for a phrase.
items.notes: Kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now (in a car, in a crowd) and can also mean 'in a bad mood'; kimochi warui (in the senses list) is queasy, but also 'gross, creepy'. Machines usually take choushi: pasokon no choushi ga warui (the computer's acting up).

items.use: For lying down to rest rather than to sleep: chotto yoko ni naru (I'll lie down a bit); to someone unwell, yoko ni natta hou ga ii yo. The ni always stays: never yoko naru.
items.verbSense: become, turn into; with yoko (side) it's 'become horizontal'
items.trap: Dictionaries give yokotawaru, which sounds written; in speech you 'become sideways', yoko ni naru. Neru also works but suggests going to sleep.

example.ja: ちょっと横になっていい？
example.english: Mind if I lie down for a bit?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto yoko ni natte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと横になってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Would it be all right if I lie down for a bit?

items.freqNote: 横 #2228; なる #29 (kanji 成る #13300); phrase entry 横になる #4874, high for a phrase.
items.notes: Related single verb: nekorobu (lie down casually, sprawl).

items.use: Used for pills, powders and syrups alike, often as a check: kusuri nonda? (did you take your medicine?).
items.verbSense: drink, swallow
items.trap: Not kusuri o toru, which would mean fetching it: medicine is 'drunk', kusuri o nomu, even pills.

example.ja: 薬飲んで、早く寝てね。
example.english: Take your medicine and get to bed early.

examplePolite.romaji: kusuri o nonde, yukkuri yasunde kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 薬を飲んで、ゆっくり休んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Take your medicine and get some rest.

items.freqNote: 薬 #1283; 飲む #229. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Eye drops take sasu (megusuri o sasu); cream takes nuru (kusuri o nuru). When it works, the medicine kiku: kono kusuri, yoku kiku (this medicine works well).

items.use: The normal way to say 'see a doctor', often as advice: byouin itta hou ga ii yo. Casual speech usually drops ni: byouin itta?
items.verbSense: go
items.trap: English 'hospital' sounds serious, but byouin is any clinic: for a cold you still go to the byouin, byouin ni iku. Isha ni iku also works; isha o miru or isha ni au doesn't.

example.romaji: sore, byouin itta hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: それ、病院行った方がいいよ。
example.english: You should get that looked at by a doctor.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, byouin ni itta hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それ、病院に行った方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You should have a doctor look at that.

items.freqNote: 病院 #651; 行く #40. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Byouin de mite morau (get it looked at) is the other natural way.

blocks.label: Aches and injuries
blocks.rationale: Saying what hurts or what's wrong with one part of the body.
blocks.interference: X ga itai is pain (atama itai, onaka itai); onaka o kowasu is an upset stomach, with o and a verb; kata ga koru is stiffness, not pain; kega o suru is the injury itself.

items.use: Body part + ga itai is the pattern for any pain, usually said without ga: atama itai. Add n da or n desu when it's the reason you can't do something.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts; on its own, 'ouch!'
items.trap: Not a 'have' sentence: the head hurts, atama ga itai. The noun zutsuu exists (zutsuu ga suru, zutsuuyaku), but in conversation atama itai comes first.

example.ja: 朝からずっと頭いたい。
example.english: I've had a headache since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa kara zutto atama ga itai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝からずっと頭が痛いんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had a headache since this morning.

items.freqNote: 頭 #375; 痛い #336; phrase entry 頭が痛い #8807, a partial count that also includes the figurative 'it's a headache'. 頭痛 #7624.
items.notes: Also used, as in English, for a problem that's a headache.

items.use: Covers any pain in the belly; usually said without ga, onaka itai, often with n da or n desu to explain. Often a polite hint that you need the toilet.
items.verbSense: painful, it hurts
items.trap: Dictionaries give i for 'stomach'; i ga itai is said too, but the everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai.

example.ja: なんかお腹痛い。食べすぎたかも。
example.english: My stomach kind of hurts. Maybe I ate too much.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka onaka ga itai n desu. tabesugita kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんかお腹が痛いんです。食べすぎたかもしれません。
examplePolite.english: My stomach kind of hurts. I might have eaten too much.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 痛い #336. No phrase entry.

items.use: Mostly in the past, onaka kowashita, after bad food, too many cold drinks or travel. It's the decent everyday way to say you have diarrhoea.
items.verbSense: break, damage (kuruma o kowasu = wreck the car)
items.trap: English 'upset stomach' has no word-for-word route: you 'break' your stomach, onaka o kowasu, with o, though nobody did it on purpose.

example.ja: 冷たいもの飲みすぎて、お腹壊した。
example.english: I had too many cold drinks and upset my stomach.

examplePolite.romaji: tsumetai mono o nomisugite, onaka o kowashimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 冷たいものを飲みすぎて、お腹を壊しました。
examplePolite.english: I had too many cold drinks and upset my stomach.

items.freqNote: おなか #1253 (お腹 #4758); 壊す #1284 counts all 'break' uses; phrase entry お腹を壊す #76983.
items.notes: Geri (diarrhoea) is the plain medical word you'd use with a doctor.

items.use: Said as kata kotta (my shoulders have gone stiff) or kata kotteru (they're stiff); the noun katakori is just as common.
items.verbSense: stiffen, harden; also be really into something (ryouri ni koru)
items.trap: English uses the adjective 'stiff', so learners look for one; Japanese uses the verb koru: kata ga kotteru.

example.ja: 一日中パソコンで、肩凝った。
example.english: A whole day at the computer, and my shoulders are stiff.

examplePolite.romaji: ichinichijuu pasokon o tsukatte ite, kata ga korimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 一日中パソコンを使っていて、肩が凝りました。
examplePolite.english: I was on the computer all day, and my shoulders have gone stiff.

items.freqNote: 肩 #1811; kana こる #4566 (kanji 凝る #6722), the higher-ranked spelling as for the other verbs here; phrase entry 肩が凝る #35013; the noun 肩こり is #33119 and 肩凝り #32224.
items.notes: Japanese complain of stiff shoulders where English speakers often say neck or back.

items.use: Heard as kega shita (I got hurt) and as the worried kega nai? (you're not hurt?) after a fall. Name the body part with o and drop kega's own o (ashi o kega shita), or use ni (ashi ni kega o shita); never two o's.
items.verbSense: do, make; here it turns the noun kega (injury) into something that happens
items.trap: Not itaku naru or kizutsuku (mostly hurt feelings): an injury is 'done', kega o suru, even by accident.

example.ja: サッカーで足怪我しちゃった。
example.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

examplePolite.romaji: sakkaa de ashi o kega shita n desu.
examplePolite.ja: サッカーで足を怪我したんです。
examplePolite.english: I hurt my leg playing football.

items.freqNote: けが #3721 (怪我 #7111); する #15. No phrase entry.

blocks.label: Catching a cold
blocks.rationale: A cold and its fever: catching it, the fever coming on, and passing it on.
blocks.interference: netsu ga deru is a fever coming on (netsu deteru = it's up now), netsu ga aru is simply having one; kaze o hiku is getting a cold, kaze ga utsuru (or kaze o morau) is catching it from someone, kaze o utsusu is giving it to them.

items.use: Kaze hiita (or hiichatta) = I've caught a cold; kaze hiiteru = I have a cold right now, not 'I'm catching one'. Usually said without o.
items.verbSense: pull, draw; with a cold it means come down with
items.trap: Not kaze o toru or tsukamu (catch a ball): you 'pull' a cold, kaze o hiku (kaze hiichatta).

example.ja: 風邪ひいちゃったみたい。
example.english: I think I've caught a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hiita mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいたみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I think I've caught a cold.

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666 (風 'wind' is #1532; kana-only かぜ #20653 mixes both); 引く #1039. Phrase entries: 風邪ひく #3998, 風邪をひく #10899, 風邪を引く #27734. These are partial counts because the tokenizer usually splits; the particle-dropped form ranking highest supports the casual drop.
alsoIn: 10-list-nouns #88 (homophone kaze 'wind'; rule S2 makes kaze o hiku the card for 'a cold')
items.notes: Kaze 'cold' sounds exactly like kaze 'wind' (kaze ga fuku = the wind blows), so this phrase is how 'a cold' is learned. Flu doesn't take hiku: infuru ni kakatta, infuru ni natta. Getting over a cold is kaze ga naoru (kaze, mou naotta?).

items.use: For a fever you have now: netsu aru (I've got a temperature), netsu aru no? (have you got a fever?). Netsu deteru also works; netsu deta is the moment it came on.
items.verbSense: there is, exist (for things)
items.trap: Not netsu o motsu: a fever 'exists', netsu ga aru (netsu aru mitai).

example.ja: 今朝からちょっと熱ある。
example.english: I've had a bit of a fever since this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa kara chotto netsu ga aru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今朝からちょっと熱があるんです。
examplePolite.english: I've had a slight fever since this morning.

items.freqNote: 熱 #1641; ある #21. No phrase entry.
items.notes: Often given in Celsius: sanjuuhachido aru (I'm running 38). Nausea and chills take suru: hakike ga suru, samuke ga suru. Taking your temperature is netsu o hakaru, not toru.

items.use: For a fever coming on, mostly past: netsu deta (I came down with a fever). For one you have now, netsu aru and netsu deteru both work. Coughs and runny noses work the same way: seki ga deru, hanamizu ga deru.
items.verbSense: come out, appear; also leave, go out
items.trap: English 'get' pulls toward morau or naru, but a fever 'comes out': netsu ga deru (netsu deta). Morau is for catching a cold from someone (kaze o morau).

example.ja: 今朝急に熱出た。
example.english: I suddenly came down with a fever this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa kyuu ni netsu ga demashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今朝急に熱が出ました。
examplePolite.english: I suddenly came down with a fever this morning.

items.freqNote: 熱 #1641; 出る #81. No phrase entry.
items.notes: The opposite is netsu ga sagaru (the fever goes down). For coughing right now, seki shiteru is also natural.

items.use: Heard as utsuru yo (you'll catch it) and kaze utsutta or utsutchatta (I caught it off someone). Say who from with kara (kodomo kara utsutta) or no (kodomo no kaze ga utsutta). Just as common: kaze o morau, 'receive' the cold (kodomo kara kaze moratchatta).
items.verbSense: move, spread (to another place or person)
items.trap: Kaze o hiku is just getting a cold; to say you caught it from someone, the cold moves to you, kaze ga utsuru.

example.ja: 子供の風邪、うつっちゃった。
example.english: I caught my kid's cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no kaze ga utsutta mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 子供の風邪がうつったみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I think I caught my child's cold.

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666; verb rank is kanji 移る #2350, which also counts 'move house or office'; kana うつる #34832 is the usual spelling for this sense. 映る #2111 and 写る #2975 are other words.

items.use: Mostly in apologies and warnings: kaze utsushichatta, gomen; utsushitara warui kara (I don't want to give it to you). The passive utsusareta = someone gave it to me.
items.verbSense: move or pass something on (to someone else)
items.trap: Not kaze o ageru, which is for gifts: you pass a cold on, kaze o utsusu.

example.ja: ごめん、風邪うつしちゃったみたい。
example.english: Sorry, I think I gave you my cold.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kaze o utsushite shimatta mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、風邪をうつしてしまったみたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I think I gave you my cold.

items.freqNote: 風邪 #2666; verb rank is kanji 移す #3371; kana うつす #12396. No phrase entry.

(past = hunger felt now, ne invites agreement); trap softened to 'no everyday hungry adjective' (himojii is old-fashioned); freqNote no longer calls 好く rare and explains the #1880 rank; notes add childish onaka pekopeko. Moved to first in its block.

Moved to first in its block.

trap no longer calls zutsuu a doctor's word (zutsuu ga suru, zutsuuyaku are everyday); trapRisk 3 -> 2 (my head hurts maps word for word); example.english matches the polite 'since this morning'; example.ja writes 頭いたい so TTS can't read 頭痛 as zutsuu.

verbRank 6722 -> 4566 (kana こる, matching the domain's higher-spelling convention) with freqNote updated; examplePolite no longer telegraphic (pasokon o tsukatte ite), without the stiff -te shimaimashita.

examplePolite uses the spoken 'kaze o hiita mitai desu' instead of the textbook -te shimatta form; both alsoIn pointers annotated as the homophone kaze 'wind'; notes warn flu takes ni kakaru / ni naru, not hiku, and give kaze ga naoru for getting better; listLinks add H-kakaru. kaze-ga-naoru was requested as a new item but not added (no-add rule); it lives in notes.

partners swap hakike (which takes suru in speech) for itami, and notes say hakike/samuke ga suru; use no longer implies netsu ga deru can't describe a current fever; trapRisk 4 -> 3; counter joined (sanjuuhachido); notes add netsu o hakaru (not toru).

trap no longer says morau is wrong for illness (kaze o morau is natural) and names get -> morau/naru; use allows netsu deteru for a current fever and absorbs seki ga deru / hanamizu ga deru from the dropped seki-ga-deru; notes add seki shiteru. Partners unchanged (seki stays, now the single home for symptom + ga deru).

use adds kara for the source and kaze o morau as an equally common way to say it; listLinks add H-morau; verbJa うつる to match ja; casual example drops the repeated mitai; examplePolite uses 'utsutta mitai desu' instead of -te shimatta; alsoIn annotated as the homophone kaze 'wind'.
verbJa うつす to match ja; freqNote states the rank is kanji 移す; alsoIn annotated as the homophone kaze 'wind'.

dropped.reason: Cut by two reviewers (traps, nuance): same symptom + ga deru frame as netsu-ga-deru, which already lists seki as a partner, and a weak trap since seki (o) suru / seki shiteru are also fine. seki ga deru and seki shiteru are folded into netsu-ga-deru's use and notes.

reviewSummaries: natural: The pairings are solid. Every headword is the verb or adjective a Tokyo speaker actually uses, the casual examples drop particles where natives do, and all the listLinks ids exist. The main problems are three. Several polite examples use the stiff textbook -te shimatta form. Two claims are misleading: ase can also take ga deru, and a cold's source takes kara as well as no. Two keep-list items, kaze-ga-naoru and kibun-ga-warui, were dropped without explanation. Nothing needs cutting; the fixes are rewording, restoring those two items and a few trap and note corrections.

traps: The trap claims are mostly sound. Every listLink id exists, and every cited rank and phrase entry matched the freq tool. Romaji, transitive/intransitive pairs (utsuru ga / utsusu o) and the casual examples are natural. Four trap/use claims are wrong or over-strict, and one partner takes a different verb. Zutsuu is not doctor-only. Kaze o morau is a natural way to catch someone's cold and is missing. 'Not netsu o morau' clashes with it. Netsu deteru is fine for a fever you have now. Hakike takes suru, not aru. The byouin trap misses its real point (byouin = any clinic; isha ni iku also works). One cut: seki-ga-deru has the same frame as netsu-ga-deru, with a weak trap. The kaze alsoIn pointers lead to 'wind' and need homophone annotation. Coverage gaps worth filling: netsu o hakaru, hana ga tsumaru, hakike/samuke ga suru, taichou o kuzusu.

nuance: Strong draft: glosses, aspect notes (kaze hiiteru, onaka suita, netsu ga aru vs deru), romaji and polite pairs are accurate. All 15 listLinks ids exist, and every frequency rank I checked matches freq.py. The main fixes: the three kaze cross-references point to kaze 'wind'; the two 'getting hungry/thirsty' polite glosses contradict the aspect point; the zutsuu claim is wrong; kaze-o-hiku needs an 'infuru ni kakaru' note; and kimochi ga warui, named in guai-ga-warui's contrast group, is missing from the block. Cutting two same-pattern items (onaka-ga-itai, seki-ga-deru) brings every block to 4–5 items; a few trapRisk scores are inflated, and the blocks need small reorders so contrast items sit together.

form: The form is very clean. Every romaji, kana and politeJa matches, every masu form is conjugated correctly, and every example's romaji matches its ja word for word. I checked all 34 noun and verb ranks and 18 phrase-entry ranks with the tool and found no wrong numbers; all 15 listLinks ids exist, there are no duplicate slugs, and block sizes are 4/4/5/6. The real errors are cross-references: three kaze items point at the 'wind' cards (vocab-trainer weather-terms, and 10-list-nouns #88 on the two utsuru/utsusu items). Two keep-list items (kibun-ga-warui, kaze-ga-naoru) were silently dropped, while byouin-ni-iku is too transparent to keep. The rest is polish: rank-spelling conventions, kanji in verbSense fields, two romaji spacing fixes, and repeated example frames. Netsu o hakaru (take your temperature, a strong 'take' trap) is also absent from the domain and the keep list.

categories.name: Clothes & wearing
categories.scope: Putting on and taking off by body part — the whole wearing system: fuku/shatsu o kiru, zubon/sukaato/kutsu/kutsushita o haku, boushi o kaburu, megane o kakeru, tokei/nekutai/masuku/mafuraa o suru, nekutai o shimeru, tebukuro/yubiwa o hameru, akusesarii/iyaringu o tsukeru, keshou o suru, fuku o nugu, kutsu o nugu, boushi o toru, megane o hazusu, tokei o hazusu, kami o musubu.

blocks.label: Clothes and shoes
blocks.rationale: The clothes and shoes people talk about every day: putting them on, taking them off at the door, and whether they fit.
blocks.interference: fuku o kiru vs kutsu/zubon o haku: kiru is for anything worn on the torso or the whole body (shirt, coat, dress, kimono); haku is for anything you step into (shoes, socks, trousers, skirts). nugu takes all of them off. saizu ga au is the plain way to say something is the right size; when it doesn't fit, people more often just say kitsui (tight), yurui (loose), ookii or chiisai.

items.use: Mostly heard as kiteru (is wearing, a state, not 'putting on now') or kiteku (wear when going out); casual speech drops o. kiteru 'wearing' is flat (ki-TE-RU) while kiteru 'has come' falls after ki (KI-te-ru), so pitch as well as context tells them apart.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the body (tops, coats, dresses)
items.trap: kiru only covers tops and whole-body clothes (shirt, coat, dress, kimono). English 'wear' also covers shoes, trousers, hats and glasses, which take other verbs (haku, kaburu, kakeru).

example.ja: 明日どんな服着てく？
example.english: What are you wearing tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa donna fuku o kite ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日はどんな服を着ていきますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you wearing tomorrow?

items.freqNote: Rank is for 着る #754. Kana きる is mostly 切る 'cut' (#546), the same sound. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Single verbs: kigaeru = change clothes; niau = suit someone (niau ne).

items.use: Said as kutsu haite (put your shoes on) at the door; casual speech drops o. haiteru means already has them on, not 'putting them on now'.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the feet and legs
items.trap: Not kutsu o kiru: anything on the feet or legs takes haku.

example.romaji: chotto matte, ima kutsu haku kara.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、今靴履くから。
example.english: Hang on, I'm putting my shoes on.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima kutsu o hakimasu node, chotto matte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今靴を履きますので、ちょっと待ってください。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm just putting my shoes on, one moment please.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 履く #3474. Kana はく is mostly 吐く 'throw up' (#1739), so the kana count was not used. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Spelled like haku 'throw up' and haku 'sweep', but the pitch differs: haku 'put on' is flat (ha-KU), the other two fall after ha (HA-ku). Context helps too.

items.use: Heard as zubon haiteru (is wearing trousers) or haite mite (try them on). Same verb as shoes; casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put on or wear on the feet and legs
items.trap: Not zubon o kiru: trousers, skirts, socks and tights take haku, like shoes (anything you step into).

example.ja: このズボン、履いてみていい？
example.english: Can I try these trousers on?

examplePolite.romaji: kono zubon, haite mite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: このズボン、履いてみてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: May I try these trousers on?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for ズボン #6081 and 履く #3474. sukaato (#6710) and kutsushita (#5748) take the same verb.
items.notes: pantsu with a flat pitch is trousers (younger speakers prefer it; zubon can sound a little old to them), but PA-ntsu, falling, is underpants, so zubon is the safe word. sutokkingu = sheer stockings or pantyhose. In shops, 'try on' is shichaku: shichaku shite mo ii desu ka?

items.use: Heard as kutsu nuide (kudasai) at home entrances, some restaurants and clinics. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: take off (clothes, shoes)
items.trap: Not kutsu o toru: shoes and clothes come off with nugu, and toru sounds like picking them up.

example.ja: ここで靴脱いでね。
example.english: Take your shoes off here, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: koko de kutsu o nuide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここで靴を脱いでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please take your shoes off here.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 靴 #1818 and 脱ぐ #2074. Pairing commonness is judged; kutsu o nuide kudasai is heard at Japanese entrances every day.
items.notes: A hat comes off with boushi o toru or nugu; glasses and accessories with hazusu.

items.use: Mostly in the negative or as a question when trying things on: saizu awanai (doesn't fit), saizu atta? (did it fit?). Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: match, fit, agree
items.trap: English makes the clothes the subject ('it fits'); Japanese says the size matches: saizu ga au / awanai. Don't reach for niau, which means 'suits you, looks good on you'. When something doesn't fit, people often just say kitsui (tight), yurui (loose) or hairanai (can't get into it). This au means 'match' and sounds the same as au 'meet'.

example.ja: このズボン、サイズ合わない。
example.english: These trousers don't fit.

examplePolite.romaji: kono zubon, saizu ga awanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: このズボン、サイズが合わないんです。
examplePolite.english: These trousers don't fit.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 合う #563. Kana あう is mostly 会う 'meet' (#110). Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: niau = suit or look good on; pittari = fits perfectly; fitto suru = a snug, body-hugging fit. Too small is often just hairanai (kono zubon hairanai); kitsui / yurui = tight / loose. iro ga au = the colours go together (the 'match' sense, not size).

blocks.label: Hats and glasses
blocks.rationale: Things worn on the head and face, each with its own verb, plus hazusu for taking glasses off.
blocks.interference: boushi o kaburu vs megane o kakeru: pulled over the head vs hung on the ears. hazusu takes glasses off, but a hat comes off with toru or nugu.

items.use: Usually boushi kabutteru (has a hat on) or boushi kabutte (put your hat on). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: pull over or put on the head
items.trap: Not boushi o kiru: anything pulled over the head (hat, cap, helmet, hood) takes kaburu.

example.ja: 今日帽子かぶってるね。
example.english: Oh, you've got a hat on today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa boushi o kabuttemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は帽子をかぶってますね。
examplePolite.english: You're wearing a hat today.

items.freqNote: Rank is for kana かぶる #1926, the usual spelling; the kanji 被る is #7902. The kana count also includes the casual 'clash/overlap' sense (yotei ga kaburu), so it overstates the wearing sense.
items.notes: Off: boushi o toru or nugu. kaburu also means 'clash', as in yotei ga kaburu.

items.use: Most often megane kaketeru (wears glasses), which describes a person, not the act of putting them on. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something
items.trap: Not megane o kiru: glasses hang on the ears, so the verb is kakeru. Casual megane shiteru is also common.

example.ja: あの眼鏡かけてる人、誰？
example.english: Who's that person with the glasses?

examplePolite.romaji: ano megane o kaketeru hito wa dare desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの眼鏡をかけてる人は誰ですか？
examplePolite.english: Who is that person wearing glasses?

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 眼鏡 #4549 (the katakana spelling メガネ is listed separately at #6067) and the kanji 掛ける #2742, used because kana かける (#244) also counts the call, sit and spend senses.
items.notes: Contact lenses go in: kontakuto o ireru (or tsukeru).

items.use: Often megane hazushite (take your glasses off) or hazusu to (when I take them off). The same verb takes off masks, watches and rings.
items.verbSense: remove, unfasten, detach
items.trap: Not megane o nugu: nugu is for things you are dressed in (clothes, shoes, hats, gloves). Glasses, watches, masks, rings and earrings come off with hazusu. English 'take off' leading to toru is fine in casual speech (megane totte, masuku totte); hazusu is the neutral verb.

example.romaji: megane hazusu to nani mo mienai.
example.ja: 眼鏡外すと何も見えない。
example.english: I can't see a thing without my glasses.

examplePolite.romaji: megane o hazusu to, nani mo mienai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 眼鏡を外すと、何も見えないんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't see a thing without my glasses.

items.freqNote: Rank is for 外す #1043, which also counts 'miss' and 'step away (seki o hazusu)'. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: Contact lenses come out with kontakuto o hazusu or toru.

blocks.label: Small items and the whole look
blocks.rationale: Small worn items, which mostly take plain suru, gloves with hameru, and kakkou o suru for the whole outfit.
blocks.interference: masuku/tokei o suru vs tebukuro o hameru: small worn items just take suru; gloves and rings fit on with hameru (suru is also fine). kakkou o suru is the whole look and needs a describing word in front.

items.use: Usually masuku shiteru (is wearing a mask); casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
items.trap: Not masuku o kiru: small worn items (mask, watch, scarf, tie) just take suru, as in masuku shiteru. masuku o tsukeru is also fine and a little more formal; masuku o kakeru is heard from some speakers too.

example.ja: 風邪ひいたからマスクしてる。
example.english: I've got a cold, so I'm wearing a mask.

examplePolite.romaji: kaze o hiita node, masuku o shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 風邪をひいたので、マスクをしてます。
examplePolite.english: I've caught a cold, so I'm wearing a mask.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for マスク #5039 and する #15. マスク may be under-ranked if the drama corpus is mostly pre-2020 (not verified); the rank was not adjusted.
items.notes: Off: masuku o hazusu or toru. tsukeru is the catch-all for anything attached: nekkuresu / piasu / kousui o tsukeru (necklace, earrings, perfume). A tie is also nekutai o shimeru (tie it), a scarf mafuraa o maku (wrap it).

items.use: Usually tokei shiteru / shitenai (wearing / not wearing a watch); casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: do; with small worn items, have on
items.trap: Not tokei o kiru: a watch takes suru (tokei shiteru). tsukeru also works but sounds stiffer.

example.ja: 今日時計してないんだ。
example.english: I'm not wearing a watch today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa tokei o shitenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は時計をしてないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm not wearing a watch today.

items.freqNote: 時計 #3262 also counts clocks; 腕時計 'wristwatch' is #10342. Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: tokei o hameru is also heard; off: tokei o hazusu.

items.use: Heard as tebukuro hamete (put your gloves on) or, just as often, tebukuro shiteru. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: fit into or onto (a snug fit)
items.trap: Not tebukuro o kiru: gloves 'fit on' (hameru), like rings; tebukuro o suru is also everyday.

example.ja: 寒いから手袋はめてく。
example.english: It's cold, so I'll wear gloves when I go out.

examplePolite.romaji: samui node, tebukuro o hamete ikimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 寒いので、手袋をはめていきます。
examplePolite.english: It's cold, so I'll wear gloves when I go out.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for 手袋 #6640 and kana はめる #2952, the usual spelling (kanji 嵌める is #65768). はめる also counts the 'trap someone' sense.
items.notes: Off: tebukuro o toru, nugu or hazusu.

items.use: Always with a describing word: sonna kakkou shite (dressed like that), kawaii kakkou shiteru. Just as common with de: sonna kakkou de iku no? (you're going like that?). Casual speech drops o and often shortens the word to kakko (sonna kakko shite).
items.verbSense: do; with a look or appearance, have it
items.trap: English 'dressed like that' or 'dress up as' has no single verb: Japanese uses kakkou (look, outfit) + suru, as in sonna kakkou shite or santa no kakkou o suru (dress as Santa). Not kakkou o kiru: kakkou is the look, not the clothes; with a garment use kiru (sonna fuku kite).
partners: kami (hair: nagai kami shiteru = has long hair)
me (eyes: aoi me shiteru = has blue eyes)

example.ja: そんな格好して、寒くない？
example.english: Aren't you cold, dressed like that?

examplePolite.romaji: sonna kakkou o shite, samukunai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そんな格好をして、寒くないですか？
examplePolite.english: Aren't you cold, dressed like that?

items.freqNote: Rank is for 格好 #1247, which also counts other senses (kakkou tsukeru 'show off'); kakkoii 'cool' is listed separately (#1899). The casual spelling カッコ is ranked separately at #6594 (it also counts 'brackets'). Pairing commonness is judged.
items.notes: kakkoii 'cool' is a separate word built on kakkou. kakkou also means posture: hen na kakkou de neteta (slept in a funny position). kao o suru is a different sense: iya na kao o suru = make a face.

changelog.change: Interference rewritten: kiru covers torso and whole-body clothes, haku anything you step into; dropped the false 'only way to say they fit' (now names kitsui/yurui/ookii/chiisai). Items reordered so the two haku items sit together: fuku-o-kiru, kutsu-o-haku, zubon-o-haku, kutsu-o-nugu, saizu-ga-au.

Relabelled 'Small items and the whole look' (it holds a hameru item); rationale adjusted. The proposed 2x5 restructure was not applied, because it depended on cutting tokei-o-suru and moving kakkou-o-suru out of the domain, and only one reviewer wanted either. Blocks stay 5/3/4.

use: kiteru homophone claim replaced with pitch cue (flat ki-TE-RU vs falling KI-te-ru); trap: 'each a different verb' corrected to 'other verbs (haku, kaburu, kakeru)'; example and examplePolite now use donna fuku ('What are you wearing tomorrow?'); trapRisk 4 -> 2; listLinks add I-te-iku.

examplePolite replaced with 'sumimasen, ima kutsu o hakimasu node, chotto matte kudasai.' (particle kept for consistency with other polite examples); notes now give the pitch difference from haku 'throw up' / 'sweep'.

partners: sutokkingu (mis-glossed as tights) replaced by taitsu (tights); notes add pantsu pitch cue, zubon sounding a bit old to younger speakers, sutokkingu = stockings/pantyhose, and the shop phrase shichaku shite mo ii desu ka.

trap rewritten: no 'no simple verb' claim; size is the subject, warns off niau, names kitsui/yurui/hairanai; partners emptied (iro ga au is a different sense, moved to notes with gloss); listLinks add H-hairu; notes add fitto suru, hairanai, kitsui/yurui.
verbJa 被る -> かぶる to match ja and the ranked spelling.

verbJa 掛ける -> かける to match ja; examples replaced with 'ano megane kaketeru hito, dare?' (describing a person, no longer a copy of the hat example), written 眼鏡 to match the headword; freqNote clarified why the kanji rank is used; listLinks add H-ireru.

trap: nugu now covers clothes, shoes, hats and gloves (no longer contradicts other items) and says casual toru is fine; trapRisk 5 -> 3; notes replaced with the contact-lens 'off' verbs; example ja spelled 眼鏡 to match headword.

trap: tsukeru described as slightly more formal (not 'what signs say'), masuku o kakeru noted; freqNote pre-2020 claim marked unverified; partners: iyaringu moved to tokei-o-suru to avoid duplication; notes add tsukeru as catch-all and nekutai o shimeru / mafuraa o maku.
partners replaced with yubiwa, nekkuresu, iyaringu, beruto so they no longer duplicate masuku-o-suru.
verbJa 嵌める -> はめる; example and examplePolite English now 'It's cold, so I'll wear gloves when I go out.' to match hameteku / hamete ikimasu.

englishVerb -> 'be dressed (like) / dress as'; trap reframed around the missing English verb (santa no kakkou o suru), with sonna fuku kite as the garment alternative; trapRisk 5 -> 3; use adds sonna kakkou de and the kakko shortening; freqNote adds カッコ #6594; partners replaced with describing-pattern kami/me; notes add posture sense and that iya na kao o suru is a different sense.

reviewSummaries: natural: All 12 pairings are the verbs a Tokyo speaker actually uses. Every casual example is natural and drops particles the way natives do, and the ranks, listLinks ids and alsoIn pointers all check out. The two major problems are overclaims: the block note calls saizu ga au the only way to say something fits, and fuku-o-kiru says the two kiteru words sound the same when pitch tells them apart, which an audio-first learner needs to hear. The rest is polish: two verbJa fields use kanji almost nobody writes, a few English glosses and one stiff polite example need fixing, kakkou-o-suru needs fixing in three fields, and one possible missing item (airon o kakeru). No cuts.

traps: This domain is solid. Every rank, listLinks id and alsoIn pointer checks out against freq.py, the versatility files, 10-list-nouns and the vocab-trainer sets, and the core kiru / haku / kaburu / kakeru / suru / nugu / hazusu traps are accurate. Their partners take the same verb in the same sense. Four items need fixing:
- saizu-ga-au: the trap and the block note both make a false exclusivity claim ('no simple verb', 'the only way').
- megane-o-hazusu: the trap targets nugu, while the English-led word toru is actually fine.
- kakkou-o-suru: the 'wear' framing is mis-aimed.
- Three homophone notes ignore pitch differences that matter to an audio-first learner.
No items need cutting.

nuance: The pairings, polite forms, romaji, aspect notes (kiteru = wearing) and particle-drop notes are accurate. Every listLinks id exists, and every rank and alsoIn pointer checks out against freq.py and the source files. The main problems: (1) the block structure: a 3-item block, plus a 'suru' block holding a hameru item and the redundant tokei o suru. (2) Two inaccurate rules: 'the only way to say fit' and 'nugu only for clothes and shoes'. (3) Homophone claims (kiteru, haku) that ignore pitch, which matters for an audio-first learner. (4) Inflated trapRisk on kakkou-o-suru and fuku-o-kiru.

form: Mechanically clean. Romaji follows the convention and matches ja and kana in every headword and example (dropped particles included). Polite masu forms are right. All 23 nounRank/verbRank values I checked match freq.py. Every listLinks id exists, the alsoIn pointers are correct, slugs are unique and block sizes are 5/3/4. What needs fixing is content: the block 1 interference and the saizu-ga-au trap overclaim ('only way', 'no simple verb'), the hazusu trap contradicts the hat and glove notes about nugu, three verbJa fields don't match the kana spelling in ja, and there are a few polish items (tights vs sutokkingu, pitch cues for the homophones, a duplicated example frame). Possible gap for the content lens: nekutai o shimeru (tie a tie) is missing.

categories.name: Home & daily routine
categories.scope: Waking, washing, switches, doors, chores, sleeping: me ga sameru, mezamashi o kakeru, ha o migaku, kao o arau, shawaa o abiru, ofuro ni hairu, ofuro o wakasu, kami o kawakasu, denki o tsukeru / kesu, denki ga tsuku / kieru, terebi o tsukeru, eakon o tsukeru / kakeru, mado o akeru / doa ga aku, kagi o kakeru, sentaku o suru? (only if a trap), sentakumono o hosu, gomi o dasu, futon o shiku, heya o katazukeru, oyu o wakasu, mizu o dasu / mizu ga deru.

blocks.label: Bathroom
blocks.rationale: Washing and the toilet, where English 'take' and 'brush' point to the wrong verb and 'use' to the less polite one.
blocks.interference: shawaa o abiru and ofuro ni hairu both translate as 'take a ___': a shower is poured over you (o abiru), a bath is gone into (ni hairu). They share the base sentence saki ni ___ kuru ne.

items.use: Used for showering at any time of day. You mostly hear shawaa abite kuru (I'll go shower) or shawaa abita (I've showered), usually without o.
items.verbSense: pour over yourself, bathe in (water, sunlight)
items.trap: Not shawaa o toru: 'take' points to toru, but a shower is poured over you, so the verb is abiru.

example.romaji: saki ni shawaa abite kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にシャワー浴びてくるね。
example.english: I'll go shower first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni shawaa o abite kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にシャワーを浴びてきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and take a shower first.

items.freqNote: Both parts ranked. abiru is used mostly for showers, sunlight and criticism, so this phrase is where learners meet it.
items.notes: Casual shawaa suru is also heard.

items.use: The everyday way to talk about bathing at home, usually at night. You hear ofuro haitte kuru and ofuro haitta? (have you had your bath?) all the time, mostly without ni.
items.verbSense: go into, enter (a room, a bath, a club)
items.trap: Not ofuro o toru or ofuro o abiru: a bath is something you go into, so it's ni hairu.

example.romaji: saki ni ofuro haitte kuru ne.
example.ja: 先にお風呂入ってくるね。
example.english: I'll go have my bath first.

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni ofuro ni haitte kimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 先にお風呂に入ってきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll go and have my bath first.

items.freqNote: お風呂 #1921 (plain 風呂 #2586); 入る #115 counts every sense of hairu.
items.notes: Running the bath is ofuro o ireru or ofuro o wakasu; the water heater announces ofuro ga wakimashita.

items.use: Part of the morning and bedtime routine: ha migaita? (did you brush your teeth?), ha migaite neru (brush and go to bed). The noun form hamigaki suru is just as common.
items.verbSense: polish, scrub until it shines (teeth, shoes)
items.trap: Not ha o arau ('wash'): teeth are polished, migaku. hamigaki suru is just as common.

example.ja: まだ歯磨いてない。
example.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada ha o migaite imasen.
examplePolite.ja: まだ歯を磨いていません。
examplePolite.english: I haven't brushed my teeth yet.

items.freqNote: 歯磨き #16183 (hamigaki suru) is the competing noun form.
items.notes: 10-list-nouns leaves out bare ha (too many homophones) and names ha o migaku as the collocation card that carries it. hamigaki (brushing) and haburashi (toothbrush) are the related nouns.

items.use: Used to ask for the toilet at a friend's home, a shop or a cafe, almost always as a request: toire karite ii? At home, going to the toilet is just toire ni iku.
items.verbSense: borrow; use something that belongs to someone else
items.trap: 'Use' points to tsukau, which friends do say (toire tsukatte ii?), but the standard request is to 'borrow' it: toire karite ii?

example.ja: ごめん、トイレ借りていい？
example.english: Sorry, can I use your bathroom?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, toire o karite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、トイレを借りてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, may I use the restroom?

items.notes: Among friends, chotto toire kashite (lend me the toilet) is just as common. otearai is the politer word for toilet, and in shops people often just ask toire arimasu ka?

blocks.label: Lights
blocks.rationale: Switching lights and machines on and off: tsukeru and kesu are the act, tsuku is the light itself, usually heard as tsuiteru.
blocks.interference: o + tsukeru/kesu means someone does it; ga + tsuku is the light coming on by itself, and tsuiteru is how it is now. Compare denki tsukete (put the light on) with denki tsuiteru (the light's on).

items.use: Said whenever a room gets dark: denki tsukete (put the light on), denki tsukeyou ka. Here denki means the light itself, and the same tsukeru works for the TV and air conditioner.
items.verbSense: attach; light or switch on (a light, fire, TV)
items.trap: Not denki o ireru: ireru (turn on) goes with suitchi (switch) and dengen (power). The room light is called denki (literally 'electricity') and takes tsukeru, like terebi and eakon: denki tsukete.

example.ja: 暗いね、電気つけようか。
example.english: It's dark, shall I put the light on?

examplePolite.romaji: kurai desu ne, denki o tsukemashou ka.
examplePolite.ja: 暗いですね、電気をつけましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's dark, shall I turn the light on?

items.freqNote: つける #393 is the kana spelling across all senses (付ける #1452, 点ける #52228); 電気 also counts 'electricity'.
items.notes: suitchi o ireru / dengen o ireru is how you switch a machine on; eakon o ireru is also heard, but tsukeru is the everyday choice. denki tsukete ends like ki o tsukete (take care), the same verb in another sense.

items.use: The other half of denki o tsukeru, used for the TV, heater and air conditioner too. You hear it as denki keshite (turn the light off) and denki keshita? (did you turn it off?).
items.verbSense: put out, make disappear (light, fire, writing)
items.trap: Not denki o tomeru, which means cutting off the power supply (denki tomerareta = they cut off my electricity). Lights and TVs are put out with kesu; for the air conditioner or a fan, kesu, kiru (eakon kitte) and tomeru are all used.

example.ja: 部屋の電気消した？
example.english: Did you turn off the light in your room?

examplePolite.romaji: heya no denki o keshimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 部屋の電気を消しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you turn off the light in your room?

items.freqNote: 消す #964 also covers erase and delete.
items.notes: Intransitive pair: denki ga kieru (the light goes out; denki kieta! = the lights went out).

items.english: the light comes on (tsuiteru = is on)
items.use: Describes the light itself, almost always as denki tsuiteru (the light's on) or denki tsukanai (it won't come on). Use tsukeru only when someone switches it on.
items.verbSense: come on, catch light; also stick, be attached
items.trap: Not denki ga tsuketeru: with ga the verb is tsuku (denki tsuiteru). denki o tsuketeru means someone is keeping it on.

example.ja: 部屋の電気ついてるよ。
example.english: The light's on in your room.

examplePolite.romaji: heya no denki ga tsuite imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋の電気がついていますよ。
examplePolite.english: The light is on in your room.

items.freqNote: つく #355 is the kana spelling across senses (付く #1570, 点く #45903); 着く 'arrive' is ranked separately at #957.
items.notes: Sounds like tsuku 'arrive' (eki ni tsuku); the particle and context tell them apart.

blocks.label: Doors and locks
blocks.rationale: Open and locked around the house. Each verb has a ga form for what happens to the door, usually heard as -teru; locking also has the doing form with o.
blocks.interference: o + kakeru means someone does it; ga + aku/kakaru is what happens to the door, and with -teru how it is now. Compare kagi kaketa? (did you lock it?) with kagi kakatteru (it's locked), and doa aiteru (the door's open) with doa o akeru (open it).

items.use: Mostly heard as doa aiteru (the door's open) or doa aita (it opened). Train and lift announcements usually say doa ga hirakimasu instead, so expect both sounds. When a person opens it, use doa o akeru.
items.verbSense: come open, be open; also become free or empty
items.trap: Not doa ga akeru: when the door opens by itself or is open, use aku (doa aiteru). akeru needs someone doing it.

example.ja: 玄関のドア開いてるよ。
example.english: The front door's open.

examplePolite.romaji: genkan no doa ga aite imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 玄関のドアが開いていますよ。
examplePolite.english: The front door is open.

items.freqNote: 開く splits by reading: ひらく #624, あく #14086. Kana あく is #3508 (it may include other words), and 空く #1498 is the 'free/vacant' aku. The tokenizer probably files most 開く under ひらく, so あく is likely understated (unverified).
items.notes: Closing follows the same pattern: doa ga shimaru / doa o shimeru.

items.use: Said when leaving the house or going to bed: kagi kaketa? (did you lock it?), kagi kakete ne (lock up, okay?).
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
items.trap: English 'lock' has no single verb here: the object is kagi (the lock), not the door, and you put it on with kakeru. In casual speech kagi o shimeru (kagi shimeta?) is just as common. rokku suru is mostly for cars and phones.

example.ja: あれ、鍵かけたっけ？
example.english: Wait, did I lock the door?

examplePolite.romaji: are, kagi o kakemashita kke?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、鍵をかけましたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Hmm, did I lock the door?

items.freqNote: かける #244 is the kana spelling across all senses (掛ける #2742); カギ #9849 is a variant spelling of the noun.
items.notes: Unlocking is kagi o akeru.

items.english: (a door) locks, gets locked (kakatteru = is locked)
items.use: Nearly always kagi kakatteru (it's locked) or kagi kakattenai (it's not locked). It describes the state, while kagi o kakeru is the act.
items.verbSense: hang, be put on; also take (time) and cost (money)
items.trap: 'It's locked' is a verb state, kagi ga kakatteru (kagi shimatteru is just as common). Not kagi ga kaketeru: with ga the verb is kakaru. kagi ga kakete aru, 'someone has locked it', is also fine.

example.ja: 大丈夫、鍵かかってるよ。
example.english: It's fine, it's locked.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu, kagi ga kakatte imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫です、鍵がかかっていますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's fine, it's locked.

items.freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses, including 'take time' and 'cost' (掛かる #5316).
items.notes: The opposite state is kagi ga aiteru (it's unlocked).

blocks.label: Home life
blocks.rationale: Chores, pets and a messy room: home life that comes up in everyday small talk.
blocks.interference: gomi o dasu (put out for collection) vs gomi o suteru (throw away), which overlap for the chore.

items.use: Used for the household chore and for collection days: gomi dashite kite (go put the trash out). gomi sutete kuru is also said for the same trip; gomi o suteru alone is throwing something away.
items.verbSense: put out, take out, send out
items.trap: English 'take out' points to toru, but gomi o toru means picking off fluff or dirt. Putting trash out for collection is dasu.

example.ja: ちょっとゴミ出してくる。
example.english: I'm just going to take the trash out.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto gomi o dashite kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとゴミを出してきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll just take the trash out.

items.freqNote: ゴミ #2709 (ごみ #8915); ゴミ出し #17427 is the noun form.
items.notes: gomidashi is the chore's name.

items.use: Almost always in the -teru form: inu katteru (I have a dog), nanika katteru? (do you have any pets?). inu ga iru (there's a dog) also works for 'I have a dog'.
items.verbSense: keep, raise (an animal); sounds the same as kau 'buy'
items.trap: Not inu o motte iru: pets are kept with kau, the sound-alike of 'buy'. inu ga iru also works.

example.ja: うち、犬飼ってるんだ。
example.english: We've got a dog at home.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi wa inu o katte iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちは犬を飼っているんです。
examplePolite.english: We have a dog at home.

items.freqNote: The homophone 買う (buy) is #238.
items.notes: katteru also means 'have bought'. In standard Tokyo speech kau 'keep' is accented on ka (KAtteru) while kau 'buy' is flat; context does the rest.

items.english: the room gets messy (chirakatteru = is a mess)
items.use: Almost always chirakatteru (it's messy right now). The host's set line is chirakatteru kedo douzo (sorry about the mess, come in).
items.verbSense: be scattered about, become cluttered
items.trap: 'Messy' isn't an adjective here: a cluttered room is chirakatteru. kitanai (dirty) is also used loosely and sounds blunter, but chirakatteru is the word for clutter.

example.ja: 部屋散らかってるけど、どうぞ。
example.english: The place is a mess, but come on in.

examplePolite.romaji: heya ga chirakatte imasu kedo, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 部屋が散らかっていますけど、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: Excuse the mess, please come in.

items.freqNote: Transitive 散らかす (make a mess) is #9673.
items.notes: Transitive pair: heya o chirakasu (make a mess); tidying up is heya o katazukeru.

blocks.label: Sleep and waking
blocks.rationale: Bedtime and morning: dreaming, setting the alarm, waking up.
blocks.interference: me ga sameru (wake from sleep) gets mixed up with okiru from the versatility list. okiru can mean waking too, but me ga sameru never means getting up: you can me ga sameru at 4 and not okiru until 7.

items.use: Used for dreams in your sleep, usually in the past: hen na yume mita (I had a weird dream). A life ambition is yume ga aru instead.
items.verbSense: see, watch, look at
items.trap: Not yume o motsu or yume ga aru, which mean having an ambition: dreams in your sleep are 'seen', yume o miru.

example.ja: 昨日変な夢見た。
example.english: I had a weird dream last night.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou hen na yume o mimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日変な夢を見ました。
examplePolite.english: I had a strange dream last night.

items.freqNote: 夢 #351 covers both night dreams and ambitions; 夢見る #4121 is the one-word 'dream of' verb.
items.notes: Bedtime set phrase: oyasumi, ii yume mite ne (good night, sweet dreams).

items.use: Said the night before, often as mezamashi kaketoku (I'll set the alarm). For phone alarms, araamu o kakeru and araamu o setto suru are just as common.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set a device going
items.trap: English 'set' gives no hint of kakeru: alarms and timers take kakeru (araamu o setto suru is also fine).

example.ja: 明日早いから、目覚ましかけとく。
example.english: I'm up early tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa hayai node, mezamashi o kakete okimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日は早いので、目覚ましをかけておきます。
examplePolite.english: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'll set an alarm.

items.freqNote: 目覚まし #15035 is the everyday short form; アラーム #12854 competes (araamu o kakeru / setto suru). かける #244 counts every sense.
items.notes: Shutting it off is mezamashi o tomeru; the alarm going off is mezamashi ga naru (mezamashi naranakatta = my alarm didn't go off).

items.english: wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)
items.use: For the moment of waking, often unplanned: yonaka ni me ga sameta (I woke in the night). It also means feeling wide awake, e.g. after coffee. Getting out of bed is okiru.
items.verbSense: wake, come out of sleep or a daze
items.trap: English 'wake up' covers two things. okiru is waking or getting up (yonaka ni okichatta is fine), but me ga sameru is only the waking and never getting out of bed: yoji ni me ga sameta kedo, okita no wa shichiji.

example.ja: 夜中に目が覚めちゃった。
example.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

examplePolite.romaji: yonaka ni me ga samete shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 夜中に目が覚めてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I woke up in the middle of the night.

items.freqNote: 覚める #6527; 目覚める #3028 is the one-word narrative/written form.
items.notes: Not the sameru of gohan ga sameru (food gets cold). mezamashi (alarm) comes from the transitive me o samasu (wake up, wake someone).

changelog.change: Split into 'Lights' (denki-o-tsukeru, denki-o-kesu, denki-ga-tsuku) and 'Doors and locks' (doa-ga-aku, kagi-o-kakeru, kagi-ga-kakaru), each with its own rationale and an interference that says the plain ga form is the event and -teru is the state. doa o akeru was not added (no new items).
Relabelled 'Home life' so inu o kau fits; new rationale; interference set to the gomi o dasu vs gomi o suteru overlap.
Rationale now says 'use' leads to the less polite verb, not a wrong one.
Interference now says okiru can mean waking too; me ga sameru never means getting up.
partners: nikkou (mostly written) replaced with hizashi.
notes: added ofuro o ireru beside ofuro o wakasu for running the bath.
trap now names ha o arau as the wrong form; windows removed from partners and verbSense; notes say 10-list-nouns names this as the collocation card for bare ha (confirmed by grep).
trapRisk 4->3; partners now in-place borrowing (denwa, daidokoro, konsento); notes replaced with toire kashite, otearai and toire arimasu ka? (no longer repeats use); added H-iku.
