Replaced the mawasu trap with the real one (ireru goes with suitchi/dengen; the light is called denki); trapRisk 4->3; notes cover eakon o ireru and the ki o tsukete sound-alike; added H-ki-o-tsukeru.
trap rewritten: denki o tomeru means cutting off the power supply; kiru and tomeru also used for the air conditioner or a fan. notes add denki kieta!.
english now 'the light comes on (tsuiteru = is on)', englishVerb 'come on'; trap names the ga + tsuketeru error and says o tsuketeru means keeping it on.

english now 'the door opens (aiteru = is open)'; use says announcements say doa ga hirakimasu; freqNote adds kana あく #3508 (checked) and marks the tokenizer explanation as unverified; added mise to partners; contrastGroup aku-akeru set to null because it has only one member.

trap rewritten: kagi is the lock, kagi o shimeru is just as common, rokku suru is for cars and phones (no folk etymology); trapRisk 5->4; english 'lock (a door, bike, locker)'; unlocking line kept only in notes; partner chein -> cheen.

english now '(a door) locks, gets locked (kakatteru = is locked)', englishVerb 'be locked'; trap names kagi ga kaketeru as the error, adds kagi shimatteru and kagi ga kakete aru; speakNeed 4->3 to match denki-ga-tsuku; partner chein -> cheen.

trap no longer marks motte iku as wrong: says gomi o toru means picking off fluff; use adds gomi sutete kuru for the chore; trapRisk 4->3; partners now the collection sense (sodaigomi, kan); notes reduced to gomidashi so it doesn't repeat use.

verbSense and trap say kau 'keep' sounds like kau 'buy' instead of relying on kanji; added H-motsu; notes add the accent difference (飼う accented on ka, 買う flat; from standard Tokyo accent dictionaries, no local data to check against).
english now 'the room gets messy (chirakatteru = is a mess)', englishVerb 'be messy'; trap allows kitanai as a loose, blunter alternative.
english 'have a dream (while asleep)'; added H-aru; notes add oyasumi, ii yume mite ne.
trap no longer uses the oku strawman; trapRisk 5->3; soujiki and eakon removed from partners; notes add mezamashi ga naru.
Fixed fatal trap that implied okiru can't mean waking; english 'wake up (from sleep); feel wide awake (me ga sameta)'; notes say mezamashi comes from me o samasu.

reviewSummaries: natural: The pairings are all correct and in scope, and every example and polite example sounds like something a Tokyo speaker would actually say, with natural particle dropping. No example needs rewriting. All listLinks ids, alsoIn pointers and frequency ranks check out. The real problems are in the glosses and traps. Three ga-headwords are glossed with their -teru meaning, so their polite forms would be misused. The denki-o-tsukeru trap misses the real confusion with ireru. Common native alternatives are undersold or marked wrong: kagi o shimeru, gomi sutete kuru, toire kashite and heya kitanai. The doa-ga-aku entry also misses that announcements say hirakimasu. The domain could also use doa o akeru and soujiki o kakeru.

traps: The draft is solid and natural. All 16 items are in scope, and every nounRank/verbRank, listLinks id and alsoIn pointer checked out against freq.py, the versatility files and the noun/vocab lists. The examples follow the app's romaji conventions (n da, -te kuru, -toku, kke). The main weakness is overclaimed traps that mark natural Japanese as wrong: okiru for waking, kagi o shimeru / kagi shimatteru, kitanai for a messy room, gomi motte iku / sutete kuru. denki o mawasu is a strawman. The domain also misses the strongest home traps: laundry, vacuuming and futon.

nuance: The entries are well made. The examples are natural casual speech with true desu/masu pairs, the romaji follows the convention, and every rank, listLinks id and alsoIn pointer checks out against freq.py, the versatility files, 10-list-nouns and utility-vocab. The main weaknesses are structural and aspect-related: Lights and doors is a 6-item block with a broken aku/akeru pair (no doa o akeru); Around the house is an incoherent 3-item leftover; and three ga-items gloss their -teru state as if it were the dictionary form. Some traps are also strawmen (mawasu, oku). Suggested additions to fill the blocks: doa o akeru, denki ga kieru, sentakumono o hosu, soujiki o kakeru, and ibiki o kaku or futon o shiku. No cuts.

form: The data is mechanically clean. All 32 nounRank/verbRank values match freq.py exactly. All 16 listLinks ids exist in 20-list-versatile.json, every alsoIn pointer resolves (10-list-nouns #2/#7/#15/#34/#49/#50/#56/#57 and the matching utility-vocab set_ids), and the romaji, kana, polite/politeJa and example ja/romaji pairs match word for word. There are no duplicate slugs and every block has 3–6 items. Real problems: the partner romaji "chein" should be cheen. Three ga-verb glosses state the -teru state instead of the dictionary form (denki ga tsuku, heya ga chirakaru, kagi ga kakaru). The aku-akeru contrast group has only one member because doa o akeru is missing, so the Lights and doors block should split in two. Three notes fields repeat their use field.

categories.name: Food & drink
categories.scope: Cooking, drinks, taste, eating out, alcohol, smoking: gohan o taku (cook rice), ocha / koohii o ireru, oyu o wakasu (if not in home), koi / usui (strong/weak coffee, taste), aji ga koi / usui, aji ga suru, osake ni you (get drunk), osake ga tsuyoi (can hold drink), tabako o suu, chuumon o suru? (only if a trap), okawari o suru, ryouri o tsukuru, niku o yaku, mizu o tsugu?

blocks.label: Meals at home
blocks.rationale: Everyday mealtime lines: having soup, making tea, food going cold, skipping breakfast.
blocks.interference: None between them; each has an English pull to resist: nomu not taberu for soup, ireru not tsukuru for tea, sameru not samui for cooling food, nuku not tobasu for skipped meals.

items.use: Said of any thin soup, miso soup included, and of ramen broth: raamen no suupu zenbu nonjatta (I drank all the ramen broth). A spoon makes no difference; thick or chunky soups can take taberu.
items.verbSense: swallow without chewing; drink
items.trap: English 'eat soup' leads to suupu o taberu; Japanese drinks soup (nomu) even with a spoon. taberu is fine for thick or chunky soups.

example.romaji: kono suupu, oishii kara nonde mite.
example.ja: このスープ、おいしいから飲んでみて。
example.english: Try this soup, it's really good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono suupu, oishii node nonde mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: このスープ、おいしいので飲んでみてください。
examplePolite.english: Try this soup, it's really good.

items.freqNote: For miso soup: 味噌汁 #9117, みそ汁 #8272. 飲む #229 counts all drinking.
items.notes: kusuri o nomu (take medicine) uses the same nomu: swallowing without chewing.

items.use: Said when offering or asking for a cup: ocha ireru ne (I'll make tea), koohii irete (make me a coffee). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: put in; for tea or coffee, brew by pouring on hot water
items.trap: English 'make tea' leads to ocha o tsukuru; for a cup or pot of tea or coffee the verb is ireru. tsukuru is used for a big jug, as in mugicha o tsukuru.

example.ja: お茶入れるけど、飲む？
example.english: I'm making tea, want some?

examplePolite.romaji: ocha iremasu kedo, ikaga desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: お茶入れますけど、いかがですか？
examplePolite.english: I'm making tea. Would you like some?

items.freqNote: 入れる #222 counts every sense of ireru (put in, include, switch on); the tea-only spelling 淹れる (#19863) is rarer only because of how it is written.
items.notes: koohii o ireru works the same way. Serving tea to a guest is ocha o dasu; ireru is the brewing.

items.use: Said at meals to get people to the table (samechau yo, it'll go cold) or about a drink left too long (koohii sameta). Hosts say samenai uchi ni douzo, 'eat it while it's hot'.
items.verbSense: lose heat and cool down (food, drinks, bath water)
items.trap: Not samuku naru: samui is for weather and how you feel; hot food or drink cooling off is sameru. tsumetaku naru is fine for something gone fully cold.

example.ja: 早く食べよう、ご飯冷めちゃうよ。
example.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

examplePolite.romaji: hayaku tabemashou, gohan ga samechaimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 早く食べましょう、ご飯が冷めちゃいますよ。
examplePolite.english: Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold.

items.freqNote: 冷める #2747 also counts feelings cooling. The verb goes with any hot food or drink (koohii, ocha, ryouri), so gohan is only the headword noun.
items.notes: samasu (let it cool) is the transitive partner; me ga sameru (wake up) is a different sameru.

items.use: Said about mornings and diets: asagohan nuita (I skipped breakfast), with o dropped and asagohan often cut to asa. For a habit you hear both itsumo asa nuku and asa wa nuiteru.
items.verbSense: pull out, take out, leave out
items.trap: English 'skip' leads to tobasu, which is odd for meals; sukippu suru is heard, but the everyday verb for leaving out a meal is nuku. asagohan tabenakatta (didn't eat breakfast) is also fine. Skipping class is saboru.

example.ja: 今日朝ご飯抜いちゃった。
example.english: I skipped breakfast today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa asagohan o nuichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は朝ご飯を抜いちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I skipped breakfast today.

items.freqNote: 朝ご飯 #5780; the kana spelling 朝ごはん (#6629) and the rough 朝飯 (asameshi, mostly male, #9447) are counted separately.
items.notes: asa nuki (going without breakfast) is the common noun form. When ordering, X nuki de means 'without X': sabi nuki de (no wasabi), koori nuki de (no ice).

blocks.label: Taste
blocks.rationale: Describing flavour: the aji ga suru frame, and the koi/usui pair for how strong it is.
blocks.interference: koi and usui are opposites that stand in for English strong/weak for coffee, tea, flavour and mixed drinks (koime/usume), so learn them together. tsuyoi osake is a high-proof drink, and osake ga yowai is about the drinker. aji ga suru names a flavour; aji ga usui judges how strong it is.

items.use: Used to say what something tastes like: hen na aji suru (tastes weird), ichigo no aji ga suru (tastes of strawberry). Casual speech drops ga, and aji shinai means it tastes of nothing.
items.verbSense: do; with a taste, smell or sound, be sensed or give off
items.trap: English 'it has a weird taste' pulls toward hen na aji ga aru, which sounds off; a taste you notice 'does': hen na aji ga suru. hen na aji da is also fine. Tasting something on purpose is ajimi suru or aji o miru, not aji ga suru.

example.ja: なんか変な味する。
example.english: This tastes kind of weird.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka hen na aji ga shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: なんか変な味がしますね。
examplePolite.english: This tastes a bit strange.

items.freqNote: Ranks are for the parts only; suru's #15 covers every use of suru. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: nioi ga suru and oto ga suru use the same frame.

items.use: The everyday verdict on food that needs more salt or soy sauce: chotto aji usui ne. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: thin, faint, weak (paper, colour, taste)
items.trap: Not aji ga yowai: food short on salt is usui (thin), the same word as weak coffee. aji ga nai is fine for food with no taste at all.

example.ja: これ、ちょっと味薄いね。
example.english: This is a bit bland.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, chotto aji ga usui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、ちょっと味が薄いですね。
examplePolite.english: This is a bit bland.

items.freqNote: 薄い #2547 also counts thin (paper, walls) and pale (colour).
items.notes: aji ga koi is the opposite: strongly seasoned, often too salty. usuaji (light seasoning) is often praise (usuaji de oishii); aji ga usui on its own is usually a complaint.

items.use: Used when ordering, making or describing coffee and tea: koi no ga ii (I like it strong). About the drink in front of you it becomes koohii ga koi (this coffee is strong).
items.verbSense: dense, strong in concentration (taste, colour)
items.trap: tsuyoi koohii sounds off: coffee, tea, flavour and even mixed drinks are koi (dense) or usui (thin), as in haibooru koime de (a strong highball, please) or usume de (a weak one). tsuyoi is for how high-proof the drink is, as in tsuyoi osake.
partners: haibooru (highball: koime de, make it strong)

example.romaji: asa wa koi koohii ga ii na.
example.ja: 朝は濃いコーヒーがいいな。
example.english: I like a strong coffee in the morning.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa koi koohii ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 朝は濃いコーヒーがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: I like a strong coffee in the morning.

items.freqNote: The rank is for the kanji 濃い (#3669). The kana こい also matches 来い and 恋, so its rank can't be trusted.
items.notes: usui koohii (weak coffee) is the opposite.

blocks.label: Eating and drinking out
blocks.rationale: What comes up on a night out: whether the place is packed, smoking, and how much you can drink.
blocks.interference: None inside the block. osake ga yowai is about the drinker, not the drink: kono osake tsuyoi means the drink itself is high-proof.

items.use: Said when choosing where to eat or go. You mostly hear konderu (it's packed now) or kondeta (it was), often without ga; plain komu means 'gets crowded', as in yoru wa komu yo.
items.verbSense: fill up with people or traffic
items.trap: English 'crowded' is an adjective, but Japanese uses the verb komu, said as konderu; komu alone means 'gets crowded'. hito ga ooi and ippai (full) are also fine.

example.ja: この店、いつも混んでるね。
example.english: This place is always packed.

examplePolite.romaji: kono omise, itsumo kondemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: このお店、いつも混んでますね。
examplePolite.english: This place is always packed.

items.freqNote: 混む #5984. The spelling 込む (#10624) is counted separately and likely includes compound-verb tails (-komu), so it isn't added in. How often the pairing comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: Opposite: mise ga suiteru (not crowded). Keep it apart from mise ga aiteru (the shop is open), from mise ga aku.

items.use: Used to ask about smoking and to say whether you smoke: tabako suu? (do you smoke?), sutte mo ii? (mind if I smoke?). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: breathe in, suck in (air, smoke)
items.trap: Dictionaries give kitsuen suru for 'smoke', but that is the word on signs and forms (kitsuenjo, kin'en); in speech you inhale the tobacco: tabako (o) suu. kemuri names only the smoke itself.

example.ja: タバコ吸ってもいい？
example.english: Mind if I smoke?

examplePolite.romaji: tabako o sutte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: タバコを吸ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you mind if I smoke?

items.freqNote: タバコ #4158 is the most frequent spelling (たばこ #7069, 煙草 #28060). 吸う #1684 also counts breathing in. 喫煙 (kitsuen) is only #18056, which fits it being a sign-and-form word.
items.notes: Restaurants ask kitsuen seki ka kin'en seki (smoking or non-smoking seat?); kin'en on a sign means no smoking. tabako o nomu is dated (older speakers); don't use it.

items.use: Said about yourself to turn down drinks gently (osake yowai n desu) or about someone who gets drunk fast. Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
items.trap: English has no set phrase here, so learners fall back on amari nomenai (fine, but blunt). Japanese says the drinker is weak: osake ga yowai (or osake ni yowai). Careful: kono osake tsuyoi is about the drink (high proof), not the drinker.
partners: asa (mornings: asa ga yowai, not a morning person)
i (stomach: i ga yowai, a delicate stomach)

example.romaji: osake yowai kara, ippai dake ni shitoku.
example.ja: お酒弱いから、一杯だけにしとく。
example.english: I'm a lightweight, so I'll just have one.

examplePolite.romaji: osake yowai n de, ippai dake ni shitokimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お酒弱いんで、一杯だけにしときます。
examplePolite.english: I'm not much of a drinker, so I'll just have the one.

items.freqNote: お酒 #1229; bare 酒 is counted separately (#1131). 弱い #970 counts every sense of weak. How often the phrase itself comes up is my judgement.
items.notes: osake ni yowai is equally fine; osake ga tsuyoi is the opposite. With conditions only ni works: samusa ni yowai (can't take the cold), atsusa ni yowai (can't take the heat), norimono ni yowai (get travel-sick); samusa ga yowai would mean the cold is mild.

changelog.change: Reordered blocks simple to complex: Meals at home, Taste, Eating and drinking out (nuance). In Meals at home, moved suupu-o-nomu first and rewrote the rationale and interference to match. Rewrote the Taste interference so that koi/usui covers mixed drinks (koime/usume) and tsuyoi osake (the drink's proof) is kept apart from osake ga yowai (the drinker). Wrote an interference line for the drinking block.

No items added, per the no-add rule. The keep list has gohan-o-taku and osake-ni-you for this domain, but the draft lacked both and added tabako-o-suu instead. Reviewers also flagged aji-ga-koi, oyu-o-wakasu, pan-o-yaku and shouyu-o-kakeru/tsukeru as gaps. Raise these in a gap pass.

Gloss is now the dictionary-form meaning ('gets crowded; konderu = is packed'). Fixed 'konde ta' to kondeta. freqNote no longer claims 込む adds to the count. Added the D-ooi link. Notes now point to mise ga aku. Kept densha/michi as partners because no densha-ga-komu is on the keep list.

Trap now names the real pull (kitsuen suru, a sign/form word) and backs it with 喫煙 #18056 in freqNote. trapRisk 4->3. Notes add kitsuen/kin'en seki and mark tabako o nomu as dated. Added the H-nomu link.

Fatal fix: replaced the samusa/atsusa partners, which reverse meaning with ga, with asa/i/karada ga yowai. The ni-only conditions (samusa/atsusa/norimono ni yowai) moved to notes. Trap rewritten around amari nomenai and the drink-vs-drinker split. trapRisk 4->3. Polite example is now the natural 'osake yowai n de, ... shitokimasu'. freqNote adds bare 酒 #1131.

Changed 淹れる to 入れる in ja/politeJa/verbJa/examples to match verbRank #222, and rewrote freqNote. Polite example now offers with ikaga desu ka. Notes replace the misspelt 'suicchi' line with the ocha o dasu contrast, and H-dasu is linked. Added 10-list-nouns #153 (koucha) to alsoIn.
Example translations now render samechau as a warning ('Come on, let's eat, the food'll get cold').

Trap now treats tobasu as the odd choice, says sukippu suru is heard, and accepts tabenakatta. trapRisk 5->4. The habit line in use now gives both nuku and nuiteru. Fixed the spelling labels in freqNote. Notes add X nuki de for ordering. Added 10-list-nouns #96 (asa) to alsoIn.
Use now gives the ramen-broth example instead of 'misoshiru nonda?'. Partners are now misoshiru and koon suupu; kusuri stays in notes because kusuri-o-nomu is its own entry.
Trap now names the real error (hen na aji ga aru) and separates tasting on purpose (ajimi suru, aji o miru). Added the D-hen link.
Gloss now 'lightly seasoned; bland (needs more salt)'. Notes add usuaji as praise versus aji ga usui as a complaint. Added haibooru (a weak mix) to partners.
Trap no longer says 'tsuyoi is for alcohol'. Mixed drinks are koime/usume, and tsuyoi osake is a drink's proof. In partners, haibooru (koime de) replaces keshou. Polite example gets ne.

reviewSummaries: natural: The draft is strong. All ten pairings are the verb or adjective a Tokyo speaker actually uses. The casual examples drop particles naturally, and the ranks, listLinks and alsoIn pointers all check out against freq.py and the source files. Two content errors need fixing: osake-ga-yowai's partners teach samusa ga yowai where it should be samusa ni yowai, and the koi/tsuyoi guidance misses that mixed drinks take koime/usui. The rest is polish on a few stiff polite examples, plus a coverage gap: gohan o taku and oyu o wakasu are missing.

traps: I checked every rank against freq.py, and every listLinks id and alsoIn pointer against the source files. All of them are correct, and the romaji and examples sound natural. One partner error is fatal: samusa/atsusa take ni, not ga. Four traps name the wrong form a learner would actually produce: osake o motenai, ajiwau and kemuri should be nomenai, aji ga aru and kitsuen suru, and 'tsuyoi is for alcohol' misses koime/usume for mixed drinks.
The domain is also thin at 10 items. It is missing the strongest kitchen traps: gohan o taku, oyu o wakasu/waku, pan o yaku, shouyu o kakeru/tsukeru and osake ni you.

nuance: Overall the food draft is solid. The glosses are mostly accurate, the examples are natural and spelled to convention, every listLinks id exists, and the ranks I checked are correct apart from one wrong spelling label in asagohan-o-nuku's freqNote. Four errors are significant: the samusa/atsusa partners take ni, not ga; the 'tsuyoi is for alcohol' rule wrongly excludes koi/usui for mixed drinks; the mise-ga-komu gloss has the wrong aspect; and gohan-o-taku, on the keep list, is missing. Structurally, two of the three blocks have only 3 items and the domain runs complex to simple. Re-chunking into Meals at home / Taste / Going out & drinking (4–5 each), restoring gohan-o-taku and osake-ni-you, and promoting aji-ga-koi fixes both problems. No item needs cutting.

form: The form is clean overall. All 27 noun and verb ranks I checked match the frequency tool. Every listLinks id exists, and the alsoIn pointers are correct (10-list-nouns #18/70/71/73/121/147; vocab-trainer sets shops/beverages/meals/taste-nouns). Slugs are unique, blocks have 3-4 items, the masu forms are right, and the example romaji matches the ja word for word, including dropped particles. Real defects: osake-ga-yowai lists samusa/atsusa as partners in a ga frame that reverses their meaning, and two romaji convention slips are in prose fields that merge.py won't fix (konde ta, suicchi). The rest is polish: the 淹れる rank mismatch, missing links, and one overstated trap. Outside this lens: the domain has only 10 items, and two are about crowds and smoking rather than food, so high-trap food pairings (gohan o taku, oyu o wakasu, shouyu o kakeru/tsukeru, niku o yaku) are worth a gap check.

categories.name: Phone, photos & screens
categories.scope: Phone, messages, photos, music, TV, battery, internet: denwa o kakeru, denwa ni deru, denwa o kiru, denwa ga naru, meeru o okuru, meeru ga kuru, shashin o toru, douga o toru, ongaku o kiku / ongaku o kakeru, terebi o miru?, juuden ga kireru (battery dies), juuden suru, denpa ga warui (bad signal), netto ni tsunagu / tsunagaru, akaunto o tsukuru?, oto o dasu / oto o sageru (volume).

blocks.label: Photos, music, messages
blocks.rationale: The everyday things you do with a phone besides calling: photos, idle scrolling, messages coming in and going out, and music on a speaker.
blocks.interference: meeru ga kuru (an email arrives, ga) vs meeru o kaesu (you reply, o): the same in/out split as denwa ga kakaru / denwa o kakeru in the next block. kaesu 'send back' sounds like kaeru 'go home', so learn it with its object. ongaku o kakeru shares kakeru with denwa o kakeru in the next block.

items.use: Said whenever photos come up, mostly as requests: shashin totte (take a photo of me or us), and shashin totte moraemasu ka? to a stranger. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: take (a photo or video)

example.ja: 一緒に写真撮ろうよ。
example.english: Let's take a picture together.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni shashin o torimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に写真を撮りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take a picture together.

items.freqNote: verbRank is the 撮る spelling (photo/film sense); 取る 'take' is #228. Phrase entry 写真を撮る is #4201 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: The one English 'take' that is toru. Take medicine is kusuri o nomu, a shower shawaa o abiru, a train densha ni noru, time jikan ga kakaru. toreru = come out in the photo: yoku toreta (it came out well).

items.use: Said about idly using a phone, usually in the -teru form: zutto sumaho ijitteru (always on their phone). About someone else it often carries a mild complaint; about yourself it admits a habit. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: fiddle with, tinker with
items.trap: Not tsukau or sumaho o asobu: idly being on your phone is sumaho (o) ijiru, and zutto sumaho miteru is just as common. tsukau is understood but sounds like using it for a task; sumaho de asobu is fine but means playing games on it.

example.ja: またスマホいじってる。
example.english: You're on your phone again.

examplePolite.romaji: neru mae ni, tsui sumaho o ijitchaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 寝る前に、ついスマホをいじっちゃいます。
examplePolite.english: I always end up on my phone before bed.

items.freqNote: nounRank is スマホ; keitai (#1458) is the older word and still common. verbRank is kana いじる; 弄る barely appears.
items.notes: With a person as the object, ijiru means tease (slangy): ijiranaide yo (stop teasing me).

items.use: Said when an email arrives, mostly as meeru kita (I got an email), with the sender marked by kara. The negative henji ga konai means there's no reply yet.
items.verbSense: come, arrive
items.trap: Not uketoru: English makes you the subject of 'got', but Japanese makes the email the subject: meeru (ga) kita ('an email came'). meeru moratta is also fine, but kita is what you hear most; uketoru sounds stiff and is for parcels and documents.

example.ja: なんか変なメール来た。
example.english: I got a weird email.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka hen na meeru ga kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: なんか変なメールが来ました。
examplePolite.english: I got a weird email.

items.notes: meeru now means email; a text from a friend is a rain (LINE): rain kita. henji and renraku work the same way: henji kita.

items.use: Said about answering emails or texts, often about being slow: kaesu no wasureteta (I forgot to reply). For chat messages the noun is rain (LINE): rain kaeshite. With henji the usual verb is suru: henji shite.
items.verbSense: give back, return something
items.trap: Not meeru ni kotaeru: replying to an email or text is kaesu ('send back'); kotaeru answers questions. henshin suru and henji suru are also fine.

example.ja: ごめん、メール返すの忘れてた。
example.english: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your email.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, meeru o kaesu no wasuretemashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、メールを返すの忘れてました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I forgot to reply to your email.

items.freqNote: nounRank is メール and verbRank is 返す, which also counts returning things; 返事 (henji) is #1075 and 返信 (henshin) #5122.
items.notes: To call someone back, the verb is orikaesu: ato de orikaeshimasu.

items.use: Said when you start music on a speaker or in the car: ongaku kakete ii? (mind if I put music on?). Music that's already playing is ongaku ga kakatteru. Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set something going (a record, a call)
items.trap: Not asobu: playing music on a speaker is ongaku o kakeru (nagasu is also fine); asobu is play for fun, hiku is play an instrument.

example.ja: なんか音楽かけていい？
example.english: Mind if I put some music on?

examplePolite.romaji: nanika ongaku o kakete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 何か音楽をかけてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Mind if I put some music on?

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かける pooling all senses; 掛ける alone is #2742. nagasu (流す) is #1234.
alsoIn: vocab-trainer utility-vocab: school-subjects (ongaku, as a subject)
items.notes: nagasu (let flow) is the alternative in shops and at events: biijiiemu o nagasu.

blocks.label: Phone calls
blocks.rationale: One phone call on the noun denwa: calling out, a call coming in, picking up, hanging up.
blocks.interference: denwa o kakeru (you call) vs denwa ga kakaru (a call comes in): o vs ga, plus kara for the caller, show the direction; with the caller as subject, add -te kuru: okaasan ga denwa kakete kita. kiru ends the call and is not a form of kakeru.

items.use: Said when you phone someone, with the person marked by ni. For a plain 'I'll call you', denwa suru is the everyday default (ato de denwa suru ne); kakeru is what you hear for dialing and trying: kakete miru, nankai kakete mo denai (they don't pick up however many times I call). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; set something going (a call, a record)
items.trap: Not yobu or iu: phoning someone is denwa o kakeru (or simply denwa suru); yobu is summon, iu is call something a name.

example.romaji: chotto okaasan ni denwa kakete miru.
example.ja: ちょっとお母さんに電話かけてみる。
example.english: Let me try calling my mom.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto haha ni denwa o kakete mimasu.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと母に電話をかけてみます。
examplePolite.english: Let me try calling my mother.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かける, which pools every sense (call, sit, spend, put on); 掛ける alone is #2742. Phrase entry 電話をかける is #7088 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: kakenaosu = call again (after a dropped or missed call). The number takes ni: kono bangou ni kakete.

items.use: Said of an incoming call, almost always as denwa kakatte kita (I got a call), with the caller marked by kara. The -te kuru shows the call coming toward you.
items.verbSense: hang, be put onto; get going (the intransitive of kakeru)
items.trap: Not okaasan kara denwa kaketa: kaketa says you made the call. An incoming call makes either the call the subject (okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita) or the caller the subject with -te kuru (okaasan ga denwa kakete kita). denwa kita and denwa moratta are also natural.

example.romaji: sakki okaasan kara denwa kakatte kita.
example.ja: さっきお母さんから電話かかってきた。
example.english: My mom called a little while ago.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki haha kara denwa ga kakatte kimashita.
examplePolite.ja: さっき母から電話がかかってきました。
examplePolite.english: My mother called a little while ago.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana かかる (掛かる alone is #5316). Phrase entries 電話がかかる #10203 and 電話がかかってくる #32857.
items.notes: denwa kita is the short everyday version; passing on a call politely is tanaka-san kara denwa ga arimashita. This -te kuru means 'toward me', not the 'go and do' sense of I-te-kuru. The partners take kakaru in its 'running' sense.

items.use: Said about picking up, mostly in the negative: denwa denai (they're not picking up). Casual speech drops ni, and denwa dete means 'can you get the phone?'
items.verbSense: come out, go out; appear
items.trap: Not denwa ni kotaeru: picking up is denwa ni deru ('come out to the phone'); kotaeru answers a question. denwa o toru (lift the receiver) is also natural, especially for office phones: denwa totte!

example.romaji: zenzen denwa denai n da kedo.
example.ja: 全然電話出ないんだけど。
example.english: They're not picking up at all.

examplePolite.romaji: zenzen denwa ni denai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 全然電話に出ないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: They're not picking up at all.

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電話に出る is #3584 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).

items.use: Said at the end of a call (jaa, kiru ne = OK, I'll hang up) and for being hung up on (kirareta). Casual speech drops o.
items.verbSense: cut; cut off
items.trap: Not kakeru ('hang'): denwa o kakeru makes the call; ending it is kiru ('cut').

example.ja: ごめん、間違えて電話切っちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, I hung up by mistake.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, machigaete denwa o kitchaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、間違えて電話を切っちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I hung up by mistake.

items.freqNote: Phrase entry 電話を切る is #16284 (the tokenizer merges only some uses).
items.notes: Not kiru 'wear' (fuku o kiru): a different verb with different pitch and conjugation. Hung up = kitta, kirimasu; wore = kita, kimasu. Intransitive: denwa ga kireta = the call cut off.

blocks.label: Battery and signal
blocks.rationale: The three ways a phone stops working, almost always said in the negative or the past as a complaint or excuse.
blocks.interference: denpa ga hairu (signal) vs netto ga tsunagaru (connection): both are said of Wi-Fi, so tie hairu to denpa and tsunagaru to netto. kireru is the intransitive of kiru: denwa o kiru = hang up (you do it), denwa ga kireta = the call cut off (it happened), and juuden ga kireta uses the same verb.

items.use: Said when a phone dies, in the past: juuden kireta / kirechatta (my phone died). About to die is juuden kiresou (or juuden yabai, slangy); low but not dead is juuden ga nai.
items.verbSense: be cut; run out (of a supply, charge or time)
items.trap: Not shinu: a dead phone is juuden kireta ('the charge ran out'). denchi kireta, juuden nakunatta and batterii kireta are also fine; sumaho shinda is slang.

example.ja: ごめん、充電切れちゃった。
example.english: Sorry, my phone died.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, juuden ga kirechaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、充電が切れちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, my phone died.

items.freqNote: juuden ranks low overall (#7708); judgement: most spoken uses are this phrase, juuden suru and juuden ga nai (the list has no phrase counts). batterii is #9633.
items.notes: Charging is the plain verb juuden suru. The same kireru is a dropped call: denwa kireta (the call cut off).

items.use: Said almost always in the negative: koko denpa hairanai (no signal here). The milder complaint is denpa ga warui (bad signal).
items.verbSense: enter, go in; come in (a signal or broadcast)
items.trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa (shingou is a traffic light), and having it is denpa ga hairu, so 'no signal' is denpa hairanai. denpa nai is also fine.

example.ja: ここ、電波入らないね。
example.english: There's no signal here, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: koko, denpa ga hairimasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: ここ、電波が入りませんね。
examplePolite.english: There's no signal here, is there.

items.freqNote: verbRank 入る pools every sense (enter, join, fit). 圏外 (kengai) is #16111.
items.notes: kengai ('out of range') is the one-word version: koko kengai da.

items.politeJa: ネットがつながります
items.use: Said mostly in the negative when Wi-Fi fails: netto tsunagaranai (the internet isn't working). The same verb covers a call going through: denwa tsunagaranai.
items.verbSense: be connected, be linked
items.trap: Not hataraku or ugoku: 'the Wi-Fi isn't working' is netto ga tsunagaranai ('doesn't connect'); ugokanai is for a frozen app or device.

example.romaji: nanka netto tsunagaranai n da kedo.
example.ja: なんかネットつながらないんだけど。
example.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

examplePolite.romaji: nanka netto ga tsunagaranai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: なんかネットがつながらないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: The internet's not working for some reason.

items.freqNote: verbRank is kana つながる (繋がる #6342) and also counts people or things being linked.
items.notes: Transitive half: netto ni tsunagu (connect to the internet). Slow internet is netto ga omoi ('heavy'): kyou netto omoi ne. Asking about Wi-Fi: koko waifai tonderu? (tobu 'fly', casual).

changelog.change: verbSense simplified to 'take (a photo or video)' (spelling detail stays in freqNote); notes now say why the item is here, as the anchor of the take-verbs (toru vs nomu/abiru/noru/kakaru), and keep toreta.

trap rewritten to lead with tsukau and rule out only 'sumaho o asobu' (sumaho de asobu = playing games, and sumaho miteru is just as common); examplePolite replaced with a self-habit sentence (neru mae ni, tsui sumaho o ijitchaimasu); use notes self vs others; notes add ijiru = tease with a person as the object.
english narrowed to 'get an email'; use says email; trap now targets uketoru and the subject flip (the email is the subject); notes say meeru = email and a friend's text is rain.
examplePolite drops the second o (kaesu no wasuretemashita); use now says rain for chats and henji takes suru; henji removed from partners and messeeji added; trap wording covers emails and texts.
notes 'BGM' respelt biijiiemu; alsoIn pointer marked as the school-subject sense.

use rewritten: denwa suru is the default for 'I'll call you', kakeru is for dialing and trying; example/examplePolite now 'chotto okaasan ni denwa kakete miru' / 'haha ni denwa o kakete mimasu'; bangou moved from partners to notes (it takes ni); trapRisk 5 -> 4.

trap rewritten: only 'okaasan kara denwa kaketa' is wrong (it says you made the call), and both 'kakatte kita' and 'okaasan ga denwa kakete kita' are taught; englishVerb 'get' -> 'call'; partners labelled with the 'running' sense; notes add 'denwa ga arimashita' for passing on a call politely and that this -te kuru is the 'toward me' sense, not I-te-kuru's; speakNeed 4 -> 3.
trap adds denwa o toru (denwa totte!) as natural, especially for office phones.

example/examplePolite replaced with hanging up by mistake (kitchatta / kitchaimashita), since nobody says 'denwa o kirimasu' politely to end a call; notes now give the conjugation cue (kitta/kirimasu vs kita/kimasu) and denwa ga kireta = call cut off.

use adds juuden kiresou (about to die); trap adds denchi kireta; denchi partner glossed as including a phone's battery; freqNote now marked as judgement; notes add denwa kireta (dropped call) with the same verb.
trap now targets shingou (= traffic light), not the straw-man morau/eru; channeru partner removed (TV uses utsuranai); listLinks add D-warui for denpa ga warui.
example/examplePolite changed to a different frame from denpa-ga-hairu (nanka netto tsunagaranai n da kedo); notes add netto ga omoi (slow) and waifai tonderu?
interference ties the meeru ga kuru / o kaesu direction to denwa ga kakaru / o kakeru.
items reordered kakeru, kakaru, deru, kiru to match the rationale; rationale reworded; interference adds the caller-as-subject + -te kuru pattern.
items reordered juuden, denpa, netto so the hairu/tsunagaru contrast pair sits together; interference now says kireru is kiru's intransitive (denwa ga kireta) instead of claiming they are unrelated.

reviewSummaries: natural: The pairings are the ones a Tokyo native uses, and the most common choice in each case. Ranks, listLinks ids and alsoIn pointers all check out, and most examples are natural with natural particle drops. Two problems matter. The sumaho and denwa-o-kiru polite examples are sentences nobody says in desu/masu. The denwa-ga-kakaru trap wrongly rules out 'okaasan ga denwa kakete kita'. The rest is nuance: suru vs kakeru for 'I'll call you', toru for picking up, asobu, meeru = email, kitta vs kita.

traps: The draft is solid. All the ranks match freq.py, every listLinks id exists, the alsoIn pointers check out, the particle and transitivity labels are right, and the examples are natural. Most traps are true and already name the acceptable alternatives. The one misleading trap is sumaho-o-ijiru's "Not asobu", which wrongly rules out *sumaho de asobu*. The rest are minor partner and sense fixes plus block reordering. The biggest gap is coverage: the "screens" part of the domain has no items, and *terebi ga tsuku / o tsukeru*, *gamen ga wareru*, *apuri o ireru* and *denwa ga naru* are missing.

nuance: The 12 entries are accurate and natural. The polite pairs are true desu/masu counterparts, examples are in real spoken form, particle drop is noted, and every rank, listLinks id and alsoIn pointer checked out (freq.py and grep). There is one wrong teaching claim (kireru is presented as unrelated to kiru when it is kiru's intransitive), two trap fields aim at the wrong error (denpa: shingou; denwa ga kakaru: kakete kita is fine), and a few traps are straw men. The chunking is loose: a grab-bag first block, the calls block out of sequence, and a 3-item last block. The domain also misses denwa ga naru, posting/entering (ageru/ireru) and anything on screens. Nothing needs cutting.

form: Mechanically the draft is clean. Romaji follows the convention throughout, including spacing for chatta, teru and -te kita. Example romaji matches the ja word for word, with dropped particles matching too, and every masu form is conjugated correctly. All 24 rank figures in nounRank, verbRank and freqNote match the frequency tool, every listLinks id exists in versatility-items.txt, and every alsoIn pointer resolves. The 12 slugs are unique and not in 21-list-collocations.json, and the blocks hold 5, 4 and 3 items. All the issues found are minor: the Phone calls items are out of the order the rationale gives, one note writes 'BGM' instead of romaji, one partners entry has a different shape, one freqNote states a judgement as fact, and a few trap or link entries could be sharper.

categories.name: Getting around
categories.scope: Trains, buses, cars, walking, directions: densha ni noru, densha o oriru, basu ni noru, takushii o hirou / yobu, kuruma o unten suru, jitensha ni noru, michi o wataru, michi ni mayou, kado o magaru, eki ni tsuku, densha ni maniau, densha ga okureru, michi ga komu (traffic is heavy), kuruma o tomeru, shingou o mamoru?, jiko ni au, nimotsu o azukeru, michi o kiku / oshieru.

blocks.label: Taking the train
blocks.rationale: Every train ride: getting on and off, finding a seat, and the timing, whether the train is late and whether you make it.
blocks.interference: densha ni noru and densha o oriru switch the particle (ni to get on, o to get off). seki ga aiteru is about a seat, while an empty train is densha ga suiteru. densha ga okureru is the train running late. Swap ga for ni (densha ni okureru) and it becomes you being late for it, which is easy to mishear, so say maniawanai before it leaves and nogashita after.

items.use: The riding and boarding itself: densha notteru (I'm on the train now), densha nottara (once I'm on). To say how you get somewhere, natives use de: densha de iku (I'll go by train), densha de kayotteru (I commute by train). Casual speech often drops ni.
items.verbSense: ride; get onto (a vehicle, a bike, a ride)
items.trap: Not densha o toru or densha o noru: you ride on a vehicle with ni noru, and 'take' is never toru here.

example.ja: 電車乗ったら、連絡するね。
example.english: I'll text you once I'm on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ni nottara, renraku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 電車に乗ったら、連絡しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll let you know once I'm on the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted, so noun and verb are ranked separately. The same frame covers basu (#2466), takushii (#1987), hikouki (#3222) and jitensha (#2927) ni noru.
items.notes: norikaeru (change trains) is a single verb. The transitive noseru is in kuruma ni noseru.

items.use: Once the train is clear, people usually name only the stop, with de: tsugi de oriru (I'm getting off at the next one). The vehicle takes o, or kara. On a packed train, sumimasen, orimasu! (excuse me, getting off) clears the way.
items.verbSense: come down; get off (a vehicle, stairs)
items.trap: Not densha ni oriru or densha kara deru: getting off is oriru, with the vehicle marked by o (kara also works). Only a car also allows kuruma kara deru, 'climb out'.

example.ja: 電車降りたら、連絡するね。
example.english: I'll text you when I get off the train.

examplePolite.romaji: densha o oritara, renraku shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 電車を降りたら、連絡しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll let you know when I get off the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. In speech the noun usually drops: tsugi de oriru.
items.notes: The same verb goes down stairs: kaidan o oriru.

items.english: a seat frees up (aiteru = a seat is free)
items.use: Almost always heard as aiteru: koko aitemasu ka? (is this seat free?) or seki aiteru (there's a free seat). aita is the moment one frees up: a, seki aita.
items.verbSense: become empty or vacant; open up (a space, a slot)
items.trap: Not kono seki tada? (that asks if it costs nothing) or seki ga hima: hima is a person or a quiet shop with nothing going on, and a free seat is aiteru ('has come open'). For your own schedule both work: ashita aiteru? / ashita hima?

example.ja: あ、あそこ席空いてるよ。
example.english: Oh, there's a free seat over there.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, kono seki aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみません、この席空いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, is this seat free?

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 空く (aku) is ranked separately from 開く (#14086, a door opening).
items.notes: A whole train being empty or packed is densha ga suiteru / konderu, not aiteru.

items.use: Heard as okureteru (it's running late) or okurete (because it was late), as in gomen, densha okurete... Casual speech drops ga, so densha okureta means the train was late. With ni instead of ga (densha ni okureru) it means you are late for the train; to say you missed it, use maniawanakatta or nogashita.
items.verbSense: be late; fall behind time
items.trap: Not densha ga chikoku suru (chikoku is people being late for school or work), and not densha ga osoi for reporting a delay: osoi works as a grumble while you wait (basu osoi ne = the bus is late), but a train running behind schedule, the one you message about, is okureteru. densha osoi can also just mean a slow train.

example.ja: ごめん、電車遅れてる。
example.english: Sorry, the train's delayed.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, densha ga okuretemasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、電車が遅れてます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, the train is running late.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. okureru's rank also covers people being late.
items.notes: When the line has stopped altogether: densha tomatteru. A clock running slow is also tokei ga okureteru (fast is susunderu).

items.use: Mostly heard as a check or a result: maniau? (will we make it?), maniatta (made it), maniawanai (we won't make it). The noun drops once the train is clear. Once it has gone, natives say nogashita or noriokureta (I missed it), above all shuuden nogashita (I missed the last train).
items.verbSense: be in time (for something); be enough
items.trap: Not densha o tsukamaeru or densha o toru: making a train in time is ni maniau ('be in time for'). 'I missed the train' is not misu shita (misu is a mistake): say maniawanakatta or nogashita.

example.romaji: isoganai to, densha ni maniawanai yo.
example.ja: 急がないと、電車に間に合わないよ。
example.english: If we don't hurry, we won't make the train.

examplePolite.romaji: isoganai to, densha ni maniaimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急がないと、電車に間に合いませんよ。
examplePolite.english: If we don't hurry, we won't make the train.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. maniau's rank covers every deadline, not just trains. For missing one: nogasu #2510, noriokureru #13876, shuuden #8326.
items.notes: maniattemasu also means 'we're fine, no thanks', a common way to turn away a door-to-door or phone salesperson.

blocks.label: Along the way
blocks.rationale: Moving through a place: turning, getting lost, staying over and stopping off.
blocks.interference: hoteru ni tomaru (stay the night) and konbini ni yoru (drop in) both come out of English 'stay' and 'stop'. There are two tomaru that sound the same: one is a night away, the other a vehicle halting (densha ga tomaru). Neither one means dropping in on the way, which is yoru.

items.use: Heard in directions with the side added: tsugi no kado o migi ni magatte (turn right at the next corner). Traffic lights take the same frame: shingou o / de hidari ni magaru.
items.verbSense: bend; turn (when moving along a road)
items.trap: Not kado ni magaru: the corner takes o or de and the direction takes ni (tsugi no kado o / de migi ni magaru). 'Turn' here is not mawaru, which means spin or go round.

example.romaji: tsugi no kado, migi ni magatte.
example.ja: 次の角、右に曲がって。
example.english: Turn right at the next corner.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi no kado o migi ni magatte kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 次の角を右に曲がってください。
examplePolite.english: Please turn right at the next corner.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 角 is ranked for the kado reading only (kaku and sumi are separate entries).
items.notes: Going straight on is massugu iku; crossing a road is michi o wataru.

items.use: Usually mayotta or mayotchatta (I've got lost) once the context is clear, like English 'I'm lost'. ima mayotteru (I'm lost right now) works just as well, and michi mayotte... explains why you're late. michi ni mayotta spells it out.
items.verbSense: lose your way; also hesitate, can't decide
items.trap: Not michi o nakusu or michi o ushinau: nakusu is for losing things, and being lost is michi ni mayou ('stray on the road').

example.ja: ごめん、道迷って、ちょっと遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I got lost, I'll be a bit late.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, michi ni mayotte, sukoshi okuremasu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、道に迷って、少し遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I got lost, so I'll be a little late.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. mayou's rank also covers its 'can't decide' sense.
items.notes: The place you got lost in takes de: eki no naka de mayotta. Asking the way is michi o kiku: sumimasen, chotto michi o kikitai n desu kedo.

items.use: Used for any night away, at a hotel or a friend's place: doko ni tomaru? (where are you staying?). It only covers overnight stays.
items.verbSense: stay the night; lodge
items.trap: Not doko ni sunderu? (that asks where someone lives), nokoru (stay behind) or hoteru ni iru (only where you are right now); sutei suru sounds like ad copy. Staying the night is tomaru, which sounds the same as tomaru, stop.

example.ja: どこのホテル泊まるの？
example.english: Which hotel are you staying at?

examplePolite.romaji: doko no hoteru ni tomaru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どこのホテルに泊まるんですか？
examplePolite.english: Which hotel are you staying at?

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 泊まる is ranked apart from 止まる (#776).
items.notes: The transitive tomeru means to put someone up: konban tomete?

items.use: Almost always followed by a direction verb: konbini yotteku (I'll stop at the konbini on the way) or yotte kaeru (stop off on the way home). Casual speech drops ni.
items.verbSense: drop in on the way; come close to
items.trap: Not konbini ni tomaru: that tomaru is a car pulling up there (konbini de tomatte = pull over at the konbini), and the overnight tomaru never fits a shop. Dropping in on the way is yoru: konbini yotteku.

example.ja: ちょっとコンビニ寄ってくね。
example.english: I'm just going to stop by the konbini.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto konbini ni yotte ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとコンビニに寄っていきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to stop by the convenience store.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. 寄る also covers 'come closer'.
items.notes: Sounds the same as yoru (night) and -ni yoru (it depends on); yotteku? also invites someone to drop in.

blocks.label: Picking up and dropping off
blocks.rationale: Offering and asking for help getting somewhere: collecting someone, taking them home or to the station, giving them a ride.
blocks.interference: mukae ni iku (go and get someone) and okuru (take someone home or to the station) go in opposite directions. okuru names the destination (ie made okuru yo = I'll take you home), while noseru is letting them ride (nosete kureru?). noseru is the giving side of noru (riding yourself).

items.use: Paired with kuru for the other direction: mukae ni iku ne (I'll come get you) and mukae ni kite (come get me). Japanese says iku where English says 'I'll come'.
items.verbSense: go (mukae is the noun of mukaeru, meet and welcome)
items.trap: Not mukae ni kuru for 'I'll come get you': you are the one going, so it is mukae ni iku (only 'come get me' is mukae ni kite). 'Pick up' is not toru here either. Among friends with a car, hirou also works for grabbing someone on the way (tochuu de hirotteku yo), but not for meeting a guest or collecting a child.

example.romaji: eki made mukae ni iku ne.
example.ja: 駅まで迎えに行くね。
example.english: I'll come pick you up at the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made mukae ni ikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで迎えに行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll come and pick you up at the station.

items.freqNote: Bare 迎え is #8575; the polite and childcare form お迎え is #2913 and the verb 迎える #1366.
items.notes: Collecting a child from nursery is omukae: hoikuen ni omukae ni iku.

items.use: Offered at the end of a visit: eki made okutteku yo (I'll take you to the station), on foot or by car. okutte kureru? asks for it.
items.verbSense: send; take someone somewhere (walk or drive them there), drop them off
items.trap: Not motte iku (that is for things) or tsurete iku, which sounds like leading someone along to a place you are both going. Taking a guest to the station or home is okuru, the 'send' verb. Waving someone off without going along is miokuru.

example.ja: 駅まで送ってくよ。
example.english: I'll take you to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made okutte ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで送っていきますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll see you to the station.

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. The destination varies (ie made, kuukou made); the fixed part is okuru with the person you take. okuru's rank also covers send (messages, parcels).
items.notes: Same verb as sending a message: meeru o okuru.

items.use: Heard as an offer or a request: noseteku yo (I'll give you a lift on my way) and nosete kureru? (can you give me a ride?). The car is often dropped once it's clear. nosete ageru is fine with friends but can sound like a favour; to a senior, offer okurimashou ka? instead.
items.verbSense: put on top of; let someone ride (transitive of noru)
items.trap: Not notte kureru? (that asks them to get in) or raido o ageru: giving a ride is noseru, the transitive of noru: nosete kureru?

example.ja: 帰り、車乗せてくれる？
example.english: Can you give me a ride home?

examplePolite.romaji: kaeri, kuruma ni nosete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 帰り、車に乗せてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Could you give me a ride home?

items.freqNote: Phrase not counted. noseru also covers putting things on top.
items.notes: Its intransitive partner is kuruma ni noru: notte (get in) vs nosete (give me a ride).

changelog.change: english now 'ride / get on the train'. use rewritten: ni noru is the riding and boarding itself, and the means of travel is de (densha de iku, densha de kayotteru).
trap now notes that only a car also allows kuruma kara deru. use adds sumimasen, orimasu! for a packed train.

english aspect fixed ('a seat frees up (aiteru = a seat is free)'). trap rewritten: kono seki tada? replaces the strawman furii, hima also covers quiet shops, and aiteru / hima overlap for schedules. examplePolite is now 'sumimasen, kono seki aitemasu ka?'. contrastGroup changed from aku-suku to null because no second member exists in this or the body domain. notes adds 'not aiteru'.

Moved into 'Taking the train'. trap rewritten: chikoku is for people, and osoi works as a grumble while waiting but not for reporting a delay (no longer contradicts D-osoi). use: densha okureta = the train was late, and densha ni okureru no longer points at the dropped card. tokei removed from partners; the slow-clock sense moved to notes.

Moved into 'Taking the train'. use and trap now cover after the fact (nogashita / noriokureta / shuuden nogashita, and misu shita is wrong). notes: maniattemasu narrowed to door-to-door and phone sales. freqNote is now factual and adds the verified ranks nogasu #2510, noriokureru #13876 and shuuden #8326.

trap: the corner takes o or de, only ni is wrong. use now shows shingou o / de. trapRisk 4 -> 3. freqNote: the untested 'dramas rarely give directions' replaced by the verified reading note (kado #4203; kaku and sumi are separate entries).
use no longer says it is past tense only; mayotteru is equally fine. notes replaced the duplicated 'can't decide' line with de for the place and michi o kiku. freqNote reworded as fact, not cause.
trap rewritten: doko ni sunderu? (lives), nokoru and hoteru ni iru are the real errors, and sutei suru is marked as ad copy, not wrong. Casual example drops ni (doko no hoteru tomaru no?).
trap rewritten: konbini ni tomaru is heard as a car pulling up (konbini de tomatte), not as staying the night. listLinks adds A-yoru. notes adds the homophone yoru (night).

trap rewritten: the direction error (mukae ni kuru) and toru are the traps, and casual hirou for a car pickup is allowed instead of called wrong. partners changed from kaimono and sanpo to eki, kuukou and hoikuen. notes gives a full omukae sentence.

verbSense no longer says 'see off', which is miokuru. trap rewritten (motte iku, tsurete iku, and miokuru for waving someone off). freqNote reworded with destinations varying and okuru's rank covering 'send'.

use: offer is noseteku yo, with a register note on nosete ageru (okurimashou ka? to a senior). trap: notte kureru? is the real slip. takushii removed from partners (different sense). commonness 3 -> 4. listLinks adds I-te-morau. notes: the intransitive partner is kuruma ni noru, not densha ni noru.

'On the train' and 'Making the train' merged into a 5-item block because dropping densha-ni-okureru left 'Making the train' with 2 items. New label and rationale. interference combines both blocks' notes and teaches the ga/ni twin and the maniawanai-before / nogashita-after split.
interference no longer says 'keep tomaru for nights'. It now explains the two tomaru (a night away, a vehicle halting) and that neither means dropping in.
Renamed from 'Giving lifts' because two of the three items are often on foot. rationale and interference no longer gloss okuru as 'see off', and interference adds the okuru vs noseru distinction.

Not applied, because this pass adds no items: kuruma-o-tomeru (on keep-list.txt but missing from the draft; wanted by the naturalness, trap and form reviews), takushii-o-hirou, michi-ga-komu, densha-ga-komu, eki-de-orosu, michi-o-wataru, and the nogasu card proposed to replace densha-ni-okureru. keep-list.txt and keep-ids.txt were not edited: they still list densha-ni-okureru and kuruma-o-tomeru and lack densha-ga-okureru. Learner-facing prose spells the two tomaru out in words instead of kanji.

dropped.reason: Two reviewers wanted it gone: the nuance review cut it and the naturalness review retargeted it to a different collocation. Before the fact it says the same thing as densha ni maniawanai (the block used one sentence for both), after the fact natives say nogashita or noriokureta, and by ear it is easily confused with densha ga okureru. Its content now lives in other cards: the ga/ni contrast in densha-ga-okureru's use, and nogashita / noriokureta / misu shita in densha-ni-maniau's use and trap. Both reviewers proposed a replacement card, densha o nogasu or shuuden o nogasu (nogasu #2510, shuuden #8326, verified). It was not added because this pass adds no items and keeps slugs unchanged. It is recommended for the next additions pass.

reviewSummaries: natural: Solid domain overall. The pairings are right, the casual examples drop particles the way Tokyo speakers do, and the polite versions keep the meaning. Every rank and listLink id checked out against freq.py and the versatility files. The real problems: densha ni okureru is not the natural way to say 'miss the train' and repeats the maniau card (retarget it to shuuden o nogasu). Three trap notes rule out or mislabel things natives actually say: hirou for a car pickup is fine, okuru is not 'see off' (that is miokuru), and konbini ni tomaru is heard as 'stop', not 'stay'. The domain is also missing michi ga konderu, kuruma o tomeru and takushii o hirou.

traps: The draft is solid. All 13 items are real, high-value pairings with accurate verbSense, correct transitivity (noru/noseru), and correct listLinks ids, frequency ranks and alsoIn pointers (all verified). Nothing needs cutting. The main weakness is traps that call acceptable forms wrong: densha osoi (contradicts the learner's own D-osoi 'late') and hito o hirou. There is also a wrong rationale in the konbini ni tomaru trap, and a few partner or notes entries that change sense (jugyou ni okureru = late for class, not miss; 'late for a person'; tokei and takushii partners).

nuance: The draft is solid. Every rank, listLink id and alsoIn pointer I checked against freq.py, the versatility files and the noun lists is correct, the examples sound natural, and the polite forms are true desu/masu counterparts. Three traps state wrong rules: konbini ni tomaru is read as 止まる (a car stopping), hirou is fine for picking up people by car, and hima is used for quiet shops and overlaps with aiteru for schedules. seki ga aku is glossed with the wrong aspect. Cut densha ni okureru: it repeats maniawanai and is less natural than nogashita / noriokureta, so replace it with densha o nogasu. Three of the four blocks have only 3 items. Add densha ga komu (which also gives the orphaned aku-suku contrast a second member) and eki de orosu (the taxi drop-off, with the otosu trap).

form: The data checks all pass: all 13 headwords, kana, polite forms and 26 example pairs match the romaji convention word for word. All 26 nounRank and verbRank values, plus the partner ranks quoted in freqNotes, match freq.py. Every listLinks id exists, the alsoIn pointers are correct (#135, #46, #59, #130, #19 and the set_ids), slugs are unique, and every block has 3–4 items. The real problems are trap claims that mark natural Japanese as wrong: hito o hirou, konbini ni tomaru, densha osoi, and the 'keep tomaru for nights' interference note. The other problem is a mismatch with the keep list: kuruma-o-tomeru was dropped and densha-ga-okureru added. Fix those and the domain is solid.

categories.name: Time, money & plans
categories.scope: Time, money, appointments, plans, bookings: jikan ga kakaru, jikan ga aru, jikan ni maniau, okane ga kakaru, okane o harau, okane o orosu, okane o kasu / kariru / kaesu, okane ga tamaru / okane o tameru, yakusoku o suru, yakusoku o mamoru / yaburu, yotei ga aru, yotei o tateru / keikaku o tateru, yoyaku o suru / toru, jikan o tsubusu, ki ga kawaru? (if not idiom).

blocks.label: Time and cost
blocks.rationale: The words for how long and how much: time and total cost both use kakaru, a thing's price uses suru, and time going by uses tatsu.
blocks.interference: kakaru vs suru: a trip costs (okane kakatta), but an item has a price (ikura shita?). kakaru vs tatsu: ichinen kakatta = it took a year, ichinen tatta = a year has gone by.

items.use: Said about how long anything takes, often with an amount in place of jikan: eki made juppun kakaru, dore gurai kakaru?. On its own, jikan kakaru means 'it takes a while'.
items.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time or money: be needed, be used up
items.trap: English 'take' leads to toru, but jikan o toru mostly means making time for someone (jikan totte kurete arigatou). How long something takes is kakaru.

example.ja: これ、けっこう時間かかるよ
example.english: This takes quite a while.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa kekkou jikan ga kakarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: これはけっこう時間がかかりますよ
examplePolite.english: This takes quite a while.

items.freqNote: かかる #385 is the kana spelling across all senses; 掛かる #5316.
items.notes: jikan o kakeru = spend time on something on purpose (jikan kakete tsukutta).

items.use: For what a trip, a hobby, a repair or daily life costs overall, often with an amount: ichiman en gurai kakatta. For the price of a thing you bought, use ikura suru.
items.verbSense: be hung on or applied; of time or money: be needed, be used up
items.trap: There is no one Japanese verb for 'cost'. A thing's price is suru (ikura shita?). What something costs you overall is kakaru, the same verb as time: shuuri ni ichiman en kakatta.

example.romaji: kuruma tte kekkou okane kakaru yo
example.ja: 車ってけっこうお金かかるよ
example.english: Having a car costs quite a bit.

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma wa kekkou okane ga kakarimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: 車はけっこうお金がかかりますよ
examplePolite.english: Having a car costs quite a bit.

items.freqNote: お金 #422; the blunter 金 (kane) is #670. かかる #385 is the kana form across all senses.
items.notes: okane o tsukau = spend (your choice); okane ga kakaru = something costs.

items.use: The shape is price + suru: ichiman en suru = it costs 10,000 yen. In the past about something bought: sore ikura shita? or ikura datta? (both common). In the present for what a thing goes for: are tte ikura suru no?, ikura suru n darou, or sanman en mo suru n da (it's a whole 30,000 yen). In a shop, the plain kore ikura desu ka is the usual question.
items.verbSense: do, make; after a price or amount: cost, be priced at
items.trap: The main list teaches kakaru as 'cost', but that is for overall spending. A single thing's price takes suru: kore ikura shita? / ichiman en shita. ikura datta? also works.

example.ja: これ、いくらした？
example.english: How much did this cost?

examplePolite.romaji: kore, ikura shimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、いくらしましたか？
examplePolite.english: How much did this cost?

items.freqNote: いくら #553 counts all uses, including 'no matter how'. The shape is price + suru, so an amount often takes the place of ikura.
items.notes: kekkou suru ne = that's pricey.

items.use: Mostly in the past, about time that has gone by: mou ichinen tatta (it's already been a year). The fixed remark is jikan tatsu no hayai ne (time flies).
items.verbSense: of time: pass, go by (sounds the same as tatsu 'stand')
items.trap: 'It's been a year' is ichinen tatta, not kakatta, which means 'it took a year'. For 'pass', use tatsu or sugiru, not tooru (pass through).

example.ja: 時間経つの早いね
example.english: Time flies, doesn't it.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga tatsu no wa hayai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 時間が経つのは早いですね
examplePolite.english: Time flies, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: 経つ #3603 is the time sense. The kana たつ is dominated by 立つ #610. sugiru (過ぎる) #701 covers all senses, including 'too much'.
items.notes: ichinen kakatta = it took a year; ichinen tatta = a year has gone by.

blocks.label: Making plans
blocks.rationale: Setting a time with someone: are you free, does it suit, I've got something on, and on the day, are you ready.
blocks.interference: aiteru means you have a gap; tsugou ga ii means the time suits you and sounds more tactful. yotei haitteru is a booked plan; youji ga atte is a vague errand, the standard excuse. Either can 'come up': youji ga dekita / yotei ga haitta.

items.use: Asking about or offering free time, nearly always as aiteru: ashita aiteru? / doyoubi nara aiteru yo. Plain aku means 'come free': jikan aitara renraku suru (I'll get in touch when I get a moment).
items.verbSense: become empty or free; open up (a seat, a room, a gap in time)
items.trap: Not jiyuu (free as in liberty) or tada (free of charge). A free slot is aku, 'open up': ashita aiteru?. ashita jikan aru? also works, and hima? is fine with friends but blunt to a senior.

example.ja: 明日時間空いてる？
example.english: Are you free tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa jikan aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は時間空いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you free tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 空く (あく) #1498. The kana あく #3508 mixes senses, and 開く read as aku (a shop or door opens) is ranked separately.
items.notes: aku also means a shop is open (mise ga aku); both come out as aiteru. Asking someone politely, people say ojikan: ojikan aitemasu ka?

items.use: The tactful way to set a time, itsu ga tsugou ii? (when suits you?), and to decline, sono hi wa chotto tsugou ga warukute (that day doesn't quite work). Casual speech drops ga. Among close friends, ashita daijoubu? is more usual.
items.verbSense: good, fine, OK
items.trap: Not benri, which is for tools and places. A time that suits someone is tsugou ga ii, and 'can't make it' is tsugou ga warui.

example.ja: 明日都合いい？
example.english: Does tomorrow work for you?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa tsugou ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は都合いいですか？
examplePolite.english: Does tomorrow work for you?

items.freqNote: いい #24 is the spoken form (良い #1474); 悪い #139 for tsugou ga warui.
items.notes: Asking someone above you: gotsugou ii desu ka? Declining politely: sono hi wa tsugou ga tsukanakute... (I can't make that day). tsugou ga tsuitara oshiete = let me know if you can make it. Said about a person, tsugou ii ne can be a dig: 'how convenient for you'.

items.use: The vague, polite reason for saying no or leaving: chotto youji ga atte..., left unfinished so the listener hears 'so I can't'. Nobody asks what the youji is. When something comes up, the verb is dekiru: kyuu ni youji ga dekichatte (something came up).
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, events)
items.trap: English 'have' leads to motsu, but having plans or errands is aru (youji ga aru). And 'something came up' is youji ga dekita, not kita or okita.

example.ja: 明日はちょっと用事あって…
example.english: Tomorrow I've got something on, so...

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa chotto youji ga aru n desu ga...
examplePolite.ja: 明日はちょっと用事があるんですが…
examplePolite.english: I've got something on tomorrow, I'm afraid...

items.use: Mostly as haitteru (is booked) or haitta (got booked): sono hi wa mou yotei haitteru. A sudden clash is kyuu ni yotei haitchatte.
items.verbSense: go in, enter; get put into something
items.trap: 'Something came up' is kyuu ni youji ga dekita or kyuu ni yotei ga haitta, not okita (that sounds like an accident). For plain 'I have plans', yotei ga aru also works, but not yotei o motteru.

example.ja: 明日はもう予定入ってる
example.english: I've already got plans tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa mou yotei ga haittemasu
examplePolite.ja: 明日はもう予定が入ってます
examplePolite.english: I've already got plans tomorrow.

items.notes: Transitive partner: yotei o ireru (book something in).

items.use: Asked and answered in the past: junbi dekita? / dekita yo / mou chotto. junbi dekitara oshiete = let me know when you're ready.
items.verbSense: be able to; come into being, get done
items.trap: English asks 'are you ready?' in the present. Japanese asks whether it is done: junbi dekita? or junbi dekiteru?. junbi dekiru? means 'can you get ready?'. Casual junbi ii? also works.
partners: shitaku (getting ready; sounds a bit old-fashioned or parental)

example.ja: もう準備できた？
example.english: Are you ready yet?

examplePolite.romaji: mou junbi dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう準備できましたか？
examplePolite.english: Are you ready yet?

items.freqNote: できる #73 is the kana form; 出来る #1313.
items.notes: Getting ready yourself is junbi suru; junbi ga dekiru is being done with it. The main list's dekiru already covers 'be ready'; the new point is asking in the past: junbi dekita?

blocks.label: Shops and cash
blocks.rationale: Running errands: is the shop open yet, has it closed, and getting cash out first.
blocks.interference: aiteru and shimatteru are the shop's own state; akeru and shimeru are the staff opening or closing it. Here aiteru means 'open', not 'free' as in ashita aiteru?.

items.use: Almost always aiteru (is open), in questions about hours: kono mise nanji made aiteru?. Plain aku is the moment it opens: juuji ni aku. yatteru (is open for business) is just as common: nanji made yatteru?
items.verbSense: of a door or shop: open, by itself
items.trap: About the shop itself, use aiteru: ano mise mou aiteru?. akeru is what the staff do, so aketemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. yatteru also works. mise o hiraku is starting a new shop.

example.ja: あの店、もう開いてる？
example.english: Is that shop open yet?

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou aitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう開いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Is that shop open yet?

items.freqNote: 開く read as aku shows #14086, but the tokenizer probably files most 開いてる under 開く read as hiraku (#624), so the real spoken rank of aku 'open' is higher. 空く #1498 is a different word.
items.notes: mise o akeru = the staff open up; mise o hiraku = start a new shop. A door opening uses the same verb: doa ga aku.

items.use: Mostly shimatteru (is closed) and shimatchau (is about to close): hayaku ikanai to shimatchau yo. Plain shimaru gives the time: kuji ni shimaru.
items.verbSense: of a door or shop: close, by itself
items.trap: For the shop's own state, use shimaru: mou shimatteru = it's already closed. shimeru is the staff closing up, so nanji ni shimemasu ka? fits only when you ask the staff. Casual owaru also works.

example.ja: あの店、もう閉まってるよ
example.english: That shop's already closed.

examplePolite.romaji: ano mise wa mou shimattemasu yo
examplePolite.ja: あの店はもう閉まってますよ
examplePolite.english: That shop's already closed.

items.notes: Closing for good is mise o tatamu, or tsubureru (go bust). Sounds like shimau (put away; the -chau ending): mou shimatta can mean 'I already put it away', and shimatta! alone means 'oops'. Context decides.

items.use: What you say on the way to the ATM or konbini: chotto okane oroshite kuru, okane orosanakya. The o usually drops.
items.verbSense: bring or take down; lower
items.trap: Not okane o toru, which sounds like taking someone's money. Cash from an ATM is orosu, 'bring down'. Casual dasu also works.

example.ja: ちょっとお金下ろしてくる
example.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto okane o oroshite kimasu
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお金を下ろしてきます
examplePolite.english: I'm just going to grab some cash.

items.freqNote: 下ろす #2775 covers all senses, including lowering things; 降ろす #4786 is letting people off.
items.notes: hikidasu is the formal word; ATM voice prompts and bank staff say ohikidashi.

blocks.label: Paying and saving
blocks.rationale: Money among friends: splitting the bill, saving up, and having nothing to spare.
blocks.interference: Money verbs: okane o tameru (save up), orosu (take out), tsukau (spend), harau (pay). warikan ni suru = split evenly; ogoru = pay for someone. yoyuu ga nai = nothing to spare (money, time or energy); okane ga nai = broke.

items.use: Said when the bill comes: warikan ni shiyou, warikan de ii?, or just warikan shiyou. People often follow with each person's share: hitori sen en ne. Between two people, hanbunko also works.
items.verbSense: do; X ni suru = make it X, go with X
items.trap: English 'split' leads to wakeru, which is fine with staff for separate bills (kaikei wakete moraemasu ka?). Splitting the total evenly is one noun, warikan: warikan ni shiyou. Each paying their own is betsubetsu.

example.ja: じゃあ、割り勘にしよう
example.english: OK, let's split it.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, warikan ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、割り勘にしましょう
examplePolite.english: OK, let's split it.

items.freqNote: 割り勘 #12038 is low in drama subtitles; commonness is judged from how often it's said at meals out.
items.notes: Paying for someone is ogoru (kyou wa ogoru yo = it's on me).

items.use: For saving toward something, usually as tameteru (I'm saving): ryokou no okane tameteru. okane ga tamatta means you've finally saved enough.
items.verbSense: let something build up; store up
items.trap: English 'save' leads to hozon suru (save a file), tasukeru (rescue) or setsuyaku (cut back). Saving up is tameru, 'pile up'. chokin suru also works.

example.romaji: ima ryokou no okane tameteru n da
example.ja: 今旅行のお金貯めてるんだ
example.english: I'm saving up for a trip.

examplePolite.romaji: ima ryokou no okane o tameteru n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今旅行のお金を貯めてるんです
examplePolite.english: I'm saving up for a trip.

items.freqNote: 貯める #10930 is the money spelling; the kana ためる #3410 covers every sense.
items.notes: Intransitive partner: okane ga tamaru (the money builds up). The same sound also means letting things pile up through neglect: shigoto o tameru, sutoresu ga tamaru (溜める).

items.use: Says you have no spare money, time or energy. A noun before it says which: okane no yoyuu, jikan no yoyuu. Plain ima yoyuu nai means 'I'm swamped right now'.
items.verbSense: there isn't; not have (negative of aru)
items.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'afford'. For one item it's kaenai (takakute kaenai = I can't afford it). For having no money to spare in general it's okane no yoyuu ga nai (or just okane nai), and yoyuu nai alone means 'I'm swamped'.
partners: okane (money: okane no yoyuu ga nai)
jikan (time: jikan no yoyuu ga nai)
kokoro (headspace: kokoro no yoyuu ga nai = too stressed to deal with anything)

example.romaji: ima okane no yoyuu nai n da
example.ja: 今お金の余裕ないんだ
example.english: Money's a bit tight right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima okane no yoyuu ga nai n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今お金の余裕がないんです
examplePolite.english: Money's a bit tight right now.

items.notes: jikan ni yoyuu ga aru = there's still plenty of time. In slang, yoyuu means 'easy': yoyuu desho / yoyuu da yo = piece of cake.

changelog.change: trap: jikan o toru now glossed as making time for someone (jikan totte kurete arigatou), not only setting time aside (traps).

trap reworded: no single verb for 'cost'; price = suru, overall cost = kakaru, with shuuri ni ichiman en kakatta (natural/traps/nuance/form). Example English now 'Having a car costs quite a bit.' (natural).

english -> 'how much it costs (price + suru)' (nuance). use rewritten to give the price + suru shape, ikura datta?, and present-tense uses (ikura suru no?, ikura suru n darou, sanman en mo suru n da) (natural/traps/nuance/form). trap now contrasts with the main list's kakaru 'cost' and adds that ikura datta? also works (nuance/traps). trapRisk 5 -> 4 (traps).

trap leads with ichinen tatta vs kakatta and allows sugiru (nuance/traps). trapRisk 5 -> 4. contrastGroup null -> take-verbs, which already links across domains (nuance/traps). listLinks: A-shibaraku replaced by A-mou and D-hayai (traps/form). freqNote adds 過ぎる #701 (form, verified). Added notes on kakatta vs tatta.

trap now allows junbi dekiteru? and junbi ii? (traps, major). shitaku partner marked as a bit old-fashioned or parental; englishVerb -> 'be ready'; notes say H-dekiru already covers 'be ready' (nuance). Moved to the end of Making plans (nuance/form).

trap adds tada (free of charge), jikan aru? as an alternative, and that hima? is blunt to a senior (traps/nuance). notes add ojikan for polite asking. The example stays as written because the natural lens accepts it between peers. Added H-aru to listLinks.

use now gives kyuu ni youji ga dekichatte and says dekiru is the verb; trap adds youji ga dekita, not kita or okita; notes set to null because they moved into use (traps). trapRisk 3 -> 2 (traps). Added H-dekiru to listLinks.

trap now gives youji ga dekita and yotei ga haitta for 'something came up' and rules out yotei o motteru, which removes the conflict with youji-ga-aru (natural/traps/nuance/form). partners: renraku replaced by kaigi, because renraku ga hairu is a different sense (traps).

use adds ashita daijoubu? for close friends (nuance). notes add gotsugou for seniors, the polite decline tsugou ga tsukanakute, and tsugou ga tsuitara oshiete (natural/traps). Added D-daijoubu to listLinks.

trap no longer calls akeru wrong: aketemasu ka? is fine when asking the staff; yatteru added (traps, major). use adds yatteru (natural/form). english -> 'a shop opens (aiteru: is open)' (nuance). partners: doa replaced by yakkyoku, and notes point to doa ga aku (traps). trapRisk 4 -> 3 (traps). Added H-yaru to listLinks.

trap no longer calls shimeru wrong: nanji ni shimemasu ka? is fine when asking the staff (traps, major). notes add the warning that it sounds like shimau, plus shimatta! (oops) (natural/nuance). english -> 'a shop closes (shimatteru: is closed)' (nuance). partners: doa and mado replaced by byouin and yuubinkyoku (traps). Added I-chau to listLinks. trapRisk stays 3, matching mise-ga-aku.
notes now refer to what is heard: ATM voice prompts and bank staff say ohikidashi (natural/nuance/form). trapRisk 5 -> 4 (traps). Added I-te-kuru to listLinks (form).
trap says wakeru is fine with staff for separate bills; warikan = an even split; betsubetsu (traps/nuance). use adds warikan shiyou and hanbunko (natural). trapRisk 5 -> 4 (nuance).

Example changed to 'ima ryokou no okane tameteru n da' / polite '...o tameteru n desu' to avoid the tame ni / tameteru sound clash; use updated to match (natural/nuance). trap adds hozon suru (traps). partners: shigoto (the 溜める sense) replaced by sutanpu; the pile-up sense (shigoto o tameru, sutoresu ga tamaru) moved to notes (traps). contrastGroup tamaru-tameru -> null because the group had no other members (traps/nuance/form).

trap gives kaenai (takakute kaenai) for a single item (natural/traps/nuance, major). partners -> okane, jikan, kokoro no yoyuu, dropping hima, which does not pair (natural/traps).
