Example English -> 'Money's a bit tight right now.' (natural). notes spell the slang as desho, matching F-desho, and add jikan ni yoyuu ga aru (natural/traps). Added H-kau to listLinks.
interference was the literal 'none'; it now gives the money verbs (tameru/orosu/tsukau/harau), warikan vs ogoru, and yoyuu ga nai vs okane ga nai (traps/form).
Items reordered to jikan-ga-aku, tsugou-ga-ii, youji-ga-aru, yotei-ga-hairu, junbi-ga-dekiru to match the rationale (nuance/form). interference now gives both ways to say 'something came up'.

NOT applied: the traps, nuance and form reviewers asked to restore the keep-list items yakusoku-o-mamoru, keikaku-o-tateru and okane-o-kariru, and suggested okane-o-kuzusu and jikan-o-tsubusu. The brief forbids adding items, so these need a decision upstream. As a result Shops and cash and Paying and saving stay at 3 items each, which is allowed. junbi-ga-dekiru was kept: no reviewer cut it, and moving it to another domain was only suggested on the condition that it be replaced.

reviewSummaries: natural: Strong domain: every pairing is the one a Tokyo speaker uses, and the casual examples drop particles naturally (jikan kakaru, yotei haitteru, okane oroshite kuru). All listLinks ids, alsoIn pointers and ranks check out against the source files and freq.py. The only substantive problems are in yoyuu-ga-nai: the trap misses kaenai as the everyday 'can't afford it', and 'hima no yoyuu' is not said. Everything else is polish: present-tense ikura suru no?, the yatteru alternative for shop hours, the shimau homophone for an audio learner, and the go-/o- forms used when asking about the listener. Gaps worth considering for this domain: yakusoku o mamoru/yaburu, yoyaku o toru, jikan ni maniau, kaado de harau.

traps: The draft is solid. All listLinks ids exist, every nounRank/verbRank matches freq.py, the alsoIn pointers check out, and the romaji is clean. The core traps hold: kakaru vs suru vs tatsu, aku for free time, tsugou vs benri, and orosu. The main weaknesses are traps that call a fine alternative wrong (akeru/shimeru when asking staff, wakeru with staff, junbi dekiteru, kaenai for 'afford') and partners used in a different sense (renraku ga hairu, shigoto o tameru, the yoyuu partners, physical doa/mado). Two high-value keep-list items were dropped without a reason: yakusoku o mamoru and yotei/keikaku o tateru. Several trapRisk scores are a notch high.

nuance: The draft is solid on accuracy. I checked every rank against freq.py, every listLinks id against the versatility files (26 of 26 exist) and every alsoIn pointer, and all are correct. The polite forms are true desu/masu pairs, and the examples are natural speech in correct romaji. The main problems are structural. Two blocks have only 3 items, and one of them has 'none' as its interference. In Making plans the item order contradicts the rationale. Three keep-list items for this domain are missing (okane-o-kariru, yakusoku-o-mamoru, keikaku-o-tateru), two of them stronger traps than the items that replaced them. A few use and trap lines need correcting: ikura suru is not mostly past-tense, and two items give conflicting phrases for 'something came up'. I recommend no cuts.

form: The form is clean. All 15 items pass the mechanical checks: romaji follows the convention and matches ja/kana sound for sound (haitchatte, shimatchau, orosanakya, juppun, koutsuuhi), masu forms are correctly conjugated, example romaji matches example ja word for word, and there are no duplicate slugs. Blocks hold 4/5/3/3 items. All 26 listLinks ids exist in versatility-items.txt, every nounRank/verbRank (all 15 items, over 30 lookups) matches freq.py, and the alsoIn pointers check out (10-list-nouns #18/#20/#138; vocab-trainer 'shops' contains mise). The main problem is selection drift: the draft swapped 3 keep-list items, including the high-trap yakusoku o mamoru, keikaku o tateru and okane o kariru, for weaker ones, with no recorded reason. The rest is polish: a literal "none" interference, block order, one over-strong usage claim, and missing links (I-te-kuru, D-hayai).

categories.name: Work & school
categories.scope: Jobs, classes, exams, homework, time off: shigoto o yasumu, yasumi o toru, kaisha ni tsutomeru, shigoto ni tsuku?, kaigi ni deru, jugyou ni deru, shiken o ukeru, shiken ni ukaru / ochiru, shukudai o dasu, shukudai o suru, ten o toru (get a score), zangyou o suru?, kaisha o yameru, shigoto ga owaru, menkyo o toru, shikaku o toru.

blocks.label: Workdays
blocks.rationale: Talking about your job day to day: when work ends, days off, meetings, and where you work.
blocks.interference: The particle carries the meaning: kaisha ni tsutomeru takes ni, but hataraku takes de (kaisha de hataraku). kaigi ni deru means attend, while kaisha o deru means leave the office.

items.use: Said when making plans around someone's workday: shigoto nanji ni owaru? Once you're done, you say shigoto owatta. Casual speech usually drops ga.
items.verbSense: end, be over (the thing itself finishes)
items.trap: English makes you the subject ('I finish work'), which tempts o with a transitive verb (shigoto o owaraseru means getting a job done). For clocking off, the work itself ends: shigoto ga owaru, so 'I'm done' is shigoto owatta.

example.ja: 今日仕事何時に終わる？
example.english: What time do you get off work today?

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa shigoto nanji ni owarimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は仕事何時に終わりますか？
examplePolite.english: What time do you finish work today?

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 終わる #190, 上がる agaru #503. Same frame: gakkou ga owaru, jugyou ga owaru.
items.notes: Leaving the building is kaisha o deru. The stiffer transitive is shigoto o oeru. Among coworkers, clocking off is also agaru: kyou nanji ni agaru?

items.english: take time off work, miss work
items.use: Said when you stay away from work, sick or not, for a day or longer: kyou shigoto yasumu. It's usually heard in the past (yasunda), and gakkou o yasumu works the same way.
items.verbSense: rest, take a break; stay away from (work, school)
items.trap: yasumu sounds like 'rest', and 'off work' or 'from work' suggests kara, giving shigoto kara yasumu. Work is the object: shigoto o yasumu, like gakkou o yasumu (miss school). yasumi o toru (take time off) is also fine.

example.ja: 今日風邪で仕事休んだ。
example.english: I took today off work with a cold.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kaze de shigoto o yasumimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は風邪で仕事を休みました。
examplePolite.english: I took today off work with a cold.

items.freqNote: 仕事 #134, 休む #584. Same frame with gakkou (#661) and kaisha (#474): kyou gakkou yasunda.
items.notes: Planned leave is yasumi o toru. 'I'm off tomorrow' is just ashita yasumi.

items.use: Said about taking part in a meeting: ashita no kaigi deru? Casual speech often drops ni, and deteru means you're in the meeting right now.
items.verbSense: go out; appear; take part in an event
items.trap: 'Attend' has no plain spoken verb: it's deru with ni. With o, deru means leaving a place (kaisha o deru = leave the office), and stepping out of a meeting is kaigi o nukeru. kaigi ni sanka suru (join) is also common at work, and shusseki suru is the formal one.

example.ja: 明日の会議出る？
example.english: Are you going to tomorrow's meeting?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no kaigi ni demasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日の会議に出ますか？
examplePolite.english: Will you be at tomorrow's meeting?

items.freqNote: 会議 #1612. 出る #81 counts every sense of deru; the 'attend' sense rests on native judgement. 参加 sanka #1164, 出席 shusseki #3831, 抜ける nukeru #1270.
items.notes: Someone in a meeting right now is ima kaigi-chuu. Joining an online meeting is kaigi ni hairu.

items.use: Said when telling someone where you work, typically in self-introductions and polite talk. Use the -te iru form, tsutometeru, because plain tsutomeru sounds like a job you'll start later. It's a notch formal: between friends, X de hataraiteru is more common.
items.verbSense: be employed (somewhere)
items.trap: 'Work at X' gives the wrong particle. tsutomeru takes ni (kaisha ni tsutometeru) and hataraku takes de (kaisha de hataraiteru); kaisha ni hataraku is wrong. X no tame ni hataraku means working for X's sake.

example.romaji: ima wa chiisai kaisha ni tsutometeru.
example.ja: 今は小さい会社に勤めてる。
example.english: I work for a small company now.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa chiisai kaisha ni tsutomete imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今は小さい会社に勤めています。
examplePolite.english: I work for a small company now.

items.freqNote: 会社 #474, 勤める #2170. The homophones 務める (#2501, serve as) and 努める (#8888, strive) are counted separately. 働く hataraku is #361.
items.notes: hataraku takes de instead. Between friends: ima chiisai kaisha de hataraiteru.

blocks.label: Exams and learning from others
blocks.rationale: Sitting, passing and failing exams (ukeru, ukaru, ochiru), then the two ways to say something was of use or taught you something (yaku ni tatsu, benkyou ni naru). All but ukeru use ni where English has a direct object or an adjective.
blocks.interference: ukeru (take) and ukaru (pass) sound alike: ukeru takes o and means taking it, ukaru takes ni and means you passed. ochiru is ukaru's opposite. yaku ni tatta = it was useful, benkyou ni natta = I learned from it.

items.use: Said about sitting a test, often when talking about plans: raishuu shiken ukeru. o is often dropped, and interviews take the same verb (mensetsu o ukeru).
items.verbSense: receive; undergo
items.trap: 'Take' leads to shiken o toru, but toru is for getting a score or a licence, or signing up for a class (jugyou o toru). Exams, tests and interviews are 'undergone': shiken o ukeru.

example.ja: 来週日本語の試験受ける。
example.english: I'm taking a Japanese exam next week.

examplePolite.romaji: raishuu nihongo no shiken o ukemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 来週日本語の試験を受けます。
examplePolite.english: I'm taking a Japanese exam next week.

items.freqNote: 試験 #3067, 受ける #356. Everyday school tests are more often tesuto (#2539), with the same verb. 面接 mensetsu (#3050, interview) takes ukeru too.
items.notes: Students often just say ashita tesuto aru (there's a test tomorrow). On its own, ukeru! is slang for 'that's hilarious'.

items.use: Said about a result, almost always in the past: shiken ukatta! Casual speech drops ni, and schools and companies work the same way (daigaku ni ukatta).
items.verbSense: pass, get in (be accepted by an exam, school or employer)
items.trap: 'Pass' gives no hint of ukaru, and the exam takes ni, not o (shiken ni ukatta). goukaku shita is just as common in speech, especially for entrance exams, and shiken ni tootta also works.

example.ja: 日本語の試験受かった！
example.english: I passed the Japanese exam!

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo no shiken ni ukarimashita!
examplePolite.ja: 日本語の試験に受かりました！
examplePolite.english: I passed the Japanese exam!

items.freqNote: 受かる #3494, 合格 goukaku #2357: both are everyday speech. ukaru is the more casual verb; goukaku also turns up in set phrases like goukaku omedetou.

items.use: Said about a result, usually as ochita or ochichatta (failed, sadly). Also used for schools, interviews and auditions: mensetsu ni ochita.
items.verbSense: fall, drop (here: fail to get through)
items.trap: 'Fail' points to shippai suru. shiken ni shippai shita is possible, but it means you blew it. For the pass/fail result, you 'fall': shiken ni ochita, or just shiken ochita. The exam takes ni, not o.

example.ja: 日本語の試験落ちちゃった。
example.english: I failed the Japanese exam, unfortunately.

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo no shiken ni ochichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語の試験に落ちちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I failed the Japanese exam, unfortunately.

items.freqNote: 試験 #3067, 落ちる #490. 落ちる counts every 'fall' sense; the exam sense rests on native judgement. 失敗 shippai #809, 滑る suberu #5017.
items.notes: Before someone's exam, avoid saying ochiru or suberu (slip): it's considered bad luck. Casually, failing is also shiken subetta. The careful polite form is ochite shimaimashita, and failing a course is tan'i o otosu.

items.use: Said about advice, information, tools or people being of real use. You hear the past yaku ni tatta (that helped) most, then yaku ni tatenakute gomen (sorry I couldn't help) and the negative yaku ni tatanai (no use; harsh if said of a person).
items.verbSense: stand (here: serve a purpose)
items.trap: 'Useful' leads to benri, which means handy or convenient to use. yaku ni tatsu means it actually helped you with something, and it's the one for advice and information: advice that helped is yaku ni tatta, not benri datta.

example.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, sugoku yaku ni tatta yo.
example.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、すごく役に立ったよ。
example.english: That app you told me about the other day was really useful.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, hontou ni yaku ni tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、本当に役に立ちました。
examplePolite.english: The app you told me about the other day was really useful.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 役に立つ has its own entry in the drama list at #1516 (役 #1534, 立つ #610). 助かる tasukaru #542.
items.notes: tasukatta (you saved me) is the warmer thanks when someone helps you. To offer help: nanika yaku ni tateru koto attara itte ne. To thank a senior for a talk, say benkyou ni narimashita instead.

items.use: Said as thanks when someone explains or shows you something: benkyou ni narimasu as a reply on the spot, especially to a senior, and benkyou ni natta or benkyou ni narimashita afterwards.
items.verbSense: become, turn into
items.trap: benkyou shita means you sat down and studied. 'I learned a lot from that' is benkyou ni natta: the thing becomes a lesson.

example.romaji: kyou no hanashi, sugoku benkyou ni natta.
example.ja: 今日の話、すごく勉強になった。
example.english: I learned a lot from today's talk.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no ohanashi, hontou ni benkyou ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 今日のお話、本当に勉強になりました。
examplePolite.english: I learned a lot from today's talk.

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 勉強になる has its own entry in the drama list at #4175 (勉強 #729, なる #29).
items.notes: Often comes after naruhodo: naruhodo, benkyou ni narimasu.

changelog.change: Trap rewritten: the invented oriru error is replaced by the real one (English makes you the subject, tempting o + transitive owaraseru); shigoto o owaru is no longer called wrong. trapRisk 3->2. Notes add colloquial agaru (kyou nanji ni agaru?); freqNote adds 上がる #503.

english -> 'take time off work, miss work'; use covers a day or longer. Trap rewritten: shigoto o toru straw man removed, real trap is kara vs o and yasumu = 'be absent' not 'rest'. trapRisk 4->3. Unrelated G-oyasumi link removed. Statement examples get final punctuation.

Trap: dropped the unused 'kaigi o deru'; with o it is kaisha o deru, stepping out of a meeting is kaigi o nukeru; sanka suru called common, shusseki suru the formal one. Partners: shiai marked 'as a player', paatii -> nomikai. Notes hyphenate kaigi-chuu and add kaigi ni hairu. listLinks add A-chuu. freqNote adds 参加/出席/抜ける ranks.

Trap rewritten around the real error (ni/de particle mix-up, kaisha ni hataraku is wrong), with tame ni as the contrast. Use and notes say it is a notch formal and give the friends' version (de hataraiteru). The register note went into use/notes because the flags enum has no 'formal' value. speakNeed 4->3. listLinks add E-tame-ni. Statement examples get final punctuation.

Partner jugyou replaced by oodishon, because jugyou o toru is correct and clashed with the trap. Trap now says toru is right for signing up for a class. Notes add the slang ukeru! ('hilarious'). Statement examples get final punctuation.
Trap and freqNote no longer call goukaku formal: goukaku shita is everyday speech (合格 #2357 outranks 受かる #3494). listLinks add H-toru (glossed 'pass') as a contrast.

Trap corrected: shippai isn't 'stiff', it means you blew it, and the exam takes ni, not o. trapRisk 5->4. Polite example -> ochichaimashita, and both English lines now carry the same regret. freqNote adds the noun rank, 失敗 and 滑る. Notes add the exam-luck taboo (ochiru/suberu), subetta, the careful form ochite shimaimashita and tan'i o otosu. The taboo went in notes because the flags enum can't hold it. Statement examples get final punctuation.

Both examples moved from the 'today's talk' frame (shared with benkyou-ni-naru) to an app that helped; the polite example uses hontou ni, not sugoku. Use adds yaku ni tatenakute gomen and marks yaku ni tatanai as harsh about a person. That warning went in use because the flags enum can't hold it. Trap sharpened (benri = handy, yaku ni tatsu = actually helped). Notes add offering help and thanking a senior for a talk. freqNote adds 助かる #542.

Use now gives the on-the-spot non-past (benkyou ni narimasu) and the past, so it no longer contradicts the notes. In the polite example, sugoku -> hontou ni. listLinks add H-naru. The statement example gets final punctuation.
Relabelled 'Exams and learning from others'. The rationale now names the exam trio and then the useful/instructive pair, since those two aren't school phrases.

reviewSummaries: natural: The list is solid. All 9 pairings are the verbs natives actually use. The ranks, listLink ids and alsoIn pointers are correct. Most casual examples drop particles the way people really do. The main problems are three. yaku-ni-tatsu reuses benkyou-ni-naru's exact 'today's talk' sentence, which erases the contrast between them. The draft calls goukaku 'formal', but it's everyday speech and outranks ukaru in the drama data. And the domain is missing high-trap pairs: kaisha ni hairu, shigoto o yameru, shukudai o dasu, jugyou o toru, gakkou ni kayou and shimekiri ni maniau. The rest is polish: some traps aren't ones learners really make (oriru, shigoto o toru, kaigi o deru), plus a few register flags and partner tweaks.

traps: Solid domain overall. All listLinks and alsoIn pointers exist, every frequency rank checks out against the drama list, and the examples are natural and correctly romanized. The weak point is the trap claims. Four of them (shigoto o yasumu, shigoto ga owaru, kaisha ni tsutomeru, shiken ni ochiru) target an error learners don't make or misstate the alternative: shippai isn't stiff, and shigoto o toru isn't 'land a job'. shiken o ukeru's jugyou partner contradicts its own toru trap. Coverage is thin: gakkou ni kayou, shukudai o dasu and jugyou o toru are the obvious missing high-trap pairings.

nuance: This domain is solid. I checked every rank, listLink and alsoIn pointer and all are correct, and the examples are natural casual speech with true desu/masu pairs. The main errors are two inaccurate trap claims: shippai is called 'stiff', and goukaku is called formal even though the data shows 合格 outranks 受かる. Also, the yaku ni tatsu and benkyou ni naru examples share one frame, so the contrast pair reads as synonyms. Smaller issues are missing register flags (ochiru avoided before exams, yaku ni tatanai about people), a few scores that run high (shigoto ga owaru trapRisk, tsutomeru speakNeed), and gaps where shigoto ga hairu and baito o suru should be added.

form: The data is clean. I checked all 18 nounRank/verbRank values and the extra ranks in the freqNotes (テスト, 面接, 合格, 働く, 務める, 努める, 学校, 役に立つ #1516, 勉強になる #4175) against freq.py, and every one is exact. All 9 listLinks ids exist, the alsoIn pointers (10-list-nouns #109/#110, office-items for shigoto/kaisha/kaigi) are correct, and romaji, kana, polite forms, masu conjugations and example romaji-to-ja alignment all pass. Slugs are unique and the blocks hold 4 and 5 items. Nothing is fatal and nothing needs cutting. The fixes are polish: hyphenate kaigi-chuu, add three missing links, tighten two trap glosses (kaigi o deru / shusseki, shigoto o toru), use totemo in the two honorific polite examples, and make example punctuation consistent.

categories.name: People & talk
categories.scope: Talking, favours, relationships, trouble: hanashi o suru, uso o tsuku, shitsumon o suru, henji o suru, koe o kakeru, aisatsu o suru, sodan ni noru, meiwaku o kakeru, shinpai o kakeru, ki o tsukau, jama o suru, kenka o suru, nakanaori o suru, tomodachi ga dekiru, kareshi / kanojo ga dekiru, sewa o suru, rei o iu, yakusoku... (in time-money), tasuke o motomeru?, hanashi ga au?

blocks.label: Making friends and getting through
blocks.rationale: Becoming and being friends, then reaching people: going up to someone, staying in touch, getting through when you don't share a language.
blocks.interference: koe o kakeru (approach or call someone over) is not hanasu (talk with); renraku o toru (keep up or manage contact) is not the one-off renraku suru from the versatility list; kotoba ga tsuujiru is about the language getting through, not wakaru.

items.use: Said once a friendship has formed, so mostly in the past: tomodachi dekita (I've made a friend). kareshi / kanojo dekita (got a boyfriend / girlfriend) works the same way.
items.verbSense: come into being, be made; also 'can do' and 'be ready'
items.trap: English 'make' leads to tomodachi o tsukuru, which natives use for setting out to make friends (tomodachi tsukuritai); 'I've made a friend' is tomodachi dekita.
partners: kodomo (child: kodomo dekita = we're expecting; akachan works too)

example.ja: こっちでもう友達できた？
example.english: Made any friends here yet?

examplePolite.romaji: kochira de tomodachi wa dekimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: こちらで友達はできましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you made any friends here?

items.freqNote: dekiru: kana できる #73 pools every sense, mostly 'can do' (出来る #1313 listed separately).
items.notes: Wanting friends is usually tomodachi hoshii or tomodachi tsukuritai.

items.use: Said about two people or a group (ano futari naka ii yo ne), or with to for you and someone: tanaka-san to naka ii n da (I'm close with Tanaka). ii becomes yo- in other forms: naka yokatta (we used to be close), nakayoku shite ne (be nice to each other). The opposite is naka ga warui.
items.verbSense: good, fine (adjective; past yokatta)
items.trap: English 'get along' splits in two: the state 'we get along' is naka ga ii (our relationship is good), and the action 'get along, be nice to each other' is nakayoku suru (nakayoku shite ne). This naka is not naka 'inside'.

example.romaji: ano futari, naka ii yo ne.
example.ja: あの二人、仲いいよね。
example.english: Those two are close, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari wa naka ga ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人は仲がいいですね。
examplePolite.english: Those two get along well, don't they.

items.freqNote: 仲 #1305; kana なか #4046 mixes in 中 'inside'. ii: kana いい #24. nakayoku (仲良く) #1816.
items.notes: Opposite: naka ga warui; close friends are nakayoshi. nakayoku suru = get along (as an action), nakayoku natta = we became friends. 10-list-nouns #23 is the homophone naka 'inside'; under its rule S2, 仲 is carded only as this phrase.

items.english: speak to, call out to; ask along
items.use: Used for going up to someone, or asking to be told: nanka attara koe kakete (give me a shout if anything comes up). Also the everyday way to invite someone along: tanaka-san ni mo koe kakeyou ka? (shall we ask Tanaka too?). koe kakerareta can mean someone came up to you, including being hit on.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, direct your voice at someone
items.trap: 'Talk to someone' leads to hanasu, which is fine once you're talking: X to hanasu is chatting with X, X ni hanasu is telling X something. Going up to someone, calling them over or giving them a shout is koe o kakeru (hanashikakeru also works for starting a chat).
partners: kotoba (words: yasashii kotoba o kakeru = say something kind to someone)

example.ja: なんかあったら声かけてね。
example.english: Give me a shout if you need anything.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika attara koe o kakete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かあったら声をかけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please let me know if you need anything.

items.freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools all senses.
items.notes: hanashikakeru (start talking to someone) is the close single verb. Same kakeru as denwa o kakeru (make a call) and meiwaku o kakeru, in a different sense.

items.use: Mostly about staying in touch or managing to reach someone: mada renraku totteru? (still in touch?), renraku ga torenai (I can't get hold of them). renraku tsukanai means the same and is just as common (renraku ga tsuku is the intransitive side). For a single message or call, renraku suru is the everyday verb.
items.verbSense: take, get hold of
items.trap: English 'keep in touch' leads to renraku suru for everything. That's right for the goodbye line (mata renraku suru ne, renraku shite ne) and for a single message, but being in contact over time or managing to reach someone is renraku o toru: mada renraku totteru?, renraku ga torenai. renraku o tsuzukeru sounds off, and renraku o tamotsu is stiff written style.
partners: kyori (distance: kyori o toru = keep your distance)
baransu (balance: baransu o toru = keep your balance)

example.ja: 彼とまだ連絡取ってる？
example.english: Are you still in touch with him?

examplePolite.romaji: kare to wa mada renraku o tottemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 彼とはまだ連絡を取ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you still in touch with him?

items.notes: Hearing from someone is renraku ga kuru or renraku moratta.

items.english: get through (of a language); be able to communicate
items.use: Heard about trips and foreigners: kotoba tsuujinakatta (we couldn't understand each other). The language itself is often the subject: eigo tsuujiru? (does English work here?), nihongo tsuujita (my Japanese got through).
items.verbSense: get through, connect (a road, a phone line, a meaning)
items.trap: Asking a person eigo wakaru? is fine, and kotoba ga wakaranai is fine for your own understanding. But saying a language works or got through, either way, is tsuujiru (eigo tsuujinakatta), not wakaru.

example.ja: 言葉通じなくて大変だった。
example.english: We couldn't understand each other. It was rough.

examplePolite.romaji: kotoba ga tsuujinakute taihen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 言葉が通じなくて大変でした。
examplePolite.english: It was hard not being able to communicate.

items.notes: hanashi ga tsuujinai = we're not on the same page. A phone call that won't connect is usually denwa ga tsunagaranai.

blocks.label: Kidding and confiding
blocks.rationale: What friends say to each other: lies and jokes, secrets, advice.
blocks.interference: uso o tsuku and joudan o iu both give a 'just kidding' reply (uso da yo / joudan da yo), but lying takes tsuku and joking takes iu; soudan ni noru (listening) vs soudan suru (asking).

items.use: Heard as denial or accusation: uso tsuitenai yo (I'm not lying), uso tsukanaide (don't lie to me). Bare uso! is the 'no way!' reaction, not an accusation.
items.verbSense: let out (breath); in speech it survives mainly in uso o tsuku and tameiki o tsuku (sigh)
items.trap: English 'tell' leads to uso o iu, which natives also say (uso bakkari itte, uso iwanaide), but the set phrase for lying is uso o tsuku: uso tsuita, uso tsukanaide.

example.romaji: uso tsuitenai yo, honto da yo.
example.ja: 嘘ついてないよ、ほんとだよ。
example.english: I'm not lying, it's true.

examplePolite.romaji: uso wa tsuitemasen. hontou desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 嘘はついてません。本当ですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not lying. It's true.

items.freqNote: uso #1544 (kana うそ #2305 counted separately). tsuku: kana つく #355 pools every kana tsuku sense (付く, 点く, 吐く); 吐く read as つく sits at the list floor (#173635, effectively unranked), so this sense has no clean rank.
items.notes: A liar is usotsuki.

items.use: Heard in teasing: mata joudan itte (there you go joking again), joudan itteru dake (I'm only joking). The short replies joudan da yo (just kidding) and joudan desho? (you're kidding, right?) leave the verb out. joudan janai yo is the annoyed opposite: this is no joke / you've got to be kidding me.
items.verbSense: say
items.trap: English 'make a joke' leads to joudan o tsukuru, which doesn't work; jokes are said (joudan o iu), and 'just kidding' is joudan da yo.

example.ja: 冗談言ってるだけだよ。
example.english: I'm only joking.

examplePolite.romaji: joudan o itteru dake desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 冗談を言ってるだけですよ。
examplePolite.english: I'm only joking.

items.use: Almost always a request: kore naisho ni shite ne (keep this between us). On its own, naisho da yo means 'it's a secret' when you won't tell.
items.verbSense: do; with ni, make something into X (kore ni suru = I'll take this one)
items.trap: English 'keep a secret' leads to mamoru. himitsu o mamoru is fine (himitsu mamotte ne works too), but naisho doesn't take mamoru: 'keep this between us' is naisho ni shite (or himitsu ni shite).

example.ja: これ内緒にしてね。
example.english: Keep this between us, okay?

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa naisho ni shite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: これは内緒にしてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please keep this to yourself.

items.freqNote: 内緒 #2414; kana ないしょ #4442 counted separately; suru #15.
items.notes: himitsu ni suru is the neutral twin.

items.use: Asked as a request or offered as support: soudan notte kurenai? (can I talk something through with you?), itsu demo soudan noru yo (I'm always here to talk). Asking for advice yourself is soudan suru.
items.verbSense: get on, ride (a train, a bike); here, take up someone's problem
items.trap: English 'give advice' leads to adobaisu: adobaisu suru is fine for a concrete tip (adobaisu o ageru can sound condescending), and hanashi kiku yo is a plain offer to listen. But helping a friend think a problem through has its own set phrase, soudan ni noru (literally 'ride on the consultation'), and asking for that help is soudan suru.
partners: sasoi (invitation: sasoi ni noru = take someone up on it)
hanashi (hanashi ni noru = go along with an idea or offer)

example.ja: ちょっと相談乗ってくれない？
example.english: Can I run something by you?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto soudan ni notte kuremasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと相談に乗ってくれませんか？
examplePolite.english: Could I ask your advice on something?

items.freqNote: 乗る #439 (載る #2368 is a different verb).

blocks.label: Favours, sorry and thanks
blocks.rationale: The social-debt phrases: asking a favour, apologising for trouble or worry, telling someone not to fuss, thanking them for their care.
blocks.interference: onegai ga aru (asking) vs onegai o kiku (granting); meiwaku / shinpai o kakeru put something on someone else, while shinpai suru is worrying yourself; ki o tsukau (fuss over others) is not ki o tsukeru (be careful) or ki ni suru (mind).

items.use: Opens a request and usually trails off with n da kedo: chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo... Natives often keep the ga in this one.
items.verbSense: there is; have (things, plans, something to bring up)
items.trap: English 'ask a favour' leads to onegai o kiku, which means granting one; asking opens with onegai ga aru (tanomi ga aru is a blunter twin, mostly heard from men).

example.romaji: chotto onegai ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっとお願いがあるんだけど。
example.english: Can I ask you a favour?

examplePolite.romaji: chotto onegai ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっとお願いがあるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: I have a small favour to ask.

items.freqNote: お願い #258 mostly counts onegai (shimasu) as 'please'; aru #21.
items.notes: hanashi ga aru n da kedo = I need to talk to you.

items.use: Mostly in apologies: meiwaku kakete gomen (sorry for the trouble), meiwaku kaketakunai (I don't want to be a burden). Bare meiwaku da means 'what a nuisance'.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, put a burden on someone
items.trap: English 'cause' leads to okosu: mondai o okosu is fine for causing an incident, but meiwaku o okosu doesn't work; trouble you put on others is kakeru (meiwaku suru means you are the one being bothered).
partners: tesuu (bother: otesuu o okake shimasu, polite/business)

example.ja: 迷惑かけてごめんね。
example.english: Sorry for all the trouble.

examplePolite.romaji: gomeiwaku o kakete sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: ご迷惑をかけてすみません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry for the trouble.

items.freqNote: kakeru: kana かける #244 pools every sense (call, put on, spend); 掛ける #2742 listed separately.
items.notes: In business you'll hear the humble gomeiwaku o okake shite sumimasen.

items.use: Said apologetically after you've had people worried: shinpai kakete gomen. Different from shinpai shinaide (don't worry), where the other person is the worrier.
items.verbSense: hang or put something onto something; here, put worry on someone
items.trap: English 'worry you' leads to shinpai suru, which means you are the one worrying; worrying someone else is shinpai o kakeru (shinpai sasete gomen also works).

example.ja: 心配かけてごめんね。
example.english: Sorry I made you worry.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai o kakete sumimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 心配をかけてすみません。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry to have worried you.

items.freqNote: 心配 #210 counts every shinpai use (shinpai da, shinpai suru); kakeru kana #244 pools all senses.

items.use: Hosts and guests say ki o tsukawanakute ii yo or ki o tsukawanaide (don't go to any trouble). About a person, ano hito to iru to ki tsukau means you have to tiptoe around them.
items.verbSense: use, spend; here, spend your attention on others
items.trap: Not ki o tsukeru (be careful): 'don't go to any trouble' is ki o tsukawanaide, and the mix-up gives ki o tsukenaide, 'don't be careful'.
partners: shinkei (nerves: shinkei tsukau = it takes a lot of care, it's nerve-racking)

example.ja: そんな気遣わなくていいよ。
example.english: You don't have to fuss over me like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ki o tsukawanakute ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんなに気を遣わなくていいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't go to any trouble.

items.freqNote: 気 #315. verbRank is 使う #171, which pools all tsukau senses (subtitles often write 気を使う); the 遣う spelling alone is #6992.
items.notes: Also written 気を使う; the noun is kizukai (thoughtfulness).

items.use: Mostly polite and set: kyou kara osewa ni narimasu when you start a stay or a job, osewa ni narimashita (thank you for everything) when you leave a host, job or school. In business you'll hear the humble osewa ni natte orimasu (recognise it, no need to say it). Casual osewa ni natta is used when describing someone who helped you.
items.verbSense: become; here, come to be in someone's care
items.trap: English 'thanks for looking after me' leads to sewa shite kurete arigatou, which fits literal care (nursing you when sick, minding your pet). Friends say iroiro arigatou; to hosts, teachers and colleagues the set thanks is osewa ni narimashita.
partners: gochisou (a treat: be treated to a meal)
yakkai (being a burden: rely on someone)

example.romaji: ano senpai ni wa honto ni osewa ni natta.
example.ja: あの先輩にはほんとにお世話になった。
example.english: That senior really looked out for me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano senpai ni wa hontou ni osewa ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの先輩には本当にお世話になりました。
examplePolite.english: That senior really looked after me.

items.freqNote: お世話 #3633 (bare 世話 #2302); naru: kana なる #29.

changelog.change: Casual example now has mou to match 'yet'; akachan partner replaced by kodomo (we're expecting); freqNote says できる #73 pools the 'can do' sense; moved nowhere, stays first in block 1.

Trap corrected: himitsu o mamoru is fine, naisho doesn't take mamoru; listLinks add I-ni-suru.
