reviewSummaries: natural: Strong domain. Every pairing is the one natives actually use. Casual and polite examples sound like real speech with the right particle drops. All listLinks ids exist, and the frequency ranks match the tool. The real errors are a wrong alsoIn pointer (naka-ga-ii → 中 'inside'), two trap texts that misstate a verb (hanasu as 'telling'; adobaisu as 'lecturing'), and partner lists that mix in other senses of kakeru. Possible gaps, unless another domain covers them: orei o iu (thank someone), yakusoku o mamoru / yaburu (keep / break a promise), henji o suru (reply).

traps: The draft is solid. All 14 items are in scope, every listLinks id exists in the versatility list, every rank matches freq.py, and the romaji and examples are natural and follow the convention. Its weak points are traps that call acceptable alternatives wrong (naisho with mamoru, soudan ni noru against adobaisu suru, hanasu called 'telling') or that miss the real use (naka yoku suru; renraku ga torenai), plus three partners in a different sense of the verb (koe o kakeru with denwa, ki o tsukau with atama, kotoba ga tsuujiru with denwa). Possible gaps for this domain, if no other domain covers them: orei o iu (say thanks), yakusoku o mamoru / yaburu (keep or break a promise), and paatii ni deru (attend).

nuance: The domain is solid overall. All 14 items are real, high-value pairings that fit the scope rules. The examples are natural, and every rank and listLinks id checks out against freq.py and the versatility files. The one wrong field is naka-ga-ii's alsoIn: it points to the homophone naka 'inside', against the noun list's rule S2. Four traps or glosses are inaccurate or invented: renraku-o-toru's tamotsu trap, koe-o-kakeru's 'hanasu means telling', the missing 'invite along' sense of koe o kakeru, and the missing renraku ga tsukanai and X to naka ga ii frames. The other fixes are scoring and chunking polish, the main one being to move onegai ga aru into the debt block. Possible gaps, if no other domain covers them: hanashi o kiku (hear me out) and yakusoku o mamoru / yaburu (keep / break a promise).

form: The form is clean. All 14 headwords, polite forms, kana, politeJa and example romaji match their Japanese sound for sound. The masu forms are right, っ→tch is right (kotchi), and slugs, block sizes (5/5/4) and noun/verb/particle fields are consistent. I checked all 28 nounRank/verbRank values with freq.py and all were correct. All 30 listLinks ids exist. One cross-reference is wrong: naka-ga-ii points to 10-list-nouns #23, which is the homophone 中 (inside). The other problems are in the trap texts: koe-o-kakeru misdescribes hanasu, and soudan-ni-noru makes a doubtful claim about adobaisu. There are also a few missing listLinks.

categories.name: Hobbies, sport & games
categories.scope: The "play" problem and other pastimes: piano / gitaa o hiku, fue o fuku, taiko o tataku, sakkaa / tenisu o suru, geemu o suru, e o kaku, uta o utau, shiai ni katsu / makeru, shiai ni deru, chiimu ni hairu, shashin? (media), sanpo o suru?, tsuri o suru?

blocks.label: Hobby verbs
blocks.rationale: Each pastime takes its own verb, and English 'play', 'draw' and 'learn' don't map onto them: suru for sports and games, hiku for instruments, kaku for pictures, narau for lessons with a teacher.
blocks.interference: asobu tempts for sports, games and instruments. After learning sakkaa o suru, keep suru/yaru for naming a hobby (piano yatteru) apart from hiku for the act of playing (piano hikeru?). Keep hiku (play an instrument) apart from kaku (draw a picture) and from its homophone in kaze o hiku, and keep piano hiiteru (plays) apart from piano naratteru (takes lessons).

items.use: Use it for playing any sport, whether regularly or right now. In speech you mostly hear sakkaa shiteru or sakkaa yatteru with o dropped, and yatteta means used to play.
items.verbSense: do; the general verb, and sports and games are things you 'do'
items.trap: Not sakkaa o asobu: asobu means playing around, so a sport takes suru, or casually yaru (sakkaa yatteru).

example.romaji: yasumi no hi wa sakkaa shiteru
example.ja: 休みの日はサッカーしてる
example.english: On my days off I play soccer.

examplePolite.romaji: yasumi no hi wa sakkaa o shitemasu
examplePolite.ja: 休みの日はサッカーをしてます
examplePolite.english: I play soccer on my days off.

items.freqNote: suru #15; yaru #45 is the casual partner for sports. tenisu #9450, yakyuu #3911 and gorufu #5148 take the same verb.

items.english: play games (video games, cards and the like)
items.use: Use it for video games, and for card or party games too. Casually it is geemu shiteru or geemu yatteru with o dropped, and zutto geemu shiteta means you were gaming the whole time.
items.verbSense: do; the general verb, and sports and games are things you 'do'
items.trap: English 'play' pulls toward asobu. For gaming in general, friends say geemu suru or yaru (geemu yatteru). With a specific title, gamers also say kono geemu asonda?, and geemu de asobu (play around with a game) is fine.

example.ja: 昨日ずっとゲームしてた
example.english: I was gaming all day yesterday.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou wa zutto geemu o shitemashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日はずっとゲームをしてました
examplePolite.english: I was playing games all day yesterday.

items.freqNote: yaru #45 is the common casual alternative (geemu yaru); asobu is #674. toranpu #9541 takes the same suru.

items.use: Use it for drawing or painting a picture, as a hobby or right now. Casually o is dropped: e kaiteru means you are drawing now or draw as a hobby.
items.verbSense: draw or paint a picture; it sounds the same as kaku (write)
items.trap: Not e o hiku (hiku draws a line: sen o hiku) or e o nuru (nuru paints a surface). A picture takes kaku whether it is drawn or painted.

example.ja: 絵描くの好き？
example.english: Do you like drawing?

examplePolite.romaji: e o kaku no ga suki desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 絵を描くのが好きですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you like drawing?

items.freqNote: The whole phrase 絵を描く is listed on its own at #4836 (えをかく). Bare 描く (#1092) is filed under the reading えがく, but the subtitles can't separate kaku from egaku, so that rank counts both. 書く (かく, write) #233 is the homophone.
items.notes: egaku is the written reading of the same kanji; in conversation it is kaku.

items.use: Use it for actually playing the instrument. The common forms are piano hikeru? (can you play the piano?) and piano hiiteru (is playing now, or plays regularly). With hikeru, ga often replaces o: piano ga hikeru.
items.verbSense: play a string or keyboard instrument (plucked, bowed or keyed); wind and drums take other verbs
items.trap: Not piano o asobu, and not piano o suru carried over from sakkaa o suru: playing the instrument is hiku (piano hiiteru, piano hikeru?). piano yatteru ('I do piano') only names it as a hobby or lessons, not playing it right now.

example.ja: ピアノ弾ける？
example.english: Can you play the piano?

examplePolite.romaji: piano o hikemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ピアノを弾けますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you play the piano?

items.freqNote: 弾く (ひく) #5832. The kana spelling ひく #2982 mixes every hiku sense, and 引く #1039 is the homophone hiku (pull; kaze o hiku). gitaa #7059 takes the same verb.
items.notes: Wind instruments take fuku (fue o fuku) and drums take tataku (taiko o tataku).

items.use: Use it for lessons with a teacher. naratteru means you take lessons now and naratteta means you used to; o is often dropped.
items.verbSense: learn from a teacher; take lessons in
items.trap: Not piano o benkyou suru (sounds like formal music study), not ressun o toru (a calque of 'take lessons'), and not oboeru (pick up, memorise). Lessons with a teacher are narau (piano naratteta), or piano no ressun o ukeru.

example.ja: 子供の頃ピアノ習ってた
example.english: I took piano lessons as a kid.

examplePolite.romaji: kodomo no koro piano o narattemashita
examplePolite.ja: 子供の頃ピアノを習ってました
examplePolite.english: I took piano lessons as a child.

items.freqNote: 習い事 (lessons taken as a hobby) #15541.
items.notes: osowaru (be taught) is the nearby verb: sensei ni osowatta.

blocks.label: Win, lose, get hooked
blocks.rationale: What happens once you play: you win or lose a match, or get hooked on a game. English says 'win the match' and 'lose the match' with a direct object, and 'into' or 'hooked on' with a preposition, but Japanese marks all three with ni.
blocks.interference: katsu and makeru both take ni, never o, for the match and for the opponent alike (Kankoku ni katta). makeru (lose a contest) is not nakusu (lose an object). hamaru also takes ni, not o.

items.use: Use it about any match or game you played or watched. It is mostly past tense (katta, or kateta for managed to win). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic and katta stands alone (kinou no shiai, katta yo). Keep ni when the match follows straight on: shiai ni katta.
items.verbSense: win; beat (both the contest and the opponent take ni)
items.trap: Not shiai o katsu: English 'win the game' takes an object, but Japanese wins at it with ni. shiai de katsu (win in the match) is also fine. The same ni marks who you beat: Kankoku ni katta = we beat Korea (not Kankoku o).

example.ja: 昨日の試合、勝ったよ
example.english: We won yesterday's match.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai ni kachimashita yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に勝ちましたよ
examplePolite.english: We won yesterday's match.

items.freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni katsu.
items.notes: English 'win' is wider: win a prize = shou o morau / toru; win the lottery = takarakuji ga ataru.

items.use: It is mostly past tense: maketa, or makechatta (lost, sadly; makechaimashita among colleagues). In speech the match is usually said first as the topic (kinou no shiai, makechatta), and the team goes unsaid. Otherwise keep ni: shiai ni maketa.
items.verbSense: lose a contest; be beaten
items.trap: Not shiai o nakusu: nakusu is losing an object. A contest is makeru with ni, never o; shiai de makeru is also fine. The same ni marks who beat you: Kankoku ni maketa = we lost to Korea.

example.ja: 昨日の試合、負けちゃった
example.english: Ugh, we lost yesterday's match.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou no shiai ni makemashita
examplePolite.ja: 昨日の試合に負けました
examplePolite.english: We lost yesterday's match.

items.freqNote: 勝負 (contest) #1203 takes the same ni makeru.

items.english: be hooked on games; be really into games
items.use: Use it for what you are into right now. It is almost always hamatteru (am hooked), as in saikin X ni hamatteru; hamatta means got hooked. It works with any hobby.
items.verbSense: fit snugly into, get stuck in; hence get hooked on
items.trap: English has no verb for being into something, so learners fall back on suki desu. suki is fine but only says you like it in general; for a current craze natives say X ni hamatteru, with ni, never o.

example.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってる
example.english: I'm hooked on this game lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin kono geemu ni hamattemasu
examplePolite.ja: 最近このゲームにハマってます
examplePolite.english: I've been hooked on this game lately.

items.freqNote: はまる #3789 and ハマる #4047 are one word in two spellings. The subtitles count them separately, so real use is higher than either rank.
items.notes: Colloquial but mainstream (dictionaries mark this sense as slang, and the katakana shows it): fine in casual and friendly polite talk; in a formal setting say X ni kyoumi ga arimasu. Milder: X ni kyoumi ga aru (interested in). Stronger: X ni muchuu ni natteru (completely absorbed in). hamatta also means got stuck: juutai ni hamatta (got stuck in traffic).

changelog.change: Rationale no longer claims every pastime is 'play or do' in English; interference limits asobu to sports, games and instruments and names the suru/yaru-vs-hiku clash (natural, traps, nuance).

Rationale reframed by meaning (what happens once you play) and corrected: 'into'/'hooked on' are prepositions, not direct objects. Interference adds that ni also marks the opponent. Moving hamaru into Hobby verbs (nuance, major) was not applied: with no new items allowed, it would leave a 2-item block.

Trap rewritten (traps, major): geemu o asobu is not 'off in chat'; gamers say kono geemu asonda? about a title. English gloss widened to 'play games (video games, cards and the like)'. Examples moved off the shared frame to kinou zutto geemu shiteta / kinou wa zutto geemu o shitemashita. Cut (nuance only) not applied: one reviewer.

Examples moved off the shared frame to e kaku no suki? / e o kaku no ga suki desu ka?, and D-suki added to listLinks. freqNote now says #1092 counts every 描く (kaku and egaku); verified with freq.py that no かく entry exists, so verbRank 1092 is kept (form and nuance) rather than nulled (natural). Use field updated, since the example now shows the suki? frame. contrastGroup set to hobby-verbs to match its block.

verbSense fixed to cover bowed violin (traps, major). Trap now also names piano o suru carried over from sakkaa o suru, and says piano yatteru only names the hobby. H-suru added to listLinks. Examples changed to piano hikeru? / piano o hikemasu ka?. Use field notes that ga often replaces o with hikeru.

contrastGroup set to hobby-verbs (all four reviewers). Trap adds the ressun o toru calque and oboeru, plus piano no ressun o ukeru. H-oboeru and H-toru added to listLinks. trapRisk kept at 4, because English 'learn' does push toward benkyou suru or oboeru.

Use no longer says ni is 'often dropped': it now describes the match said first as a topic, and says to keep ni otherwise (nuance, major). Trap adds that ni marks the opponent (Kankoku ni katta). verbSense covers the opponent too. Notes added for prize and lottery 'win'.

Use rewritten to describe topicalisation instead of ni-drop, and mentions makechaimashita. Trap adds Kankoku ni maketa. Casual English is now 'Ugh, we lost...' to carry the chatta regret. examplePolite changed to the plain kinou no shiai ni makemashita (form, nuance).

trapRisk 5→3 (natural, traps, nuance). Trap rewritten: suki is fine but general, and the real slip is the particle (ni, never o). English is now the state ('be hooked on / be really into games'). flags set to ["slang"] for the colloquial sense, because the schema has no 'colloquial' value; notes explain it is mainstream. Notes fix 'X ni muchuu' to X ni muchuu ni natteru and add the 'got stuck' sense (juutai ni hamatta).
Coverage additions (shiai ni deru, jimu ni kayou, bu/bukatsu ni hairu) not applied: the brief says never add items. Flag them for a later pass.

reviewSummaries: natural: This is a strong domain. All eight pairings are the ones a Tokyo speaker actually uses (suru, kaku, hiku, narau, ni katsu, ni makeru, ni hamaru), every example sentence is natural, and the polite versions keep the meaning. I checked every rank against freq.py and every listLinks id against the versatility files, and all of them match. No item should be cut, and nothing here is wrong or misleading. The fixes are trap and use wording, one rank taken from a different reading (e o kaku), a missing colloquial flag on hamaru, and coverage: shiai ni deru is the clearest missing high-trap item, and jimu ni kayou and bu ni hairu are worth adding.

traps: The domain is solid. I checked every rank against freq.py and all match; listLinks ids exist, and alsoIn is correctly empty (none of the nouns are in 10-list-nouns or vocab-trainer). Romaji and polite forms are clean, and every partner takes the same verb. There are three trap-truth problems: piano-o-hiku's verbSense excludes bowed violin, geemu-o-suru overstates that geemu o asobu is off in chat, and geemu-ni-hamaru implies suki desu isn't native. The rest is polish: ni-drop wording, block rationale claims, repeated example frames, an unset contrast group, and two worthwhile gap items (shiai ni deru, bukatsu ni hairu). Nothing needs cutting.

nuance: The Japanese is natural throughout. All romaji, ja/kana and polite pairs are correct. I re-ran every frequency rank and each matches the frequency tool, and every listLinks id exists in the versatility files. The main problems are structural. Block 2 is grouped by particle, not meaning (hamaru sits with win/lose). The use lines for katsu/makeru wrongly say ni is 'often dropped' when the examples actually show the match said first as a topic. hamaru's trapRisk of 5 is inflated. geemu-o-suru duplicates sakkaa-o-suru's pairing.
Fix: cut geemu-o-suru and move hamaru into Hobby verbs. Rebuild block 2 as 'Matches' with shiai ni deru (H-deru) and optionally X-bu ni hairu (H-hairu). Vary the four identical 'yasumi no hi wa X -teru' example frames so the audio cards stay distinct.

form: The form side is clean. Romaji follows the convention throughout: long vowels as spelled (sakkaa, geemu), っ doubling, auxiliaries joined (hiiteru, naratteta, makechatta, hamatteru). Every kana reading, masu conjugation and politeJa form is correct, every example's romaji matches its ja word for word (dropped particles included), and the noun/particle/verb fields agree with the headwords. Slugs are unique, the blocks hold 5 and 3 items, and all listLinks ids exist in versatility-items.txt (H-suru, H-yaru, H-asobu, H-benkyou-suru, H-oshieru, D-suki). The empty alsoIn fields are correct: none of these nouns appear in 10-list-nouns or utility-vocab. All 30-plus ranks checked against freq.py match exactly. The only problems are minor: one missing contrastGroup, an incomplete muchuu phrase, a missing colloquial flag, a -chaimashita polite model, and two wording fixes.

categories.name: Senses & mind
categories.scope: Perceiving and noticing: oto ga suru, nioi ga suru, aji ga suru (if not food), koe ga suru, kanji ga suru, samuke ga suru (if not body), yume o miru, ki ga tsuku (notice), ki ni iru (like, be pleased with), kyoumi ga aru, kioku ga aru?, me ni hairu?, oto ga kikoeru, me ga sameru (if not home), kotae ga wakaru?

blocks.label: Likes and reactions
blocks.rationale: How you react to something: it feels nice, it's gross, you love it, you want to know more.
blocks.interference: ki ni itta (I love it) and ki ni natta (it bugged me, I got curious) sound almost the same. kimochi warui is nausea or disgust; guai ga warui is feeling unwell. ki ni iru is liking a thing you have or tried; kyoumi ga aru is wanting to know more about it.

items.use: A reaction to a bath, a breeze, a massage or a stretch, almost always said as one word without ga: aa, kimochi ii. kimochi ii ne asks the other person to agree.
items.verbSense: good, fine; here the feeling is good
items.trap: English 'feel good' covers mood and health, but kimochi ii is only a physical sensation: a bath, a breeze, a massage. For 'I feel good today', say kyou choushi ii or kibun ii. A bath isn't tanoshii (fun) either; it's kimochi ii.
partners: kibun (kibun ga ii: in a good mood)
choushi (choushi ga ii: in good shape)

example.romaji: aa, kaze ga kimochi ii ne.
example.ja: ああ、風が気持ちいいね。
example.english: Ah, the breeze feels nice.

examplePolite.romaji: aa, kaze ga kimochi ii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: ああ、風が気持ちいいですね。
examplePolite.english: Ah, the breeze feels nice, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: Usually said without ga: 気持ちいい #2005 vs 気持ちがいい #13062.
items.notes: Also used for 'satisfying', like a tidy desk or a crisp sound.

items.english: feel queasy, feel nauseous; gross, creepy
items.use: Usually said as one word, kimochi warui. It covers both 'gross/creepy' (a bug, a weird message) and 'I feel queasy' (chotto kimochi warui).
items.verbSense: bad
items.trap: English 'feel sick' covers both nausea and illness, but kimochi warui is only nausea or disgust. With a cold or the flu, say guai ga warui; kimochi warui sounds like you're about to throw up. For 'gross', learners say kirai, which only means dislike.
partners: guai (guai ga warui: feel unwell, not queasy)
kibun (kibun ga warui: feel unwell; be in a bad mood)

example.ja: 飲みすぎてちょっと気持ち悪い。
example.english: I drank too much, I feel a bit sick.

examplePolite.romaji: nomisugite, chotto kimochi ga warui desu.
examplePolite.ja: 飲みすぎて、ちょっと気持ちが悪いです。
examplePolite.english: I drank too much, I feel a bit sick.

items.freqNote: Usually said as one word: 気持ち悪い #1740 (気持ちが悪い #23002). The slang clip キモい is #4580.
items.notes: About a person, kimochi warui means creepy and is insulting, and the slang clip kimoi (キモい), which only means gross or creepy, is ruder still. To say someone looks unwell, say guai warui sou.

items.use: Nearly always past or -te ru: ki ni itta (I love it, about a gift, purchase or place) and ki ni itteru (I really like it, I've taken to it). The thing you like takes ga or o, and casual speech drops both: kore ki ni itta. Giving a gift: ki ni itte kureru to ii na (I hope you like it).
items.verbSense: enter, go in (an old reading of hairu); the thing gets into your heart
items.trap: English says 'I love it' in the present, but Japanese says the past, ki ni itta. iru here conjugates like hairu (itta, irimasu), not like iru 'be' (ita, imasu).

example.ja: これすごい気に入った！
example.english: I love this!

examplePolite.romaji: kore, sugoku ki ni irimashita.
examplePolite.ja: これ、すごく気に入りました。
examplePolite.english: I really love this.

items.freqNote: 入る read iru (#63142) survives almost only inside this phrase; the whole expression 気に入る is #889, and the noun お気に入り (favourite) #3558.
items.notes: The negative ki ni iranai (I don't like it) is mostly said about someone's attitude and sounds combative: ano taido ga ki ni iranai. okiniiri means favourite: kore, okiniiri na no.

items.use: The topic takes ni, and casual speech often drops ga: X ni kyoumi aru? The blunt reply kyoumi nai (not interested) is very common.
items.verbSense: there is, exist; here you have (an) interest
items.trap: For 'I'm interested', learners say watashi wa omoshiroi, which means 'I'm funny', or kyoumi desu. Japanese says the interest exists, and the topic takes ni: X ni kyoumi ga aru. X ga omoshiroi (X is interesting) is also fine, but it describes the thing, not you.

example.ja: アニメとか興味ある？
example.english: Are you into anime or anything?

examplePolite.romaji: anime toka ni kyoumi ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: アニメとかに興味がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you interested in anime or anything like that?

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the ga-aru expression because its tokenizer splits it. 興味ない is #1906 and 興味を持つ #4531.
items.notes: kyoumi o motsu (take an interest in) is the version for an interest someone develops: anime ni kyoumi o motta.

blocks.label: Noticing things
blocks.rationale: Ways of perceiving: a smell or sound 'does' (ga suru), a sound reaches you (kikoeru), your attention catches on something (ki ga tsuku).
blocks.interference: oto ga suru means there's a noise, oto ga kikoeru means I can hear it, and kiku means listening on purpose. ki ga tsuku (notice) sounds almost like ki o tsukeru (be careful).

items.use: Said the moment you notice a smell, usually without ga: ii nioi suru! or nanka hen na nioi shinai? To name the source, add no: gasu no nioi ga suru (I smell gas).
items.verbSense: do; here, be perceived: a smell, sound, taste or feeling makes itself felt
items.trap: For 'I smell something', learners use kagu, but kagu means sniffing on purpose. The smell is the subject: nanka nioi ga suru. ii nioi! on its own is also fine.

example.ja: なんかいい匂いするね。
example.english: Something smells good.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika ii nioi ga shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何かいい匂いがしますね。
examplePolite.english: Something smells good, doesn't it.

items.freqNote: nounRank is the kana spelling におい; 匂い is #2171 and 臭い (bad smell) #7168. The expression 匂いがする is #7128.
items.notes: For a bad smell, natives often just say kusai (it stinks).

items.english: hear a noise, there's a sound
items.use: The normal way to report a noise, with the noise as the subject, not you: nanka oto shita (I heard something). Use the past shita for a sound just now. ga is usually dropped.
items.verbSense: do; here, be perceived: a sound, smell or taste makes itself felt
items.trap: For 'I heard a noise' just now, learners say oto o kiita. That works when you tell the story later, but in the moment natives make the sound the subject: oto shita, or oto ga kikoeta.

example.ja: 今なんか音しなかった？
example.english: Did you just hear something?

examplePolite.romaji: ima nanika oto ga shimasen deshita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今何か音がしませんでしたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you just hear a noise?

items.freqNote: The expression 音がする is #5813.
items.notes: Often comes with a sound word: gatan tte oto shita (there was a thud).

items.use: A phone and video-call staple: kikoeru? / kikoenai. The thing heard takes ga, which is usually dropped. For a person's voice, use koe: koe ga kikoenai.
items.verbSense: be audible, reach your ears without effort (unlike kiku, listen)
items.trap: For 'Can you hear me?', learners say kiiteru?, which means 'Are you listening?'. The question is kikoeru?: kiku is deliberate, kikoeru just happens. The sound is the subject: oto ga kikoeru, not oto o kikoeru (mieru works the same way).

example.ja: 音小さくて聞こえない。
example.english: It's too quiet, I can't hear it.

examplePolite.romaji: oto ga chiisakute kikoemasen.
examplePolite.ja: 音が小さくて聞こえません。
examplePolite.english: The sound is too low, I can't hear it.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for 音が聞こえる, so the noun and verb are ranked separately.
items.notes: Sight has the same pair: mieru (be visible) vs miru (look).

items.use: Mostly past: ki ga tsuita (I noticed, I realised) and zenzen ki ga tsukanakatta (I didn't notice at all). The thing noticed takes ni: machigai ni ki ga tsuita. ki ga tsuitara is the everyday 'before I knew it': ki ga tsuitara asa datta (next thing I knew, it was morning).
items.verbSense: stick, get attached; here your attention catches on something
items.trap: For 'I noticed', learners say mita or wakatta. The phrase is ki ga tsuita. Keep it apart from ki o tsukeru (be careful), which sounds almost the same.

example.ja: ごめん、全然気つかなかった。
example.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, zenzen ki ga tsukimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、全然気が付きませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

items.freqNote: verbRank is 付く; kana つく (#355) mixes several tsuku verbs. The list also holds the whole expression, 気が付く #2832 and 気がつく #3139. The one-word kizuku ranks higher: 気付く #1083, 気づく #1239.
items.notes: The one-word kizuku means the same and is even more common in drama speech: zenzen kizukanakatta.

blocks.label: Mood and energy
blocks.rationale: Talking about your energy and mood: getting motivated, cheering someone up, getting stressed, getting hyped.
blocks.interference: With yaruki ga deru the energy comes out by itself (deru); with genki o dasu you bring it out (dasu). Mood goes up or down (tenshon ga agaru / sagaru), while stress piles up (tamaru). tenshon means hype, not tension, which is kinchou.

items.use: Mostly said in the negative about yourself: yaruki denai (I can't be bothered, no motivation). yaruki aru means keen or motivated and is often said about others; asked as yaruki aru no?, it's a reproach: are you even trying?
items.verbSense: come out, appear
items.trap: Learners look for an adjective for 'motivated', but everyday Japanese has none. The will to do it 'comes out' (deru): yaruki ga denai. yaruki ga aru (be keen) and mochibeeshon ga agaru are also fine.

example.ja: 今日全然やる気出ない。
example.english: I can't get motivated at all today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa zenzen yaruki ga demasen.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は全然やる気が出ません。
examplePolite.english: I just can't get motivated today.

items.freqNote: The list has no entry for the whole phrase, so the noun and verb are ranked separately.
items.notes: yaruki is literally 'do-feeling', from yaru + ki.

items.use: Almost always the request genki dashite (cheer up!), said to someone who is down. The intransitive genki ga deru means feel better or perk up: kore tabetara genki deta.
items.verbSense: put out, bring out
items.trap: For 'cheer up', learners say ganbatte, which means 'hang in there' and can feel like pressure to someone who's sad. genki ni natte is said mostly to someone ill (get well). For someone down right now, the set phrase is genki dashite.

example.ja: 大丈夫だよ、元気出して。
example.english: It's okay, cheer up.

examplePolite.romaji: daijoubu desu yo, genki o dashite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大丈夫ですよ、元気を出してください。
examplePolite.english: It's okay, please cheer up.

items.freqNote: The expression 元気を出す is #13529, the request 元気出して #7639, and the intransitive 元気が出る #8964.
items.notes: Pairs with genki ga nai (feeling down), which is in the describing-people set. To a superior, genki o dashite kudasai can sound presumptuous, like ganbatte kudasai.

items.politeJa: ストレスが溜まります
items.use: Usually in -te ru for how you are now: sutoresu tamatteru (I'm stressed out). Getting rid of it is sutoresu kaishou, and blowing off steam is sutoresu hassan: karaoke de sutoresu hassan shita.
items.verbSense: pile up, accumulate
items.trap: For 'I'm stressed', learners turn 'stress' into a verb: sutoresu shiteru, which isn't Japanese. Stress piles up: sutoresu tamatteru. sutoresu o kanjiru (feel stress) and shigoto ga sutoresu (work stresses me out) are also fine.

example.ja: 最近ストレス溜まってる。
example.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin sutoresu ga tamattemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近ストレスが溜まってます。
examplePolite.english: Stress has been piling up lately.

items.freqNote: verbRank is the kana spelling たまる (#1650); 溜まる is #16850. The whole phrase has no entry.
items.notes: The transitive is tameru, as in okane o tameru: sutoresu tamenai you ni ne (don't let the stress build up).

items.politeJa: テンションが上がります
items.use: For being hyped right now: tenshon agaru! or tenshon agatte kita. The opposite is tenshon sagaru (get bummed out), and tenshon takai means hyper. It's an informal word: fine with friends and coworkers, but not in formal speech.
items.verbSense: go up, rise
items.trap: For 'I'm excited', learners say koufun shiteru, which sounds worked-up and, in some contexts, sexual. Say tenshon agaru for hyped right now, and tanoshimi or wakuwaku suru for a plan. False friend: tenshon is energy or mood, not tension.

example.ja: やばい、テンション上がってきた！
example.english: Oh man, I'm getting so hyped!

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu ne, tenshon ga agatte kimashita!
examplePolite.ja: いいですね、テンションが上がってきました！
examplePolite.english: This is great, I'm getting excited!

items.freqNote: The phrase entry テンションが上がる is #30223 because the tokenizer usually splits it.
items.notes: English 'tension' or 'nervousness' is kinchou (kinchou suru, get nervous).

changelog.change: Trap rewritten around the real interference (English 'feel good' for mood/health -> choushi ii / kibun ii), tanoshii kept as a short aside; added kibun and choushi partners; casual example now keeps ga (kaze ga kimochi ii ne); added D-tanoshii link; contrastGroup set to null because kimochi-ga-warui moved into the cross-domain guai-kimochi-warui group.

english now 'feel queasy, feel nauseous; gross, creepy'; trap says kimochi warui is nausea/disgust only and points to guai ga warui for a cold or flu; partners guai and kibun added; notes warn that kimochi warui about a person is insulting (kimoi ruder still) and give guai warui sou for 'looks unwell'; contrastGroup changed to guai-kimochi-warui to match body's guai-ga-warui. Flags left empty: the schema's flag enum has no 'insulting about a person' value, so the warning sits in notes.

use: ki ni itteru glossed 'I really like it, I've taken to it' (not 'favourite'), the liked thing takes ga or o, gift line ki ni itte kureru to ii na added; notes: ki ni iranai framed as combative, okiniiri = favourite added; freqNote adds お気に入り #3558 (verified).

Trap rewritten: real errors are watashi wa omoshiroi ('I'm funny') and kyoumi desu, X ga omoshiroi noted as fine; verbSense no longer reads as 'interest in you'; H-motsu linked; notes reworded with an example (anime ni kyoumi o motta). The 'kyoumi nai is blunt' flag was not added because the flag enum has no fitting value; use already says it.
use: 'kusai nioi' replaced by 'hen na nioi'; polite example uses nanika instead of nanka; contrastGroup renamed sense-ga-suru -> sense-perception.
Trap no longer calls oto o kiita wrong: fine when recounting, unnatural in the moment; trapRisk 5 -> 4; contrastGroup renamed to sense-perception.

Trap adds the particle error (oto ga kikoeru, not oto o kikoeru); H-miru linked; contrastGroup renamed to sense-perception. The suggested koe polite example was not applied because it would break the oto pairing with the casual example.

use adds ki ga tsuitara ('before I knew it'); casual example drops ga (zenzen ki tsukanakatta); notes say kizuku is even more common, and freqNote adds 気づく #1239; H-miru linked. contrastGroup ki-tsuku-tsukau kept because ki-o-tsukau is on the keep list for another domain, so it should carry the same group.
Trap now says 'everyday Japanese has none'; use adds the reproach yaruki aru no? (are you even trying?).

Trap rewritten: ganbatte can feel like pressure, and genki ni natte is said mostly to someone ill (not wrong); polite example keeps o (genki o dashite kudasai); freqNote adds 元気が出る #8964; I-ku-naru linked; notes add that genki o dashite kudasai can sound presumptuous to a superior (in notes because the flag enum has no fitting value).

Trap targets the calque sutoresu shiteru and adds shigoto ga sutoresu as fine; examples' English no longer adds intensifiers ('Stress has been piling up lately'); use adds sutoresu hassan beside kaishou; notes now read 'don't let the stress build up' instead of 'bottle it up'.
Flag 'slang' added (the schema enum has no 'informal' value); trap adds the koufun shiteru error and wakuwaku suru; commonness 5 -> 4; polite example keeps ga; moved to the end of its block.

Reordered to yaruki-ga-deru, genki-o-dasu, sutoresu-ga-tamaru, tenshon-ga-agaru so deru/dasu sit together and the slangiest item comes last; rationale and interference rewritten to match (agaru/sagaru vs tamaru, tenshon vs kinchou).
Interference rewritten around the real confusions: ki ni itta vs ki ni natta, and kimochi warui vs guai ga warui.

reviewSummaries: natural: The domain is strong. Every pairing is the one natives actually use, most examples sound like real speech, and all the listLinks ids, ranks and the 10-list-nouns pointers check out. The two main problems are the kimochi-ga-warui gloss ('feel sick' should be queasy, with guai ga warui for feeling unwell in general) and the kimochi-ga-ii trap, which misses the real 'I feel good today' interference. The rest is polish: trap wording, missing flags, ki ga tsuitara, and English that adds emphasis the Japanese doesn't have. Possible gaps for this domain: kibun ga ii/warui, aji ga suru, guai ga warui.

traps: The draft is solid. All 12 items are in scope, every listLinks id and alsoIn pointer exists, the frequency ranks match freq.py, the transitive/intransitive pairs (deru/dasu, tamaru/tameru) are labelled correctly, and every partner noun takes the verb in the same sense. The weak point is trap truth. Four traps overclaim or give the wrong error: kimochi warui is glossed 'feel sick' (pushes cold/flu misuse), oto o kiita is called wrong though kiku also means hear, X ga omoshiroi is not an error, and genki ni natte is acceptable. These need rewriting before shipping. Possible gaps in this domain: aji ga suru, kanji ga suru, and kibun/guai ga warui if the body domain doesn't cover them.

nuance: The draft is solid. Every nounRank, verbRank and freqNote figure matches freq.py, every listLinks id exists, the alsoIn pointers (#74 nioi, #113 oto) are correct, and the examples are natural casual and polite speech in the app's romaji spelling. The main gaps are meaning and register. kimochi warui is glossed ambiguously as 'feel sick', and its contrast with guai ga warui is split across the senses and body domains. Two flags are missing: tenshon is casual, and kimochi warui insults when said about a person. ki ga tsuitara ('before I knew it') is missing, and the tenshon trap leaves out koufun shiteru. Nothing needs cutting. Note that the keep-list placed kanji-ga-suru and kigen-ga-warui near this domain, but neither appears in this draft; confirm they landed in another domain.

form: The data is clean overall and nothing is fatal. All 21 listLinks ids exist, both alsoIn pointers (10-list-nouns #74 nioi, #113 oto) are correct, and all 22 noun/verb ranks plus the 15 phrase ranks cited in freqNotes match the frequency tool. Romaji, kana, polite forms and examples line up word for word, slugs are unique, and every block has 4 items. Remaining fixes: tenshon-ga-agaru needs an informal flag, some polite examples keep the particle and others drop it, the kizuku frequency claim is understated, and a few use/trap/notes lines overstate or leave something out.

categories.name: Describing people
categories.scope: The X ga ADJ way of describing someone, which English says with one word: se ga takai / hikui (tall / short), atama ga ii (smart), me ga warui / ii (eyesight), mimi ga ii?, ashi ga hayai (fast runner), kami ga nagai / mijikai, kao ga chiisai?, karada ga yowai (often ill), genki ga nai (low), toshi ue / toshi shita?

blocks.label: Height, age, hair
blocks.rationale: The physical basics you mention when describing someone: how tall they are, how old they are compared with you, and a new haircut.
blocks.interference: Short is se ga hikui, never mijikai. Older is toshi ga ue (toshiue), not furui, which on a person means long-standing or old-fashioned. Kami kitta (cut) is not kita (wore).

items.use: The plain way to call someone tall: ano hito, se takai ne, with ga dropped in casual speech. Before a noun, ga often becomes no: se no takai hito (a tall person).
items.verbSense: takai: high; also expensive
items.trap: Not kare wa takai: takai on its own is for things (high, expensive), so a person's height needs se ga takai.

example.romaji: uchi no ani, se takai n da.
example.ja: うちの兄、背高いんだ。
example.english: My big brother's tall.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no ani wa se ga takai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちの兄は背が高いんです。
examplePolite.english: My older brother is tall.

items.freqNote: 背 (せ) #5388, plus 背 (せい) #39147 for the sei ga takai variant. The bare noun ranks low because se almost only occurs inside this phrase. 身長 shinchou #4523.
items.notes: Sei ga takai is a common spoken variant. The 'tall' sense of takai applies to a person only inside this phrase. For an exact height, use shinchou: shinchou nan senchi? (how tall are you?).

items.use: The opposite of se ga takai, often said about yourself: watashi, se hikui kara... Casual speech drops ga.
items.verbSense: hikui: low, not high
items.trap: Not se ga mijikai: in Japanese height is high or low, so short is hikui. Mijikai is for length and duration, never height.

example.romaji: watashi, se hikui kara, ue no tana todokanai n da.
example.ja: 私、背低いから、上の棚届かないんだ。
example.english: I'm short, so I can't reach the top shelf.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi wa se ga hikui node, ue no tana ni todokanai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 私は背が低いので、上の棚に届かないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm short, so I can't reach the top shelf.

items.notes: Casual speech also says chiisai (chiisai hito); chibi is teasing slang.

items.use: Mostly heard in the past tense with o dropped: kami kitta? (did you get a haircut?), a stock small-talk line. For the salon trip itself, say kami kiri ni iku (go get a haircut).
items.verbSense: kiru: cut (with a blade or scissors)
items.trap: English 'get a haircut' suggests kitte morau or the dictionary word sanpatsu suru (old-fashioned). Kitte morau works, but natives just say kami kitta (or katto shita), even when a stylist did it.

example.ja: あれ、髪切った？
example.english: Oh, did you get a haircut?

examplePolite.romaji: are, kami kirimashita?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、髪切りました？
examplePolite.english: Oh, did you get your hair cut?

items.freqNote: 髪 #1752 (髪の毛 kami no ke #3658); 切る #546; カット #3084; 散髪 sanpatsu #24840.
items.notes: Don't mix it up with kiru 'wear' (fuku o kiru): cut is kitta / kirimasu, wear is kita / kimasu. By ear, cut drops after ki (KI-tta) and wear is flat (kita). Kami (hair) sounds the same as kami 'paper' (10-list-nouns #14), so kami o kiru can also mean cut paper. Context decides, and kami no ke makes 'hair' explicit.

items.use: Mostly heard as the fused compound toshiue (ano hito, toshiue da yo). The full phrase usually carries a number of years: toshi ga mittsu ue (three years older), or just mittsu ue. Younger is toshi ga shita, or toshishita.
items.verbSense: ue: above, higher (a noun, not an adjective)
items.trap: Not furui: on a person, furui means long-standing or old-fashioned (kare no hou ga furui = he's been here longer), not older in age. 'Older than me' is watashi yori toshi ga ue, or just toshiue.

example.romaji: suzuki-san, watashi yori toshi ga mittsu ue na n da.
example.ja: 鈴木さん、私より年が三つ上なんだ。
example.english: Suzuki's three years older than me.

examplePolite.romaji: suzuki-san wa watashi yori toshi ga mittsu ue na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 鈴木さんは私より年が三つ上なんです。
examplePolite.english: Suzuki is three years older than me.

items.freqNote: 年 (とし) #1354; 上 (うえ) #321. The compound 年上 toshiue is #3068 and 年下 toshishita is #4076. Commonness rates the full phrase toshi ga ue; the fused toshiue is said more often.
items.notes: To say someone is getting old, use toshi o toru (toshi totta naa = I'm getting old; 年取る #8003), not furuku naru, which is for things.

blocks.label: Traits, abilities, mood
blocks.rationale: Each names a quality as noun + ga + ii / warui / aru / nai, where English uses one adjective or a short phrase (smart, poor eyesight, athletic, popular, down).
blocks.interference: Atama, me and undou shinkei share the X ga ii / warui frame; only the noun changes. 'Athletic' is not undou ga jouzu: jouzu is for skills you practise (e ga jouzu). Ii becomes yokatta / yokunai, never iikatta. Atama ii (smart) is one sound away from atama itai (headache).

items.use: The everyday 'smart': ano hito, atama ii ne, with ga dropped in casual speech. Ii conjugates from yoi, so the past is atama yokatta and the negative is atama yokunai.
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not sumaato (in Japanese that means slim or sleek): 'smart' is atama ga ii. Kashikoi is also correct but less everyday, and often said to children or pets.

example.ja: 田中さん、頭いいよね。
example.english: Tanaka's smart, right?

examplePolite.romaji: tanaka-san wa atama ga ii desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 田中さんは頭がいいですよね。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka is smart, right?

items.freqNote: 頭 #375; いい #24 (良い #1474, よい #120). The fused casual form 頭いい appears as its own entry at #7901, which is direct evidence for the phrase. 賢い kashikoi #3471; スマート #11064.
items.notes: Atama ga warui is fine about yourself but rude about others.

items.use: Said about yourself to explain glasses or squinting: me warui kara... Casual speech drops ga. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta.
items.verbSense: warui: bad, in poor condition
items.trap: Not warui me o motteru ('have bad eyes'): Japanese makes the eyes the subject, me ga warui. English 'short-sighted' has no everyday one-word match either: kinshi and shiryoku ga warui are the terms you hear at eye exams. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta, not warui ni natta.

example.romaji: me warui kara, megane nai to nanimo mienai n da.
example.ja: 目悪いから、メガネないと何も見えないんだ。
example.english: My eyesight's bad, so I can't see a thing without my glasses.

examplePolite.romaji: me ga warui node, megane ga nai to nanimo mienai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 目が悪いので、メガネがないと何も見えないんです。
examplePolite.english: My eyesight is poor, so I can't see anything without glasses.

items.freqNote: 目 #216; 悪い #139; 視力 shiryoku #11362; 近視 kinshi #61905.
items.notes: The opposite, me ga ii, means good eyesight. 'Has a good eye' (for people or things) is miru me ga aru.

items.kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
items.use: The everyday 'athletic, coordinated': ano hito, undou shinkei ii yo ne. The opposite, undou shinkei ga nai, is common self-deprecation, and so is undou onchi (uncoordinated).
items.verbSense: ii: good
items.trap: Not asurechikku (in Japanese that's an obstacle-course playground): say undou shinkei ga ii. Supootsu ga tokui (good at sports) is also natural.

example.romaji: otouto, undou shinkei ii kara, supootsu nara nandemo dekiru yo.
example.ja: 弟、運動神経いいから、スポーツなら何でもできるよ。
example.english: My little brother's athletic, so he's good at any sport.

examplePolite.romaji: otouto wa undou shinkei ga ii node, supootsu nara nandemo dekimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 弟は運動神経がいいので、スポーツなら何でもできますよ。
examplePolite.english: My younger brother is athletic, so he can do any sport.

items.freqNote: 運動神経 #12050 as a whole compound. It occurs almost only in this phrase and in undou shinkei ga nai / warui, so the phrase is more common than the rank suggests. 運動音痴 undou onchi #37364.
items.notes: Literally 'motor nerves are good'.

items.use: For people, shops, shows and products: ano mise, ninki aru yo ne. Casual speech drops ga, and also says ninki da yo or sugoi ninki da yo. 'Popular with X' is X ni ninki ga aru, very popular is ninki ga takai, and unpopular is ninki nai. Before a noun: ninki no aru mise, or just ninki no mise (a popular shop).
items.verbSense: aru: there is; have (things, qualities)
items.trap: Not popyuraa: in Japanese it's for things that are widely known or standard (popyuraa na kyoku), never for a person. A person or shop that people like ninki ga aru.

example.romaji: ano sensei, seito ni ninki aru yo.
example.ja: あの先生、生徒に人気あるよ。
example.english: That teacher's popular with the students.

examplePolite.romaji: ano sensei wa seito ni ninki ga arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの先生は生徒に人気がありますよ。
examplePolite.english: That teacher is popular with the students.

items.freqNote: 人気 #1303; ある #21. Ninkimono (#5320, 'a popular person') is a related noun, noted only; モテる #2224; ポピュラー #37551.
items.notes: Popular with the opposite sex is the single verb moteru.

items.use: Said when you notice someone seems low: genki nai ne, dou shita no? Casual speech drops ga. In polite speech genki nai desu ne is just as common as genki ga arimasen. The opposite is genki ga aru (full of energy).
items.verbSense: nai: there isn't, have none (negative of aru)
items.trap: Not kanashii (sad, too strong), and not genki ja nai, which leans toward 'unwell': for 'you seem down', say genki nai ne. If something has upset them, ochikonderu? (are you feeling down?) is also natural.

example.romaji: genki nai ne. dou shita no?
example.ja: 元気ないね。どうしたの？
example.english: You seem down. What's up?

examplePolite.romaji: genki nai desu ne. dou shita n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 元気ないですね。どうしたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You seem down. Is something wrong?

items.freqNote: 元気 #297; ない #43 (無い #6807); 落ち込む ochikomu #1647.
items.notes: Here genki is a noun (energy), not the adjective genki da. Genki dashite (cheer up) is the usual response. Keep apart: genki nai = low, flat; kigen warui = grumpy; kibun warui = feel sick; guai warui = unwell.

reviewSummaries: natural: All nine pairings are the ones a Tokyo speaker would naturally use, and the casual examples drop particles the way natives do. All listLinks ids and alsoIn pointers exist, and the frequency ranks check out against freq.py. Three things need fixing: toshi-ga-ue's examples never use the headword (and casual 'kare' reads as 'my boyfriend'), the me-ga-warui note wrongly says me ga ii means 'has a good eye for things', and genki-ga-nai's contrastGroup has no other member and misses kigen/kibun/guai ga warui. Two pairs of examples copy each other's frame, and the domain leaves out high-trap items such as ni niteru, se ga nobiru and kami o nobasu.

traps: This is a solid domain. All 9 items are in scope (none are figurative idioms or guessable verbs), and every listLink id, alsoIn pointer and frequency rank checks out against the source files. The examples are natural and the romaji follows the convention. There are four inaccurate claims about loanwords and alternative words to fix: furui on people (long-standing, not 'only things'), popyuraa (exists, but only for things), me ga ii ('good eye' is miru me ga aru), and the toshi-ga-ue examples, which never say the headword. The rest is polish. Possible additions for this domain: toshi o toru (get old), kami o nobasu or hige o hayasu (grow hair or a beard; sodateru is the trap), and seikaku ga ii (good-natured).

nuance: This is a solid domain. All 9 items are clear in-scope collocations, all listLinks ids exist in the versatility files, and the frequency ranks and alsoIn pointers check out against freq.py and the source files. The use lines name the ga-dropped forms people actually say, and the English loanword traps (sumaato, popyuraa, asurechikku) are accurate. The main faults are in toshi-ga-ue: its examples never say the headword, and 'kare, ... toshiue da yo' reads as 'my boyfriend'. Two high-trap gaps are missing: toshi o toru (get old) and koe ga ookii / takai (loud vs high voice). The 'Traits and mood' block needs relabelling and reordering. The rest are minor: inflated trapRisk on me-ga-warui, and small notes and links.

form: The form checks are clean. All headword, kana, polite and example romaji match the Japanese with no macrons and correct particles, the masu forms are right, all 10 listLinks ids exist, and all 27 frequency ranks I checked match the tool exactly. There are no duplicate slugs and both blocks are 4–5 items. The real problems: the toshi-ga-ue examples never use the headword, the kami-o-kiru card doesn't warn that it sounds the same as 'cut paper' (the learner's only kami is paper), and genki-ga-nai points at a contrast partner that doesn't exist. The rest is polish: near-duplicate example frames, extra words in the English glosses, and inconsistent spacing in a partner.

checks.consNotes:
WHAT I COULD CHECK: Full entries are on disk only for the body domain (/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-main-Developer-Projects-claude-projects/666a0dd4-1c14-46e0-80e1-0fbb2656b52c/scratchpad/body/final.json, 18 items). The other 12 domains were checked from the summary rows in the task only. So check (6), englishVerb, could only be run on body. There every value is a single plain word (take, catch, have, get, give, feel, lie, see, upset, stiff, hurt, sweat, hungry, full, thirsty), so nothing needed changing. Partners, use and notes for the other domains were not visible.

(4) LINKS: All 120 distinct listLinks ids across the 158 items exist in versatility-items.txt (checked with comm against the id column), so no link fixes. Body alsoIn pointers also resolve: 10-list-nouns #29 yoko, #40 atama, #88 kaze, and the vocab-trainer set_ids physical-sensations, body-external, position-nouns, town-places and weather-terms. One link looks wrong but was not changed: c-kaisha-ni-tsutomeru -> E-tame-ni. The E-tame-ni entry's example is "ryokou suru tame ni, chokin shiteru" (saving up), and tsutomeru is neither built on tame ni nor confusable with it. It looks like it belongs on c-okane-o-tameru (tameru / tame ni sound alike). I left it because I couldn't see whether tsutomeru's own example uses tame ni.

(3) CONTRAST GROUPS: Three groups had only one member. sense-ga-suru (aji ga suru only) is the same X-ga-suru perception frame as sense-perception (nioi ga suru, oto ga suru), so I merged it in. play-verbs (ongaku o kakeru only) is the same English-'play' trap as hobby-verbs (sakkaa/geemu o suru, piano o hiku), so I merged it in. ki-phrases (ki o tsukau) and ki-tsuku-tsukau (ki ga tsuku) were each a one-member group for the same ki family, so I unified them as ki-phrases and added ki ni iru (it had no group). The clothing verbs were split across three groups (kiru-haku-nugu, head-face-wear, wear-suru). That kept hazusu apart from tokei/masuku/tebukuro, which also take hazusu, and nugu apart from boushi (boushi o nugu). It also went against the plan to keep the clothing verbs together. I unified all 11 wear and take-off items as wear-verbs; saizu ga au stays without a group. I added genki ga nai (describing) to energy-mood beside genki o dasu (senses), the natural 'genki nai ne / genki dashite' pair. Groups that already spanned domains with one name were fine: take-verbs, guai-kimochi-warui and free-or-busy. The tsuku/tsukeru pair (denki ga tsuku / o tsukeru / o kesu) was already linked, and so were the kakeru/kakaru pairs (kagi, denwa) and kaze ga utsuru / o utsusu.

(1)/(5) ROMAJI: There are no macrons, wo, capitals or kana in any romaji. Loanwords and long vowels are spelled one way everywhere: koohii, suupu, shawaa, meeru, geemu, sakkaa, saizu, konbini, denpa, shinpai, ninki, juuden, tenshon, sutoresu. Contracted state forms are also consistent (tsuiteru, aiteru, kakatteru, chirakatteru, konderu, shimatteru). All polite forms are correct, including yoyuu ga arimasen and genki ga arimasen. The body examples are clean, including utsutchatta and utsushichatta. The one notation slip was in the English glosses: mise-ga-aku and mise-ga-shimaru wrote "(aiteru: is open)" where every other entry writes "(X = ...)", and mise-ga-komu added its state form after a semicolon. Those three are fixed above.

(2) DUPLICATES: There are none. Same-noun items across domains are different pairings: genki o dasu / genki ga nai, geemu o suru / ni hamaru, atama ga itai / ii, onaka ga itai / o kowasu.

LEFT AS IS (for the next step to decide):
- jikan ga tatsu sits in take-verbs, but English 'take' plays no part in it. It is presumably there to sit beside jikan ga kakaru.
- Some sound-alikes in different domains can't share a contrast group because each item has one group slot: me ga sameru / gohan ga sameru (覚める/冷める), and kaze o hiku / kaze ga tsuyoi. Also aiteru covers four items: doa and mise (開く) and seki and jikan (空く).
- Text-to-speech risk, the same issue the body domain already fixed for お腹がすく: 店が開く and ドアが開く can be read hiraku, and 席が空く can be read suku. Consider kana あく in ja/politeJa/example ja for c-mise-ga-aku, c-doa-ga-aku and c-seki-ga-aku. I didn't change these because I couldn't see their example ja fields.

selectorNotes:
I kept 167 items. Per domain: weather 12, body 18, clothes 12, home 16, food 11, media 13, travel 13, time-money 16, work-school 11, people 15, hobbies 9, senses 12, describing 9. Body and time-money run over their guidance on purpose. Under a commonness-first lens those are the domains where c4–c5 pairings are densest and said every week.

Hardest calls:
(1) Guessable but very common items. I kept shashin-o-toru (t1) and eki-ni-tsuku (t2) because they're c5 and n5. I also kept ongaku-o-kiku (t1) only because it forms a contrast set with ongaku-o-kakeru. I dropped hanashi-o-suru (t2) and uta-o-utau (t1).
(2) Near-duplicates where I kept one side and made the other a partner:
- densha-ni-maniau over jikan-ni-maniau, so the train set stays whole: densha ga okureru / ni okureru / ni maniau.
- kimochi-ga-warui over kibun-ga-warui.
- mise-ga-komu over michi-ga-komu.
- eki-made-okuru over uchi-made-okuru.
- denwa-ga-kakatte-kuru over denwa-ga-kakaru, since that is the form actually said.
- inu-o-kau over petto-o-kau, since the noun is far more frequent.
- yoyuu-ga-nai over yoyuu-ga-aru.
- youji-ga-aru over youji-ga-dekiru and yotei-ga-hairu.
- renraku-o-toru over renraku-ga-kuru and renraku-ga-toreru; meeru-ga-kuru already carries the kuru pattern.
- tomodachi-ga-dekiru over kareshi-ga-dekiru.
- piano-o-hiku stands for the instrument verbs. I left out tataku and fuku (fue-o-fuku is c2) rather than include a half set; mention them in partners.
- nodo-ga-itai is dropped as a partner of atama-ga-itai, since it follows the same pattern.
- terebi-o-tsukeru and eakon-o-tsukeru are dropped as partners of denki-o-tsukeru.
(3) Contrast sets kept whole:
- Wearing verbs: kiru, haku, kaburu, kakeru, suru (masuku and tokei), plus nugu and hazusu for taking things off.
- denki ga tsuku / o tsukeru / o kesu.
- kagi o kakeru / ga kakaru.
- kaze ga utsuru / o utsusu. I added utsusu at c3 so this pair stays whole.
- shiken ni ukaru / ochiru, shiai ni katsu / makeru, mise ga aku / shimaru, se ga takai / hikui, kimochi ga ii / warui, densha ni noru / o oriru.
doa-ga-aku is kept as the task's named example. There is no doa-o-akeru in the pool, so akeru goes in its partners. I left mado-o-akeru out (t2).
(4) Scope rule:
- I dropped kango+suru items where the suru pairing is guessable: shitsumon, henji, kenka, jama, nakanaori, iiwake.
- wasuremono-o-suru and okawari-o-suru were cut as borderline.
- I kept atama-ga-ii, naka-ga-ii, ki-o-tsukau, soudan-ni-noru, osewa-ni-naru, yoko-ni-naru and kata-ga-koru as the plain way to say each thing, not metaphor. atama-ga-ii is the one most open to challenge under the body-part rule.
(5) Flags: tenshon-ga-agaru is casual-only but c5, so I kept it with the flag. The pool has no rank for ikura (question word), so ikura-suru's freqNote should say so.
(6) Notable c4 items cut for size: toshi-o-toru, seki-ga-deru, onaka-o-kowasu, tsukare-ga-toreru, sentakumono-o-hosu, nimotsu-ga-todoku, oyu-o-wakasu, tabako-o-suu, shashin-o-kesu, shashin-ga-toreru, kuruma-o-tomeru, yakusoku-ga-aru, okane-o-tsukau, okane-o-kariru, yasumi-o-toru, monku-o-iu, baka-ni-suru, genki-o-dasu, oto-ga-kikoeru, sutairu-ga-ii, kaze-ga-fuku, tenki-yohou-ga-hazureru. These are the first candidates if there is room to grow toward 170.

I kept 165 collocations, counted and checked for duplicates. The lens was trap-first. With trapRisk 1–2, only items at c5/n5 stayed: tenki-ga-ii and shashin-o-toru.

Domain counts: weather 11, body 19, clothes 12, home 17, food 11, media 12, travel 13, time-money 15, work-school 10, people 15, hobbies 8, senses 12, describing 10.

Body and home go over their guidance because nearly every candidate there is t4–5 with n4–5. Weather, work-school and hobbies come in under.

Contrast sets kept whole:
- **Putting on:** fuku-o-kiru, kutsu-o-haku and zubon-o-haku (trousers are the real trap), boushi-o-kaburu, megane-o-kakeru, masuku-o-suru, tokei-o-suru, tebukuro-o-hameru.
- **Taking off:** kutsu-o-nugu, megane-o-hazusu.
- **Lights:** denki-o-tsukeru, denki-ga-tsuku, denki-o-kesu, denki-ga-kieru. I added kieru, a c3 item, only to complete the set.
- **Locks:** kagi-o-kakeru, kagi-ga-kakaru.
- **Catching a cold from someone:** kaze-ga-utsuru, kaze-o-utsusu.
- **Exams:** shiken-o-ukeru, ni-ukaru, ni-ochiru.
- **Matches:** shiai-ni-katsu, ni-makeru.
- **Trains:** densha-ga-okureru and densha-ni-okureru (switching the particle flips the meaning).
- **Phone:** denwa-o-kakeru, ga-kakaru, ni-deru, o-kiru.
- **"Play":** suru for sports and games, hiku for instruments.

Where two entries teach the same pairing, I kept one and the other becomes a partner note:
- jikan-ni-maniau kept; densha-ni-maniau dropped.
- mise-ga-komu kept (c5); michi-ga-komu dropped.
- eki-made-okuru kept; uchi-made-okuru dropped.
- petto-o-kau kept; inu-o-kau dropped.
- denwa-ga-kakaru kept; denwa-ga-kakatte-kuru dropped.
- denpa-ga-hairu kept (the verb is the trap); denpa-ga-warui dropped.
- tomodachi-ga-dekiru kept; kareshi-ga-dekiru dropped.
- Of the "feel unwell" phrases, guai-ga-warui and kimochi-ga-warui stay. kibun-ga-warui, choushi-ga-warui and kigen-ga-warui become partner notes. That was a close call, since the kibun/kigen confusion is itself a trap.
- takarakuji-ni-ataru and takarakuji-ga-ataru are near-duplicates; I dropped both.

Hardest calls:
1. **atama-ga-ii** is kept. It could be read as a body-part metaphor, but it is the plain everyday way to say "smart". mimi-ga-tooi, kan-ga-ii and kuchi-ni-au were dropped as closer to idiom, or as describing character.

FINAL: 160 - 7 + 8 = 161 items. Domains: weather 12, body 19, clothes 12, home 16, food 10, media 12, travel 13, time-money 15, work-school 9, people 14, hobbies 8, senses 12, describing 9. Body runs over its guidance because all three selectors found it the domain with the most traps. Work-school runs under because its 1-vote candidates are weak (shigoto-ga-mitsukaru, ten-o-toru, kekka-ga-deru are all t3).

WHY THE 7 REMOVALS. Each partner is already taught by a gloss in the versatility list (grepped versatility-items.txt), so each failed the 'cannot guess the partner' test:
- oto-o-ookiku-suru: an application of I-ku-suru ('-ku suru, make it (adj)'). listLink I-ku-suru from any volume note.
- tanoshimi-ni-suru: D-tanoshimi ('looking forward to it') is already an item. Same rule as the ki- phrases.
- kodomo-ga-iru: H-iru-exist is glossed 'have (people, pets)'. Put kyoudai/kareshi iru in partners where relevant.
- yotei-ga-aru: H-aru is glossed 'have (things)', and yotei ga hairu says the same thing ('I've got something on') with the real trap verb. Make it a partner of yotei-ga-hairu.
- gohan-ga-dekiru: H-dekiru is glossed 'be ready'. junbi-ga-dekiru keeps that sense; gohan dekita yo goes in its examples or partners.
- shigoto-ga-hairu: the same ga-hairu pairing as yotei-ga-hairu; shigoto ga haitchatta goes in its partners.
- osake-ni-you: really a single verb. Natives say yotta / yotchatta without osake. Move it to partners of osake-ga-yowai.

WHY THE 8 ADDITIONS.
- kaze-ga-fuku: the plan the user approved names 'kaze ga fuku next to kaze o hiku' as an example of a confusable set. I'd rate it c4, not c3 (kaze fuiteru is everyday). It also anchors fuku for the fue/fuku partner note.
- genki-o-dasu (c4 t5 n4): pairs with genki-ga-nai; link D-genki.
- oto-ga-kikoeru (c4 t4 n4): contrast with oto-ga-suru, and with H-kiku, whose gloss 'hear' pushes learners to oto o kiita; kikoeru? on calls makes n5 arguable.
- onaka-o-kowasu (c4 t5 n4): the commonest travel-health complaint.
- yoyuu-ga-nai (c4 t4 n4): no verb for 'afford'.
- tabako-o-suu (c4 t4 n3): classic trap with suu, and brings food back to 10.
- kotoba-ga-tsuujiru: high speakNeed for this learner (eigo tsuujiru? / nihongo tsuujita).
- denpa-ga-hairu: restores media to 12 after the volume item left.

DUP RULE APPLIED. Same noun with a different verb, or same verb with a different noun, counts as a near-duplicate only when it teaches the same pairing or meaning. These were kept as contrasts, not dups: netsu ga aru / deru, kaze ga tsuyoi / ame ga tsuyoi, kutsu o haku / zubon o haku, masuku o suru / tokei o suru, atama ga itai / onaka ga itai, the four aku items (doa, mise, seki, jikan: different meanings, and doa ga aku is the task's named transitive/intransitive example), sakkaa o suru / geemu o suru.
