outOfScope: weather: kaze o hiku (catch a cold): belongs to body. List it next to kaze ga fuku when grouping, because both use the sound kaze.
weather: ase o kaku (sweat): belongs to body, as the brief says.
weather: hiyake suru / hi ni yakeru (get a tan or sunburn): belongs to body. hi ni ataru (sit in the sun) is too narrow.
weather: atsui, samui, suzushii, atatakai, mushiatsui, hieru as standalone words: atsui and samui are already D-atsui and D-samui, and the rest are single adjectives or verbs.
weather: hareru, kumoru, hieru, yureru, furidasu: single verbs, so they go in partner notes only (yureru is in the jishin entry).
weather: atsuku naru, samuku naru, kuraku naru: these are the -ku naru pattern (I-ku-naru), not collocations. kuraku naru is noted as the casual alternative to hi ga kureru.
weather: taifuu ga kuru: fully guessable (come = kuru), even though it's common.

weather: hi ga deru, taiyou ga deru, tsuki ga deru, hoshi ga deru: the same 'appear in the sky = deru' pattern, folded into niji ga deru. hi ga dete kita could replace niji ga deru if the selector wants the more common case.
weather: hi ga noboru / hi ga shizumu (sunrise, sunset): mostly narrative or written. Conversation uses hi no de or yuuhi.
weather: kiri ga deru / kiri ga kakaru (fog): rare in conversation.

weather: Partners folded into their main entry instead of getting slots: sakura ga chiru (in hana ga saku), tsuyu ga akeru (in tsuyu ni hairu), kion ga sagaru (in kion ga agaru), yohou ga ataru (in tenki yohou ga hazureru), ame ga agaru and kaze ga yamu (variants of ame ga yamu).
weather: shitsudo ga takai / shikke ga ooi (humid): news or technical register. People say mushiatsui or jimejime suru.
weather: ooame, doshaburi, yuudachi, niwakaame, kosame, amayadori: single nouns or compounds, not pairings.
weather: kasa o motte iku (take an umbrella along): guessable from motsu + iku, so it's used only as a contrast link on kasa o sasu.
weather: denwa ga naru (the phone rings): belongs to media. It shares naru (鳴る) with kaminari ga naru.
weather: yama ni noboru (climb a mountain): belongs to hobbies or travel.
weather: Figurative idioms, proverbs and four-character compounds: ame futte ji katamaru, seiten no hekireki, arashi no mae no shizukesa, kaze no uwasa, kaze no fuki mawashi. Out per the rules.
weather: ame ga furisou / ame futte kita: the F-sou-looks and I-te-kuru patterns applied to ame ga furu. These are usage forms, not separate collocations.

body: hara ga heru / hara hetta (#6497 / #4970): masculine, rough variant of onaka ga suku. Note it as a flagged variant in that entry, not as its own item. Onaka peko peko is a mimetic intensifier of the same item.

body: choushi ga warui (phrase entry #8863): near-synonym of guai ga warui that also covers machines and sports form. The learner needs only one 'unwell' phrase first, so it fits better as a note or in a general list.
body: taichou ga warui / taichou furyou: semi-formal (sick-day emails, news). Guai ga warui covers speech.
body: kimochi warui (#1740): a single compound adjective that also means 'gross'. Mention it under kibun ga warui and hakike ga suru.
body: i ga itai: organ-specific. Onaka ga itai is the everyday form, and the trap line already contrasts them.

body: koshi ga itai, ha ga itai, me ga itai, ashi ga itai: same body part + ga itai frame, guessable once atama, onaka and nodo are known. Koshi vs senaka for 'back' is a vocabulary issue, not a collocation.
body: kushami ga deru / kushami o suru: same ga deru frame, and rarely something a learner needs to say.
body: hana o kamu (blow one's nose): unguessable verb but too narrow.
body: yakedo o suru (get burned): same pattern as kega o suru; narrow.
body: hone o oru: listed figurative idiom ('take pains'). The literal 'break a bone' is usually kossetsu suru.
body: onaka o kowasu (upset stomach): borderline metaphor and narrow. Onaka ga itai covers it.
body: isha ni mite morau: wordier. Byouin ni iku is what people say; mention it as an extension.
body: atama ga itai / mimi ga itai in the figurative sense ('it's a headache', 'hits a nerve'): idioms, left for the idiom list. Only the literal atama ga itai is a candidate.
body: me ga sameru (wake up): home and daily routine domain.
body: futoru / yaseru (gain or lose weight), netsuppoi, kazegimi, nenza suru, kossetsu suru: single words or transparent kango + suru verbs.
body: shawaa o abiru, ha o migaku, kami o arau: grooming and bathing belong to the home domain. Se ga takai and me ga warui (eyesight) belong to describing.
body: ki o ushinau (faint), iki o suu (breathe in for the doctor), chi ga tomaru: too narrow or clinical for everyday speech.

clothes: Single verbs, mentioned as partners or notes rather than entries: kigaeru 'change clothes' (#1536), niau 'suit/look good on' (#941), haoru 'throw on' (#18847), kiseru/hakaseru 'dress someone'.

clothes: Same verb as a kept item, so folded into its notes instead of separate entries: shatsu/kooto/seetaa/kimono/yukata o kiru (kiru); sukaato/kutsushita/sandaru/buutsu o haku (haku); uwagi o nugu (nugu); tebukuro o hameru (hameru); piasu o tsukeru / piasu shiteru (tsukeru); masuku/tokei/yubiwa o hazusu (hazusu); nekutai o suru / nekutai shiteru (nekutai o shimeru); beruto o shimeru (shimeru); mafuraa o maku (mafuraa o suru); meiku suru / okeshou suru (keshou o suru).
clothes: kasa o sasu: an umbrella is carried, not worn. It pairs with ame ga furu, so it belongs to weather.
clothes: shiitoberuto o shimeru: belongs to travel.
clothes: kami o kiru, kami o arau, kami o kawakasu: hair cutting and washing go to body/home, as the brief says.
clothes: fuku o tatamu, sentakumono o hosu, fuku ga yogoreru, shimi o otosu: laundry, so home.
clothes: ki ni iru (kore ki ni itta): belongs to senses/mind.
clothes: kakkou ga ii / kakkoii, oshare: describing people; kakkoii is a single adjective.
clothes: botan o tomeru/kakeru, chakku o shimeru/akeru (chakku #14719, jippaa #46414), sode o makuru, shatsu o ireru (tuck in), piasu no ana o akeru (pierce ears): too narrow for a ~160-item list.
clothes: atsugi/usugi suru: compound verbs, transparent once the noun is known.
clothes: fuku ga kitsui/yurui: the adjective is the English one (tight/loose), so the pairing is guessable.
clothes: kontakuto o toru: the 'get in touch' sense, not lenses; business register.

clothes: Figurative idioms built on wear verbs, kept for the later idiom list: neko o kaburu (play innocent), on ni kiru (feel indebted), kasa ni kiru (abuse a position), nureginu o kiseru (falsely accuse), hachimaki/fundoshi o shimete kakaru (buckle down), megane ni kanau (win someone's approval).
home: kao o arau (wash your face): fully guessable (wash = arau), trapRisk 1
home: heya o katazukeru (tidy the room): the lesson is the single verb katazukeru, not the pairing; guessable once the verb is known
home: sentaku o suru / souji suru / kaji o suru: transparent noun + suru; sentakuki o mawasu and sentakumono o hosu carry the real laundry traps
home: ofuro o wakasu / ofuro ga waku (heat the bath / the bath is ready): reserve; uses the same wakasu as oyu o wakasu and is specific to households with a bath heater
home: futon o shiku / futon o tatamu (lay out / fold up the futon): a real trap but limited to futon households, low speakNeed; reserve if the selector wants a sleeping item
home: mizu o dasu / mizu ga deru / mizu o tomeru (run / stop the tap): low need, and dasu/deru are already taught (H-dasu, H-deru)
home: mezamashi ga naru (the alarm goes off): naru 'ring' is guessable from 'the alarm rang'; belongs in the notes for mezamashi o kakeru
home: terebi o kesu / eakon o kesu / kagi o akeru: same verbs as kept entries (kesu, akeru); belong in the notes for denki o kesu and kagi o kakeru
home: doa o shimeru / doa ga shimaru: a second open/close pair that follows the aku/akeru pattern exactly; reserve
home: hamigaki o suru: variant of ha o migaku; mention as a partner
home: me o samasu: transitive of me ga sameru, rare in conversation
home: nebou suru (oversleep), norikaeru-style single verbs: single verbs, not pairings
home: hige o soru, keshou o suru: grooming and makeup belong to the body/clothes domains
home: ocha o ireru, gohan o taku: food domain; sumaho o juuden suru: media domain
home: toire o nagasu, denki ga kireru (bulb burns out), ofuro ga aku (bath is free): too narrow
home: rusu ni suru (be away from home): rusu desu is the common form; narrow
home: uchi ni kaeru: already covered by H-kaeru-return in the versatility list
home: ashi o arau (go straight), asameshi mae: figurative idioms, left for the idiom list
food: ryouri o tsukuru: easy to guess, and the versatility list already glosses H-tsukuru as 'make; cook'.
food: chuumon (o) suru: a plain kango + suru verb, and H-tanomu ('order') already covers it.
food: gohan ga dekiru (gohan dekita yo): built on H-dekiru 'be ready', so it's guessable once that's learned, and it fits the home domain better. Contrasted in gohan ga takeru.
food: osake o nomu / nomi ni iku: easy to guess from H-nomu, and nomi ni iku is a grammar pattern, not a noun-verb pairing.
food: osake o tsugu / otsugi suru (pour drinks for others): drinking-party etiquette, so narrow and leaning polite. The frequency list can't separate tsugu from sosogu (注ぐ is listed only as そそぐ).
food: ocha o samasu / samasu (let it cool): the rarer partner of sameru, mentioned under gohan ga sameru instead of getting its own slot.
food: usui koohii: the opposite of koi koohii, mentioned under that entry. Add it if the selector wants the adjective pair complete.
food: kusuri o nomu, onaka ga suku, onaka ga ippai, nodo ga kawaku, shokuyoku ga nai, futsukayoi: body and health domain.
food: kuruma ni you (carsick): body or travel domain, though it uses the same verb as osake ni you.
food: hi ni yakeru (sunburn): body or weather domain, though it uses the same verb as niku ga yakeru.
food: ofuro o wakasu / ofuro ga waku: home domain, with the same verbs as oyu o wakasu / oyu ga waku.
food: biiru o hiyasu / biiru ga hieteru: about the fridge, so home domain, and tsumetai biiru is guessable and fine.
food: bentou o atatameru (the konbini question 'atatamemasu ka?'): atatameru = warm is guessable, so it is a phrase to recognise when heard, not a collocation to learn.
food: kome o togu (wash rice), shio o furu (sprinkle salt), aji o tsukeru (season): cooking phrases too narrow for everyday conversation.
food: kuchi ni au (suits one's taste), amai mono ni me ga nai, nekojita: body-part metaphors and idioms, so they go to the idiom list.
food: meshi o kuu / meshi iku: a rough, masculine swap for gohan o taberu, not a pairing a learner has to learn. Flag it for a register list if wanted.
food: tabako o yameru, osake o yameru: easy to guess from H-yameru.
food: okaikei / kanjou (paying the bill), seki ga aiteru (is there a free table): time-money and travel domains.
media: terebi o miru: fully guessable (miru = watch); add it only if the selector wants a plain anchor beside terebi de yaru / terebi ni deru
media: juuden suru (charge the phone): transparent kango + suru; named inside juuden ga kireru
media: denwa suru: transparent noun + suru; noted as the casual alternative under denwa o kakeru
media: henji suru (reply): transparent noun + suru; henji ga konai (no reply) is covered by the meeru ga kuru frame
media: renraku suru: already in the versatility list (H-renraku-suru); renraku ga kuru is noted under meeru ga kuru
media: akaunto o tsukuru: guessable (tsukuru = make) and narrow
media: terebi o tsukeru / terebi o kesu: home domain, with the other switches
media: oto o dasu / oto ga deru (make a sound / sound comes out): fits senses (next to oto ga suru) or home (noise); the media need, volume, is covered by oto o ookiku suru
media: denwa ga tooi ('the line is faint', lit. the phone is far): real but narrow phone etiquette, mostly polite or older speakers
media: denwa o kawaru (hand the phone over): narrow
media: manaa moodo ni suru (set phone to silent): mostly heard in announcements; narrow
media: kidoku ga tsuku / kidoku suruu (read receipt shows / leave on read): LINE-specific and slangy, too narrow
media: rain o koukan suru (swap LINE IDs): brand-specific; a general renrakusaki o koukan suru could go to people
media: orikaesu (call back): single verb and business register; can go in partner notes
media: rokuga suru (record a programme): transparent kango + suru
media: geemu o suru, eiga o miru, uta o utau, piano o hiku: hobbies domain (asobu vs suru vs hiku traps belong there)
media: netto de shiraberu (look it up online): guessable from shiraberu; generic research verb
media: fuirutaa o kakeru, pinto ga au (apply a filter, be in focus): camera-hobby narrow
media: sumaho o otosu (drop or lose your phone): guessable from otosu; the lose sense belongs to home/time-money
media: QR koodo o yomu (scan a QR code): narrow, transactional
media: rusuden ni ireru (leave a voicemail): narrow and declining
media: douga o miru: guessable; noted under douga o toru
travel: basu / takushii / hikouki / jitensha ni noru: same verb and particle as densha ni noru, so they're folded into it as variants in freqNote and why rather than kept as separate items.
travel: densha ga komu / mise ga komu: folded into michi ga komu as the same komu pairing; the selector can swap the headword noun if trains suit better than roads.
travel: kuruma o unten suru (drive): a transparent kango + suru verb; once you know unten, nothing about the pairing is unguessable.
travel: ryokou ni iku / kaimono ni iku: the purpose-ni + iku pattern is grammar, and ryokou suru is a transparent kango verb.
travel: norikaeru, noriokureru, oriru on its own: single verbs. They are mentioned in the partner notes (noriokureru under densha ni okureru).
travel: michi ga wakaru (know the way): guessable from H-wakaru, and michi shitteru? is equally natural, so there's no trap.
travel: michi o machigaeru (take a wrong turn): guessable straight from H-machigaeru.
travel: kippu o kau (buy a ticket), basu o matsu (wait for the bus): fully guessable pairings.
travel: kuruma ni hikareru (get hit by a car): an unguessable verb but mostly heard as a warning or in the news, so it's too narrow to say; a possible later reserve.
travel: shiitoberuto o shimeru: the shimeru pairing belongs to the clothes domain (beruto / nekutai o shimeru), and the seatbelt alone is too narrow.
travel: gasorin o ireru, enjin o kakeru, shingou o mamoru: only for drivers or road-safety talk, too narrow for an everyday list.
travel: jikan ga kakaru (it takes time): belongs to the time-money domain even though it comes up constantly when travelling.
travel: okureru as 'be late' (a time word): already H-okureru in the versatility list; only the noun pairings densha ni okureru / densha ga okureru are kept.
travel: ashi ga nai (have no way to get there): a figurative body-part idiom, saved for the idiom list.
travel: ki o tsukete (take care on your trip): already G-ki-o-tsukete / H-ki-o-tsukeru in the versatility list.
time-money: okane o harau / kaado de harau: 'pay' maps directly to harau, so the pairing can be guessed, and 'de' for the means of payment is general grammar.
time-money: yakusoku (o) suru: a transparent kango + suru verb. Its useful nuance (= make plans to meet) is covered under yakusoku ga aru.
time-money: yoyaku suru, chokin suru, setsuyaku suru, kyanseru suru: transparent kango or loanword + suru verbs. yoyaku is kept only through the unguessable yoyaku o toru.
time-money: jikan ni okureru / densha ni okureru: the verb is already H-okureru in the versatility list. It is named as the opposite of jikan ni maniau.
time-money: okane ga tariru / tarinai: the verb is already H-tariru, and the pairing with money is guessable.
time-money: jikan ga nai, okane ga nai, hima ga aru: guessable once aru and nai are known, and hima is already D-hima.
time-money: tsugou ga warui: folded into tsugou ga ii as its opposite instead of a separate entry.
time-money: okane o kakeru: folded into jikan o kakeru (same verb, same pattern).
time-money: yotei o tateru: folded into keikaku o tateru (same verb).
time-money: jikan o mamoru: folded into yakusoku o mamoru (same verb).
time-money: okane o kasegu: a single verb whose English 'earn' maps directly to kasegu.
time-money: okane o kuzusu (break a bill into change): the pairing can't be guessed, but it is too narrow (asking for change at a till). It could be a reserve for a later pass.
time-money: tokei ga susumu / tokei ga okureru (a clock running fast or slow): narrow, and better in the home domain if anywhere.
time-money: warikan ni suru (split the bill): the item is really the noun warikan, and ni suru is the general I-ni-suru pattern.
time-money: machiawase (o) suru: a native-word noun + suru whose suru is transparent.
time-money: jikan ga sugiru: a more formal alternative to jikan ga tatsu.
time-money: yasumi o toru (take a day off): belongs to the work-school domain.
time-money: seki ga aku / mise ga aku (seat free, shop opens): belong to the travel and food domains. The aku sense is taught here through jikan ga aku.
time-money: Figurative money and time idioms (kane ga mawaranai, futokoro ga sabishii, saifu no himo ga katai, te ga hanasenai): kept for the later idiom list.
time-money: Proverbs (toki wa kane nari, isogaba maware): out of scope.
work-school: jugyou o toru (take/sign up for a class): toru works as in English. It is kept only as the contrast inside shiken-o-ukeru's trap.
work-school: mensetsu o ukeru (have a job interview): same frame as shiken o ukeru, folded into its freqNote.
work-school: shikaku o toru (get a qualification): same frame as menkyo o toru, folded into it.
work-school: yuukyuu o toru (take paid leave): folded into yasumi o toru.
work-school: kaisha ni hairu (join a company): guessable, because the versatility list already glosses hairu as 'enter; join' (H-hairu).
work-school: shigoto o suru / shukudai o suru / shukudai o yaru: guessable (do = suru/yaru).
work-school: shigoto ga aru / shiken ga aru / kaigi ga aru: guessable (have = aru).
work-school: shigoto ni iku / kaisha ni iku / shigoto o sagasu: guessable.
work-school: zangyou (o) suru, shuushoku suru, sotsugyou suru, nyuugaku suru, shusseki suru, teishutsu suru, tenshoku suru: transparent kango + suru verbs.
work-school: baito (o) suru: transparent noun + suru (do a part-time job).
work-school: goukaku suru / pasu suru: kango or loanword + suru, noted as the formal and casual alternatives to ukaru.
work-school: kubi ni naru (get fired): body-part metaphor idiom, left for the idiom list.
work-school: yotei ga hairu, shimekiri ni ma ni au: plans and deadlines belong to time-money.
work-school: nooto o toru / memo o toru (take notes): guessable from English 'take'.
work-school: tan'i o toru / tan'i o otosu (earn/fail a university credit): too narrow, university-only.
work-school: mondai o toku (solve a problem): narrow (maths and exam questions).
work-school: jugyou o saboru (skip class): saboru is a slangy standalone verb that pairs freely, not a fixed noun pairing.
work-school: kaisha ga tsubureru (company goes bust): too narrow for this list.
work-school: shigoto ni nareru (get used to the job): nareru + ni is a general frame, not specific to this noun.
work-school: sensei ni naru, jugyou ga hajimaru, shiken ni okureru: guessable from verbs already in the versatility list.
work-school: te o ageru (raise your hand in class): a literal body action, better placed in body.
people: ki ni naru, ki ni suru, ki o tsukeru / ki o tsukete: already in the versatility list (H-ki-ni-naru, H-ki-ni-suru, H-ki-o-tsukeru, G-ki-o-tsukete); linked from ki o tsukau, not repeated.
people: renraku suru: already in the versatility list (H-renraku-suru); the new pairing is renraku o toru instead.
people: ki ga au, hanashi ga au (hit it off): figurative idioms that describe chemistry; they go to the idiom list.
people: kao ga hiroi, kao o dasu (show up), mimi o kasu, kuchi ga warui, kuchi o kiku, te o kasu: body-part metaphors, so they go to the idiom list.

people: aisatsu o suru, akushu o suru, shoukai suru, kokuhaku suru, deeto suru: transparent noun + suru verbs; the greetings themselves are already in the versatility list (G-ohayou, G-konnichiwa ...).
people: X ni au (meet), X to kekkon suru: particle choices rather than an unguessable partner word; covered by H-au-meet, and kekkon suru is a transparent kango verb.
people: tsukiau (date), wakareru (break up), furareru (get dumped), ayamaru (apologise), homeru (praise): single verbs; mention as partners in notes.
people: yakusoku o suru / mamoru / yaburu: time-money domain.
people: denwa o kakeru, denwa ni deru, meeru o okuru: media domain.
people: tasuke o motomeru: formal or written; speech uses tasukete.
people: yoroshiku tsutaeru (say hi to X for me): an adverb + verb chunk, not a noun pairing; better as an extension of G-yoroshiku.
people: guchi o iu / guchi o kobosu: near-duplicate of monku o iu (noted there); kobosu is figurative.
people: himitsu o mamoru, himitsu ni suru: formal twins of naisho ni suru (noted there).
people: tanomi ga aru, onegai o kiku: twins and contrasts noted inside onegai ga aru.
people: tomodachi o tsukuru: a less natural variant, noted in the tomodachi ga dekiru trap.
people: kyoudai ga iru, kareshi ga iru: slot-swaps of kodomo ga iru, noted there.
people: te o furu (wave): body domain.
people: hito ga ii, yasashii: describing domain.
people: aite o suru / aite ni shinai (keep company / ignore): partly figurative and narrow.
people: Proverbs, four-character compounds, keigo beyond desu/masu (osewa ni natte orimasu).
hobbies: shougi o sasu / go o utsu (play shogi / go): strong trap verbs, but narrow for everyday conversation, and casual shougi suru is accepted, so the trap is soft.
hobbies: janken o suru, toranpu o suru: the same suru slot as geemu o suru, which covers them. janken de kimeru is a possible note.
hobbies: karaoke ni iku: karaoke is a venue, so 'go to karaoke' maps straight across; noted under tsuri ni iku.
hobbies: sanpo o suru, undou suru, renshuu suru, ouen suru, yuushou suru: transparent kango + suru verbs. sanpo ni iku is noted under tsuri ni iku.
hobbies: booru o nageru / booru o keru, odori o odoru / dansu o suru, yama ni noboru, shiai o suru, shiai o miru: guessable, since English leads to the right verb.

hobbies: gooru o kimeru (score a goal), ten o ireru / ten o toru (score points), bando o kumu (form a band), tako o ageru (fly a kite): good traps but too narrow for an everyday list. Test scores belong to work-school.
hobbies: ude ga agaru / ude o migaku (skill improves / hone a skill): body-part metaphor idioms, so they go to the later idiom list.
hobbies: X ga umai / X ga jouzu / X ga tokui (good at): describing-people domain, and jouzu and nigate are already versatility items (D-jouzu, D-nigate).
hobbies: shashin o toru: media domain. ongaku o kiku: media domain. kuji ni ataru (win the lottery): time-money domain. karada o kitaeru / kintore o suru: body domain.
hobbies: oyogi ni iku, asobi ni iku: verb stem + ni iku is already the versatility pattern I-ni-iku.
hobbies: Existing material: only uta (10-list-nouns #114) overlaps. vocab-trainer utility-vocab has no hobby or sport set, and its fuku is clothing, not blow.

senses: ki ga suru, ki ni naru, ki ni suru, ki o tsukeru / ki o tsukete: already in the versatility list (H-ki-ga-suru, H-ki-ni-naru, H-ki-ni-suru, H-ki-o-tsukeru, G-ki-o-tsukete). Linked from ki ga tsuku, ki ni iru, kanji ga suru and yokan ga suru instead.
senses: samuke ga suru (get chills): belongs to the body domain. Its noun is in vocab-trainer physical-sensations.
senses: kioku ga nai / kioku ni nai (#11720): guessable (memory + not have), and oboete nai covers it in speech. Mostly drama amnesia or blackout talk.
senses: me ni hairu (catch the eye, #6687): fairly guessable and leans written.
senses: atama ni ukabu (come to mind, #14562): low frequency and semi-figurative. omoitsuku is a single verb.

senses: ki ga sumu (be satisfied, #3762), ki ga muku (feel like it, #10750), ki ga susumanai (#21043), ki ga raku (#8269): ki expressions with lower learner need and an idiomatic flavour. Leave them to the idiom list.
senses: ki ga aru (have a crush on, #6413), ki ga au, ki ga tsuyoi, ki ga mijikai, ki ga omoi, ki ni kuwanai: figurative or character idioms. Out under the borderline rule.
senses: ki o ushinau (faint, #8021): belongs to the body domain.
senses: kyoumi o motsu (take an interest, #4531): mentioned under kyoumi ga aru. It is rarer in speech and the same pairing logic.
senses: kehai ga suru (sense a presence): too narrow (horror and drama).
senses: mieru (Fuji-san ga mieru): the ga + mieru frame works with any noun, so it is a verb, not a noun-specific collocation. Mention it beside oto ga kikoeru.
senses: kibun ga ii (#13225): left as a note under kibun ga warui. In speech kimochi ii covers most of 'feel good'.
senses: omoide ga aru (have memories): a guessable pairing.
senses: kimoi (キモい #4580): slang clip of kimochi warui, recorded in freqNote rather than as its own item.
senses: kotae ga wakaru: just wakaru with an object, no collocational trap.

describing: kao ga hiroi, ki ga mijikai, kuchi ga warui, ki ga tsuyoi / ki ga yowai, atama ga katai, me ga takai, hana ga takai: figurative character idioms (hana ga takai is literal only in a narrow sense), so they go to the idiom list.
describing: atama ga warui: mentioned under atama ga ii. It is derivable from it, and rude when said about others.
describing: me ga ii: mentioned under me ga warui. It is rarer, derivable, and also figurative ('has a good eye').
describing: mimi ga tooi (hard of hearing): plain and literal, but a learner rarely needs to say it. Reserve if the domain runs short.
describing: mimi ga ii: split between 'good hearing' and 'good ear for music', and rare.
describing: kao ga chiisai: a culture-specific compliment, narrow, and low need to say it.
describing: karada ga katai (inflexible): a strong trap, but it belongs to body or hobbies (stretching, sport). Flagged to those domains.
describing: tairyoku ga nai (no stamina): common, but the English 'no stamina' maps straight across, so it is guessable.
describing: onaka ga deru (pot belly), kami ga usui (thinning hair): narrow and touchy appearance remarks. Body could take onaka ga deru.
describing: hige o hayasu (grow a beard): unguessable verb but narrow. Hige o soru belongs to home routine.
describing: kami o kiru (get a haircut, even at a salon): a strong trap, but home routine or body, not describing.
describing: megane o kakeru: clothes domain (wearing verbs).
describing: sake ni tsuyoi / yowai (can or can't hold drink): food and drink domain.
describing: hi ni yakeru (get tanned): weather or body domain.
describing: genki o dasu / genki ga deru (cheer up / perk up): an unguessable transitive/intransitive pair, but senses and mind domain, not describing.
describing: toshi ue / toshi shita / onaji toshi: nouns, not noun + partner pairings. Toshi ga chikai is too narrow.
describing: futoru / yaseru / fukeru: single verbs (note the futotteru / yaseteru state form in teaching).
describing: kakkoii, kawaii, kashikoi, sumaato, ninkimono: single words. Sumaato is used as the false-friend note under atama ga ii.
describing: X ni niteru (resemble): a grammar pattern not tied to one noun, so it belongs with the versatility patterns.
describing: ashi ga nagai, me ga ookii, chikara ga tsuyoi, hada ga kirei: fully guessable from English.
describing: se no takai hito: just the relative-clause form of se ga takai, not a separate item.

cuts.trap: 'Get wet' is the single verb nureru, with no 'get' or naru added. The rain takes ni (ame de nureta is also heard).
cuts.reason: The lesson is the single verb nureru (get wet); 'ame ni' is a free add-on, and ame ni furareru is kept for the rain itself.

cuts.trap: Not taiyou ga tsuyoi or taiyou ga atsui: strong sun is hizashi (sunlight) ga tsuyoi.
cuts.reason: Correct and a real trap, but it's mostly a summer remark; atsui does most of the work in casual talk.

cuts.trap: English 'it thunders' is one verb. Japanese makes the thunder sound: kaminari ga naru (鳴る 'ring', a homophone of naru 'become').
cuts.reason: Correct, but thunder doesn't come up often; people mostly just say kaminari!

cuts.trap: A forecast doesn't machigaeru (that is a person's mistake) or chigau. It misses, hazureru, or hits, ataru.
cuts.reason: Strong trap: a forecast 'misses' (hazureta) or 'hits' (atatta). 'yohou hazureta ja n' is common weather grumbling.

cuts.trap: Not ichinichi ga nagai, which means 'it was a long day': daylight hours are hi ga nagai / hi ga mijikai.
cuts.reason: Natural seasonal small talk (hi ga nagaku natta ne), but only a couple of times a year.

cuts.trap: English 'the weather turns/breaks' points to kawaru or kowareru. Worsening weather 'crumbles': kuzureru.
cuts.reason: Mostly forecast language; in conversation people say tenki warui or ame furisou.

cuts.trap: English 'come out/open' points to deru or hiraku. Flowers bloom with saku, and petals fall with chiru, not ochiru.
cuts.reason: Saku is simply the verb 'bloom'; once you know it the pairing comes free.

cuts.trap: English 'an earthquake hit/struck' has no matching verb. Say jishin ga okiru (casually jishin ga atta / kita). The shaking itself is yureru.
cuts.reason: Sounds like the news; in conversation people say jishin atta or yureta.

cuts.trap: English 'the snow is sticking/settling' has no match: snow piles up, tsumoru, not tsuku or nokoru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but only useful where it snows heavily; yuki ga furu covers most snow talk.

cuts.trap: English has no verb for it: the rainy season is 'entered', tsuyu ni hairu, and when it ends it 'opens', tsuyu ga akeru.
cuts.reason: Rainy-season talk only, a few weeks a year.

cuts.trap: English 'there's a rainbow' points to niji ga aru. A rainbow comes out: niji ga deru (or niji ga kakaru).
cuts.reason: Correct, but rainbows rarely come up; niji da! works on the spot.
'Temperature goes up' maps straight onto agaru; no trap.

cuts.trap: Not samui kaze by default: wind you feel on your skin is tsumetai (cold to the touch). Samui describes the air or how you feel.
cuts.reason: The tsumetai/samui split is real, but a cold wind isn't something you say often.

cuts.trap: No 'sore' adjective: the throat hurts, nodo ga itai.
cuts.reason: Same 'body part ga itai' pattern as atama ga itai; swap in nodo for a sore throat.

cuts.trap: Means physically sick or queasy, not 'grumpy' (that is kigen ga warui); kimochi warui is the casual twin.
cuts.reason: Casual speech uses kimochi warui for feeling sick, which is kept; guai ga warui covers feeling unwell.

cuts.trap: Not hana ga hashiru: 'nose water comes out', hanamizu ga deru.
cuts.reason: Same 'symptom ga deru' frame as netsu ga deru; its card can list hanamizu as a partner.

cuts.trap: Not koeru: the cold itself 'heals', kaze ga naoru (kaze naotta?); you cure it with kaze o naosu.
cuts.reason: Very common ('kaze naotta?') and nothing kept covers getting better; English 'get over' gives no clue to naoru.

cuts.trap: Not netsu ga oriru or heru: a fever 'drops', netsu ga sagaru (netsu sagatta?).
cuts.reason: The natural follow-up to netsu ga aru ('netsu sagatta?'), said constantly when someone is ill.

cuts.trap: Not furuku naru (that's for things): people 'take years', toshi o toru (toshi totta naa).
cuts.reason: Common and unguessable: people 'take years' (toshi totta naa); nothing kept says 'get older'.

cuts.trap: Not kusuri ga hataraku: medicine 'takes effect', kusuri ga kiku, a homophone of kiku 'listen'.
cuts.reason: Pairs naturally with kusuri o nomu ('kiita?'), and kiku = 'take effect' is a real trap.

cuts.trap: Not samui alone: chills 'do', samuke ga suru; samui means the room is cold.
cuts.reason: Correct, but a specific symptom; most people just say samui or zokuzoku suru.

cuts.trap: No 'dizzy' adjective: dizziness 'does', memai ga suru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but dizziness is a less common thing to report; kurakura suru is the casual version.

cuts.trap: Not hakike ga aru: nausea 'does', hakike ga suru; in casual talk people say kimochi warui.
cuts.reason: In conversation people say kimochi warui for nausea, which is kept.

cuts.trap: Not netsu o toru: you 'measure' a fever, netsu o hakaru (netsu hakatta?).
cuts.reason: Real trap (hakaru, not toru), but you rarely need to say it yourself.

cuts.trap: 'Bleed' is one verb in English; Japanese says blood comes out, chi ga deru (chi deteru yo).
cuts.reason: Correct, but only for injuries; kega o suru is kept for the event itself.

cuts.trap: Not warui kaze: a bad cold is hidoi kaze; warui means wrong or at fault.
cuts.reason: Hidoi (terrible) goes with anything bad; it's a free combination, not a fixed pair.

cuts.trap: No 'stuffy' adjective: the nose clogs, hana ga tsumaru (hana tsumatteru).
cuts.reason: Correct, but cold symptoms beyond fever and headache come up less; hana tsumatteru is still worth knowing.

cuts.trap: Guessable; only the tense trips people: tired eyes now is me ga tsukareta / tsukareteru.
cuts.reason: 'Eyes get tired' translates word for word.

cuts.trap: Shots are 'hit', chuusha o utsu; as the patient say chuusha utte moratta or utareta.
cuts.reason: Mostly a clinic word; you hear it more than you say it.

cuts.trap: The ankle isn't named: you sprain the ashi, ashi o kujiku (ashi kujiita), or nenza shita.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare; nenza shita or ashi hinetta are also heard.
'High fever' maps straight onto takai.

cuts.trap: Not fuku o toru: every garment comes off with nugu, whichever verb put it on.
cuts.reason: Kutsu o nugu teaches that nugu takes off any garment.

cuts.trap: Not keshou o tsukeru or kiru: makeup takes suru. Many speakers say okeshou suru, and younger ones meiku suru.
cuts.reason: Keshou (o) suru is a plain noun + suru verb; the lesson is the noun keshou or meiku.

cuts.trap: Not yubiwa o kiru: things you push a finger or hand into (rings, gloves) take hameru. yubiwa shiteru is also common for wearing one.
cuts.reason: Tebukuro o hameru teaches hameru for things you push a finger or hand into.

cuts.ja: アクセサリーを付ける
cuts.trap: Not akusesarii o kiru: earrings, necklaces and badges take tsukeru, or just suru (piasu shiteru).
cuts.reason: Correct, but people usually name the item and use suru (piasu shiteru).

cuts.trap: Not keshou o nugu or toru: makeup is 'dropped' with otosu, the same verb used for dirt and stains.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but a narrow routine phrase; you rarely need to say it.

cuts.trap: Not nekutai o kiru: a tie is 'tightened' with shimeru, which sounds like shimeru 'close'. Wearing one is just nekutai shiteru.
cuts.reason: Shimeru is the set verb, but in conversation people say nekutai shiteru, like tokei o suru.

cuts.trap: Not kontakuto o kakeru like glasses: lenses go in with ireru and come out with hazusu or toru.
cuts.reason: Only relevant to lens wearers; megane o kakeru covers the common case.

cuts.trap: Not mafuraa o kiru: a scarf takes suru (mafuraa shiteru), or maku 'wrap' for the act of putting it on.
cuts.reason: Same 'accessory + suru' frame as tokei o suru and masuku o suru.

cuts.trap: English 'put your hair up' doesn't carry over; the verb is musubu 'tie' (casually kami shibaru or matomeru).
cuts.reason: 'Tie your hair' maps straight onto musubu.

cuts.trap: Not boushi o hazusu: hats come off with toru (boushi o nugu also works), not with the accessory verb hazusu.
cuts.reason: 'Take off' as toru is a natural guess; no real trap.

cuts.trap: Not uchi o hanareru or nokosu: leaving home for the day is deru, and the place you leave takes o.
cuts.reason: One of the most-said daily lines ('nanji ni uchi deru?'), with o on the place you leave.

cuts.trap: Not terebi o akeru or on ni suru: screens, like lights, are tsukeru'd, and off is kesu.
cuts.reason: Same tsukeru/kesu as the light; the denki card can list terebi as a partner.

cuts.trap: English 'vacuum' is a verb, but Japanese says soujiki o kakeru, not soujiki suru or soujiki o tsukau.
cuts.reason: Everyday chore with an unguessable verb (kakeru); English 'vacuum' gives no hint.

cuts.trap: Same tsukeru as lights, and eakon o kakeru (run it) is equally natural; not on ni suru or mawasu.
cuts.reason: Same tsukeru as the light; the denki card can list eakon as a partner.

cuts.trap: Not mizu o niru: you boil 'hot water' (oyu), and the verb is wakasu; niru is for cooking food.
cuts.reason: Daily kitchen phrase with two traps at once: you boil oyu (not mizu) and the verb is wakasu.

cuts.trap: Not kakeru or tsurusu: laundry put out to dry is hosu, and the noun is sentakumono (the clothes), not sentaku.
cuts.reason: Daily household chore in Japan, and neither the noun nor hosu is guessable.

cuts.trap: Not denki ga kesu: the intransitive is kieru, and 'the light is off' is denki kieteru.
cuts.reason: The denki ga tsuku / denki o kesu cards already teach the on/off pair; kieteru fits in their notes.

cuts.trap: English uses one verb; Japanese needs ibiki + kaku, the same kaku as ase o kaku (sweat).
cuts.reason: Good trap (same kaku as ase o kaku), but snoring doesn't come up much.

cuts.trap: No English verb leads here: bed hair 'sticks on' (neguse ga tsuku), as in neguse tsuiteru yo.
cuts.reason: A cute everyday line, but a rare noun; mostly heard as 'neguse tsuiteru yo'.

cuts.trap: Not sentakuki o hashiraseru or ugokasu: you 'spin' (mawasu) the washer.
cuts.reason: Correct, but people usually just say sentaku suru.

cuts.trap: The pairing itself is guessable; the risk is transitivity, mado o akeru (you do it) vs mado ga aiteru (it's open).
cuts.reason: 'Open the window' maps straight onto akeru; doa ga aku already teaches the ga/o switch.

cuts.trap: English 'water' is a verb; Japanese 'gives' water, (hana ni) mizu o yaru, or politely ageru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but only for plant owners.

cuts.trap: English 'iron' is a verb; Japanese says airon o kakeru, not airon suru.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but ironing rarely comes up in conversation.

cuts.trap: Not kami o kawaku or fuku: drying it yourself is the transitive kawakasu, while kami ga kawaku means it dries.
cuts.reason: Correct, but a narrow routine phrase.

cuts.trap: Not gohan o ryouri suru or niru: rice has its own verb, taku.
cuts.reason: Daily in Japanese homes, and taku is a verb used only for rice that you can't guess.

cuts.trap: There is no 'get' to translate: it is the verb you, and the drink takes ni (not o).
cuts.reason: Two reviewers wanted it: 'yotta' is everyday drinking talk, and the drink takes ni.

cuts.trap: English splits grill, roast, bake, toast and fry; Japanese uses yaku for all dry-heat cooking (pan o yaku = make toast).
cuts.reason: The lesson is the verb yaku (grill/bake/toast), which goes with any food.

cuts.trap: Not osake o takusan moteru: a heavy drinker is 'strong at alcohol'; with the drink as topic (kono osake wa tsuyoi) it means the drink is strong.
cuts.reason: Osake ga yowai is kept; tsuyoi is just its opposite.

cuts.trap: Not aji ga tsuyoi: heavy salt or sauce flavour is koi.
cuts.reason: Koi koohii and aji ga usui already teach koi/usui for flavour.

cuts.trap: Not shouyu o oku or ireru: sauce poured over food is kakeru (also mayo, dressing, sauce).
cuts.reason: Correct, but a mealtime detail you rarely need to say.

cuts.trap: Intransitive half: 'the kettle's boiled' is oyu ga waita, not oyu ga wakashita.
cuts.reason: The intransitive half of oyu o wakasu; heard less than the transitive form.

cuts.trap: There is no word for 'seconds' or 'refill' to translate; it is the noun okawari, used with suru or on its own (okawari kudasai).
cuts.reason: The lesson is the noun okawari, which works alone (okawari kudasai).

cuts.trap: Checking the seasoning is aji o miru ('look at the taste') or ajimi suru; ajiwau means savour.
cuts.reason: A cook's phrase; you rarely need it in conversation.

cuts.trap: The rice cooker finishing is gohan ga taketa; gohan ga dekita means the whole meal is ready.
cuts.reason: Rare outside the kitchen; gohan dekita covers 'food's ready'.

cuts.trap: Meat being cooked through is yakeru ('it got grilled'), not niku ga dekita.
cuts.reason: Mostly at a barbecue table; narrow use.

cuts.trap: English 'connect' covers both: you tsunagu a device (waifai ni tsunaide), but the net tsunagaru on its own.
cuts.reason: Netto ga tsunagaru is kept; tsunagu can go in its notes as the transitive partner.

cuts.trap: There is no 'turn up' verb: volume up is oto o ookiku suru ('make the sound big') and down is chiisaku suru; oto o ageru / sageru also work.
cuts.reason: Two reviewers wanted it: 'turn it up' is a daily request, and you need the noun oto plus -ku suru.

cuts.trap: Not deru: 'it came out nice' is kirei ni toreta / yoku toreteru (it got taken well).
cuts.reason: Toreta is the 'can/did get taken' form of toru; the shashin o toru card can carry kirei ni toreta.

cuts.trap: Sounds like naru 'become', but this is 鳴る 'ring': keitai natteru yo = 'your phone's ringing'.
cuts.reason: Correct, but you mostly hear it rather than say it.

cuts.trap: Not terebi ni aru: 'the film is on TV tonight' is konban terebi de yaru ('TV is doing it'); ni deru is for people.
cuts.reason: Natural (terebi de yatteru), but less needed now that people stream.

cuts.trap: Not shingou: phone signal is denpa ('radio waves'); shingou is a traffic light.
cuts.reason: Denpa ga hairu is kept and teaches the noun denpa.

cuts.trap: Not just insutooru suru: everyday 'get the app' is apuri o ireru ('put in'); deleting it is kesu.
cuts.reason: Useful modern phrase, but mainly when helping someone set up a phone.

cuts.trap: Not okuru: okuru sends to a person; putting a photo up online is ageru ('raise') or appu suru, as in insuta ni ageta.
cuts.reason: Correct, mostly among social-media users; appu suru is also common.

cuts.trap: Not terebi ni iru: a person on TV terebi ni deru ('comes out on'); a programme is terebi de yaru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but being on TV rarely comes up in daily talk.

cuts.trap: Not kowareru: a cracked screen wareru ('splits'); kowareru means the phone stopped working.
cuts.reason: Only for a cracked phone screen.
'Send a message' maps straight onto okuru.
'Listen to music' translates word for word.

cuts.trap: For a phone or online video the everyday word is douga; bideo suggests a camcorder or tape. The verb is the same toru as for photos.
cuts.reason: Same toru as shashin o toru; douga is just the noun for video.

cuts.trap: waifai aru? is fine, but natives often ask waifai tonderu? ('is Wi-Fi flying?'), which is opaque if you only know tobu as 'fly'.
cuts.reason: Casual-only and niche; waifai aru? works everywhere.

cuts.trap: Not jiko o shita or jiko o motta: being in an accident is jiko ni au, the same sound as meeting someone. A driver who causes one jiko o okosu.
cuts.reason: Good trap (ni au), but accidents rarely come up; you'd mostly hear it.

cuts.trap: Not michi ga isogashii (busy is for people) or kuruma ga ooi: crowded roads, trains and shops are konderu.
cuts.reason: Same komu/konderu as mise ga komu; that card can list michi as a partner.

cuts.trap: Not kuruma o paaku suru: parking is just 'stopping' the car, tomeru (chuusha suru is the word on signs). Not yameru, which means quitting.
cuts.reason: Daily for anyone who drives ('doko ni tomeru?'), and English 'park' gives no hint of tomeru.

cuts.trap: Not densha ga yameru: yameru is quitting. A train stopping (at a station, or halted) is tomaru.
cuts.reason: 'The train stops' maps onto tomaru once you know the verb.

cuts.trap: Not takushii o toru or takushii o tsukamu: hailing one in the street is hirou ('pick up'). tsukamaeru also works; phoning for one is yobu.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but taxis are an occasional topic; takushii yobu covers most needs.

cuts.trap: Not shuuden o misu suru: Japanese says the last train 'is gone', as in shuuden nakunatchau!
cuts.reason: Real nightlife line, but reviewers suggest shuuden o nogasu as the better card to add.

cuts.trap: Not kuruma de byouki ni naru: motion sickness uses you, the verb for getting drunk (kuruma yoi, fune ni you).
cuts.reason: Good trap, but carsickness is an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not nimotsu o oku or nimotsu o nokosu: handing bags over to be kept (hotel, locker, airport check-in) is azukeru. Leaving them behind by mistake is wasureru.
cuts.reason: Hotel, locker and airport situations only.

cuts.trap: Not michi ga karappo or michi ga hima: an uncrowded road or train is suiteru, the same suku as in onaka ga suku.
cuts.reason: Correct (suiteru), but roads being clear rarely comes up.

cuts.trap: Not michi o iu or michi o hanasu: telling someone the way is oshieru ('teach'), as in eki made no michi oshiete kuremasen ka?
cuts.reason: Learners already reach for oshiete when asking the way; it's a natural guess.

cuts.trap: Not eki o tsuku or eki ni kita for 'I'm here': arriving is tsuku with ni, as in ima eki tsuita.
cuts.reason: The versatility list already teaches tsuku = arrive with ni.

cuts.trap: Not densha ga hanareru or densha ga saru: a train or bus leaving is just deru, as in tsugi no densha nanji ni deru?
cuts.reason: Deru = leave is the obvious guess.

cuts.trap: Not michi o tanomu or michi o shitsumon suru: asking the way is kiku, the verb for listening.
cuts.reason: Kiku = ask is in the versatility list; the pairing is a natural guess.

cuts.trap: Not seki o ageru: offering your seat to someone is yuzuru ('hand over').
cuts.reason: Correct, but you'd mostly see it on signs; rarely said.

cuts.trap: Not michi ni wataru or kurosu suru: what you cross takes o (michi, hashi, shingou o wataru).
cuts.reason: 'Cross the road' maps onto wataru; only the o needs noticing.

cuts.trap: Not takushii o kakeru: kakeru goes with denwa (the phone call), while the taxi you summon is yobu.
cuts.reason: 'Call a taxi' maps onto yobu (call, summon).

cuts.trap: Not yotei o motsu: having plans is aru (yotei aru kara = I've got plans).
cuts.reason: Two reviewers wanted it: 'yotei aru kara' is the standard way to say 'I've got plans'.

cuts.trap: Not jikan ni tsuku or dekiru: making it in time is maniau, with ni on the deadline or train (densha ni maniatta).
cuts.reason: Densha ni maniau already teaches maniau with ni.

cuts.trap: Learners swap kariru (borrow) and kasu (lend). The lender takes ni or kara (tomodachi ni karita).
cuts.reason: Toire o kariru teaches kariru = borrow; the kasu/kariru swap is a single-verb lesson.

cuts.trap: Not yakusoku o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a promise is mamoru, 'protect' (jikan o mamoru = be on time).
cuts.reason: Common and a true trap: promises are 'protected' (mamoru), not kept or held.

cuts.trap: Not okane o sugosu: money is spent with tsukau, 'use'; sugosu is only for spending time.
cuts.reason: 'Use money' is the natural guess, and it's right.

cuts.trap: Not jikan o korosu: killing time is tsubusu, 'crush' (kafe de jikan tsubushiteta).
cuts.reason: Good trap (crush, not kill), but it comes up less than the kept time phrases.

cuts.trap: yakusoku isn't only 'promise': it means any arrangement to meet, so kyou wa yakusoku ga aru = I'm meeting someone today.
cuts.reason: Youji ga aru and yotei ga hairu already cover having plans.

cuts.trap: Not keikaku o tsukuru: plans are tateru, 'stand up'. yotei o tateru works the same way.
cuts.reason: Somewhat formal; in conversation people say keikaku suru or just kimeru.

cuts.trap: Not yoyaku o tsukuru: you 'take' a booking (yoyaku toreta? = did you get one?). Plain yoyaku suru also works.
cuts.reason: Correct, but plain yoyaku suru is what most people say.

cuts.trap: Not jikan o tsukau or sugosu: putting time into something is kakeru (jikan kakete tsukutta), the transitive of kakaru.
cuts.reason: Its card is jikan ga kakaru; kakeru can sit in its notes as the transitive partner.

cuts.trap: Not kokoro o kaeru: changing your mind is ki ga kawaru, with ki as the subject (ki ga kawattara itte).
cuts.reason: Natural, but less frequent than the ki phrases you already have.

cuts.trap: When the money is the subject the verb is tamaru (okane tamattara = once I've saved up), not transitive tameru.
cuts.reason: Okane o tameru is kept; tamaru is its intransitive partner for the notes.

cuts.trap: Swapped with kariru: kashite = lend me; karite ii? = can I borrow?
cuts.reason: The versatility list already teaches kasu = lend.

cuts.trap: Not okane o harau: paying back a loan is kaesu, 'give back' (ashita kaesu ne).
cuts.reason: 'Give back money' maps straight onto kaesu.

cuts.trap: Not yotei o tsukuru or oku: you 'put in' a plan (raishuu ni ireta = I put it in for next week).
cuts.reason: Yotei ga hairu is kept; ireru is its transitive partner for the notes.

cuts.trap: Not yakusoku o kowasu: breaking a promise is yaburu, 'tear'.
cuts.reason: Correct, but heavier and rarer than yakusoku o mamoru.

cuts.trap: Not jikan o jiyuu ni suru: clearing time for someone is akeru (ashita akete oku ne).
cuts.reason: Jikan ga aku is kept; akeru is its transitive partner for the notes.

cuts.trap: 'Something came up at work' is shigoto ga haitchatta (work 'entered' the schedule), not okiru or kuru.
cuts.reason: Same hairu as yotei ga hairu ('something got booked in'); that card can list shigoto.

cuts.trap: Attending a class is deru with ni. jugyou o deru would mean walking out of it, and shusseki suru is the formal word.
cuts.reason: Kaigi ni deru already teaches ni deru = attend.

cuts.trap: Landing a job is usually intransitive, shigoto ga mitsukatta (a job turned up). English 'I found' pushes toward shigoto o mitsuketa, which sounds less natural.
cuts.reason: Correct and natural, but job-hunting talk is occasional.

cuts.trap: English 'take' works here. The trap is the contrast: a day off sick is shigoto o yasumu, while a planned break is yasumi o toru.
cuts.reason: 'Take time off' maps straight onto toru.

cuts.trap: Handing in is dasu ('put out'), not ageru or teishutsu suru in speech. When a teacher says it, dasu means 'set homework'.
cuts.reason: The versatility list's dasu already includes 'hand in'; homework is also school-only.

cuts.trap: Scores are 'taken', not received: hyakuten totta, ii ten toreta (not ten o morau).
cuts.reason: Test scores only; mostly student talk.

cuts.trap: Not menkyo o morau: you 'take' a licence by earning it (menkyo totta). The same goes for qualifications: shikaku o toru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but getting a licence is an occasional topic; toru = get is in the versatility list.

cuts.trap: 'I go to a Japanese school' as a routine is kayotteru, not itteru: iku is one trip, kayou is regular attendance.
cuts.reason: The real lesson is the verb kayou (go regularly), which works with any place.

cuts.trap: Not shukudai o morau: homework 'comes out', shukudai ga deta (we got homework). It is the intransitive half of shukudai o dasu.
cuts.reason: School only.

cuts.trap: A topic that's on the test 'comes out' in it, kore tesuto ni deru?, not shiken ni aru.
cuts.reason: Exam prep only.

cuts.trap: Mostly guessable from yameru = quit. The catch is that you quit the company or the job (kaisha/shigoto o yameru), and 辞める sounds identical to 止める 'stop'.
cuts.reason: Yameru = quit is the obvious guess.

cuts.trap: 'I got paid' is the pay 'coming in', kyuuryou haitta (or kyuuryou ga deta), not a passive of harau.
cuts.reason: Natural, but payday talk is occasional; kyuuryou-bi covers a lot.

cuts.trap: Not kodomo o motte iru or kodomo ga aru: people you 'have' take ga iru (kodomo iru? kyoudai iru? kareshi iru?).
cuts.reason: The versatility list's iru already covers 'have (people, pets)'.

cuts.trap: Not kareshi o eru or morau: a partner 'comes into being' with ga dekiru (kanojo dekita!).
cuts.reason: Same ga dekiru as tomodachi ga dekiru; that card can list kareshi/kanojo.

cuts.trap: Not shitsumon o kiku: 'ask a question' is shitsumon (o) suru, and kiku alone means 'ask' without the noun.
cuts.reason: A plain noun + suru verb; the lesson is the noun shitsumon.

cuts.trap: English 'answer' leads to kotae, which is an answer to a question; replying to a person, message or call is henji (o) suru.
cuts.reason: A plain noun + suru verb; meeru o kaesu covers replying to messages.

cuts.trap: English 'disturb/bother' has no matching verb: it is jama (o) suru, and entering someone's home is the set phrase ojama shimasu.
cuts.reason: A noun + suru verb (jama shinaide); the lesson is the noun jama.

cuts.trap: There is no verb for 'thank': you 'say thanks' with orei o iu (orei also means a thank-you gift).
cuts.reason: A bit formal; in conversation people say arigatou tte itta.

cuts.trap: Not hanasu hitsuyou ga aru: 'I need to talk to you' is chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
cuts.reason: 'Chotto hanashi ga aru n da kedo' is the standard opener for 'I need to talk to you', and English gives no hint.

cuts.trap: Mostly guessable, but 'talk about X' is usually X no hanashi (o suru), shorter than X ni tsuite hanasu.
cuts.reason: 'Do a talk' is close to English and easy to guess.

cuts.trap: Not ai kontakuto o suru: eyes 'meet' with au 合う (fit), not au 会う (meet a person).
cuts.reason: Correct, but eye contact rarely comes up in conversation.

cuts.trap: English 'take care of' gives no clue: you 'see to the bother' with mendou o miru. Keep it apart from mendokusai (what a hassle).
cuts.reason: Correct, but sewa o suru and other phrases do most of this job.

cuts.trap: There is no verb for 'complain': you 'say complaints', as in monku iwanaide (guchi o iu = grumble, vent).
cuts.reason: Very common ('monku iwanaide'), and there's no verb for 'complain' to translate.

cuts.trap: Not tatakau, which means battle: a fight or argument between people is kenka suru (kare to kenka shita, with to).
cuts.reason: A plain noun + suru verb (kenka shita); the lesson is the noun kenka.

cuts.trap: Not ki o tsukeru: caring for a pet, child or plant is sewa o suru (inu no sewa).
cuts.reason: Correct, but mostly pet- or child-care talk.

cuts.trap: There is no phrasal verb for 'make up': it is nakanaori suru ('mending the relationship'), never tsukuru.
cuts.reason: A plain noun + suru verb; the lesson is the noun nakanaori.

cuts.trap: Not gitaa o suru: guitar takes hiku like the piano (gitaa hikeru? = can you play guitar?).
cuts.reason: Piano o hiku teaches hiku for stringed and keyboard instruments.

cuts.trap: Not shiai o suru for 'play in the game': taking part is deru (nichiyou shiai deru), and so is taikai ni deru (enter a tournament).
cuts.reason: Same ni deru = take part as kaigi ni deru.

cuts.trap: Not taiko o hiku or suru: drums are hit, tataku, and a drum kit works the same way (doramu o tataku).
cuts.reason: Only for people who play drums.

cuts.trap: Not chiimu o sanka suru: you 'enter' a team, club or circle with ni hairu (saakuru ni haitta).
cuts.reason: Correct, but joining a team is an occasional topic; hairu = join is in the versatility list.

cuts.trap: Not tsuri o iku or tsuri suru ni iku: an activity noun takes ni iku directly (tsuri ni itta).
cuts.reason: Same 'activity ni iku' pattern as mukae ni iku.

cuts.trap: Not fue o hiku or suru: wind instruments are blown with fuku, the verb of kaze ga fuku (the wind blows).
cuts.reason: Only for wind-instrument players.

cuts.trap: Not shumi o motsu in speech: having a hobby is ga aru (nanka shumi aru?), like jikan ga aru.
cuts.reason: 'Have a hobby' maps onto ga aru like most 'have' phrases.
'Sing a song' translates word for word.

cuts.trap: Not kanjiru for 'it feels like...': the everyday form is ~ kanji ga suru (or ~ tte kanji).
cuts.reason: The versatility list has tte kanji and ki ga suru, which do the same job.
cuts.coveredBy: tte kanji / ki ga suru (versatility list)

cuts.trap: 'I know how you feel' is sono kimochi wakaru, not shitteru: shiru is for knowing facts.
cuts.reason: 'Sono kimochi wakaru' is a very common empathy line, and English 'know' pushes you to the wrong verb (shiru).

cuts.trap: 'I had a scary experience' is kowai omoi o shita, not kowai keiken o motta: the feeling is the object of suru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but used mainly in storytelling; a bit advanced for this list.

cuts.trap: 'I heard someone's voice' is koe ga shita (suru) when it just reaches you, not koe o kiita.
cuts.reason: Same frame as oto ga suru; that card can list koe.

cuts.trap: 'I have a bad feeling about this' is iya na yokan ga suru, not warui kimochi ga aru, which sounds like nausea.
cuts.reason: A memorable phrase, but a set expression you rarely need.

cuts.trap: 'Distracted/distracting' has no adjective in Japanese: ki ga chiru (urusakute ki ga chiru); learners only manage shuuchuu dekinai.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but less frequent than the kept ki phrases.

cuts.trap: 'Smell this!' is kaide mite: actively smelling is kagu, not nioi o suru or kiku.
cuts.reason: Correct, but mostly heard as 'kaide mite'; nioi ga suru covers most smell talk.

cuts.trap: Not koe ga takai, which means high-pitched, and not just urusai: a loud voice is ookii (big).
cuts.reason: Common remark ('koe ookii yo'), and the trap is real: koe ga takai means high-pitched, not loud.

cuts.trap: False friend: sutairu ga ii means a good figure (slim, well-proportioned), not good fashion sense. Fashion is oshare.
cuts.reason: A false friend you'll hear often: it means a good figure, not good fashion sense.

cuts.trap: Not 'nagai kami ga aru' for 'she has long hair': say kanojo wa kami ga nagai.
cuts.reason: Same 'feature ga adjective' frame as se ga takai; swap in kami.

cuts.trap: Not kami ga hikui: hair length is mijikai. Hikui is only for height (se ga hikui).
cuts.reason: Same 'feature ga adjective' frame as se ga takai.

cuts.trap: Not 'hayai rannaa': a fast runner is ashi ga hayai ('legs are fast'). Ashi ga osoi is slow.
cuts.reason: Natural, but describing someone's running speed is occasional.

cuts.trap: Not 'sugu byouki ni naru hito' as the default: 'gets sick a lot' is karada ga yowai. Karada ga joubu is the sturdy opposite.
cuts.reason: Correct, but less frequent than the kept health phrases.

cuts.trap: Not se ga sodatsu: 'you've grown!' is se nobita ne (or ookiku natta ne).
cuts.reason: Mostly said to children ('se nobita ne'); ookiku natta also works.

cuts.trap: Not kami ga sodatsu: hair grows = nobiru. 'Your hair's grown' is kami nobita ne.
cuts.reason: Natural, but an occasional remark.

cuts.trap: Not kami o sodateru: growing your hair out is nobasu ('lengthen'), e.g. ima kami nobashiteru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not 'shiroi hito', which reads as 'a white person': fair skin is iro ga shiroi ('colour is white'). Iro ga kuroi means tanned.
cuts.reason: Correct, but commenting on skin tone is uncommon and can be touchy.

cuts.trap: Not hi o morau or hi ga kuru: a sunny room is one the sun 'hits' (hi ga ataru); hiatari ga ii = gets lots of sun.
cuts.reason: Mostly flat-hunting talk (hiatari ga ii).

cuts.trap: Not tsuyu ga owaru: the rainy season 'opens out' (akeru), the same akeru as yo ga akeru (day breaks).
cuts.reason: Rainy-season talk only, once a year.

cuts.trap: English has a verb, but in Japanese a sneeze 'comes out' (kushami ga deru); kushami o suru also works.
cuts.reason: Same 'symptom ga deru' frame as netsu ga deru.

cuts.english: one's leg goes numb, falls asleep
cuts.trap: Not ashi ga neru: a leg doesn't 'sleep' in Japanese, it goes numb (shibireru). The classic case is after sitting seiza.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but mainly after sitting seiza.

cuts.english: get a cramp in one's leg
cuts.trap: Not ashi ni kuranpu ga aru: a cramping leg 'tsuru' (pulls tight). It's usually said in the past: ashi tsutta!
cuts.reason: Correct, but a rare situation.

cuts.trap: Not koe o nakusu: a voice 'withers' (kareru, like a plant) after karaoke, cheering or a cold.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but an occasional complaint.

cuts.trap: Not kusuri o nomu or tsukeru: creams, ointment and sunscreen are 'spread' on (nuru); nomu is only for swallowing.
cuts.reason: Correct (nuru for creams), but less common than kusuri o nomu.

cuts.trap: Not bansoukou o kiru or kakeru: anything stuck on flat (plasters, compresses, stickers, posters) is haru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but a rare noun and situation.

cuts.trap: Not shujutsu o motsu: the patient 'receives' an operation (ukeru), like shiken o ukeru. Casually a patient can also say shujutsu suru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but operations rarely come up; shiken o ukeru teaches the same ukeru.

cuts.trap: Not te o moyasu or yaku: a burn is a noun you 'do' (yakedo o suru), like kega o suru. Casually: yakedo shita.
cuts.reason: Same 'injury + suru' frame as kega o suru.

cuts.trap: Not atama o tataku or naguru, which mean hitting on purpose: knocking your head on something is butsukeru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional mishap.

cuts.english: be off, not working right (body, form or a device)
cuts.trap: English splits 'feel off' and 'act up', but Japanese uses choushi ga warui for both your body and a phone or PC.
cuts.reason: Guai ga warui covers feeling off; choushi can go in its notes, including for devices.

cuts.trap: Not kenkouteki, which is stiff and written: 'healthy food' is karada ni ii tabemono, and unhealthy is karada ni warui.
cuts.reason: Said all the time about food and habits ('karada ni ii yo'); kenkouteki sounds stiff.

cuts.trap: Not taichou ga byouki ni naru: you 'crumble' your condition (taichou o kuzusu). It's the neutral everyday way to say you got sick.
cuts.reason: A bit formal; guai ga warui is the everyday version.

cuts.trap: Not tsukare ga naoru: tiredness 'comes off' (toreru), like a stain. It's mostly negative: tsukare ga torenai.
cuts.reason: 'Tsukare ga torenai' is a very common complaint, and toreru is unguessable.

cuts.trap: Not nikibi o morau or toru: spots, blisters and bruises 'form' (dekiru), as in mame ga dekiru and aza ga dekiru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not me o shimeru: eyes are shut with tsuburu (or tojiru); shimeru is for doors and windows.
cuts.reason: Mostly heard from photographers or doctors; you rarely say it.

cuts.english: see a doctor, get checked out
cuts.trap: Not isha o miru, which means looking at a doctor: the doctor sees you, so it's isha ni mite morau.
cuts.reason: Byouin ni iku is the everyday way to say 'see a doctor'.

cuts.trap: Not iki ga nakunaru: breath 'snaps' (kireru), the same kireru as juuden ga kireru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional remark.

cuts.trap: Not just atatakai fuku o kiru: 'wrap up warm' is one noun, atsugi ('thick wearing'), plus suru.
cuts.reason: Rare noun; most people say attakai kakkou shite.

cuts.trap: Not kami o migaku: teeth are brushed with migaku, hair with tokasu.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but a narrow routine phrase.

cuts.trap: English 'shave' needs no object, but Japanese names what comes off: hige o soru (face), ashi no ke o soru (legs).
cuts.reason: Correct, but the lesson is mostly the verb soru; an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not mezamashi ga deru or iku: an alarm 'rings' (naru), like denwa ga naru.
cuts.reason: Mezamashi o kakeru is kept; naru fits in its notes.

cuts.trap: Not ofuro o tsukuru or ireru: you 'boil' the bath (wakasu), and the tub itself announces ofuro ga wakimashita.
cuts.reason: Common in Japanese homes, but modern tubs make ofuro o ireru / ofuro waita more typical.

cuts.trap: 'Get out' pushes learners to deru, but for the bath natives mostly say agaru ('come up'): ofuro agatta yo.
cuts.reason: Natural, but a narrow home-routine line.

cuts.english: turn on the tap / the water
cuts.trap: Not mizu o tsukeru: tsukeru is for lights and power, while water is 'let out' (dasu).
cuts.reason: Correct, but rarely needs saying.

cuts.english: turn off the tap / the water
cuts.trap: Not mizu o kesu: kesu is for lights and fire, while water is 'stopped' (tomeru).
cuts.reason: Correct, but rarely needs saying.

cuts.trap: Japanese has no word for 'flush': you make the toilet 'flow' (nagasu), as in toire nagashite or mizu o nagasu.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but mostly said to children.

cuts.trap: Not kabi ga sodatsu or naru: mould 'sprouts' (haeru), the same verb as hair and weeds. Example: pan ni kabi haeteru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not sentakumono o ireru or motte kuru: laundry is 'taken in' (torikomu). Example: ame futte kita, sentakumono torikonde!
cuts.reason: Common in Japanese homes, but less than putting laundry out.

cuts.trap: Not nimotsu ga tsuku: deliveries 'reach' you (todoku); tsuku is for people and trains arriving.
cuts.reason: Daily online-shopping talk ('nimotsu todoita?'), and English 'arrive' pushes you to tsuku.

cuts.trap: Switches are 'put in' (ireru) to turn on and 'cut' (kiru) to turn off, not tsukeru and kesu.
cuts.reason: Correct, but most devices just take tsukeru in speech.

cuts.english: lay out the futon, make up the bed
cuts.trap: Not futon o oku or hiraku: a futon is 'spread' (shiku) at night and folded away with tatamu.
cuts.reason: Only if you sleep on a futon.

cuts.trap: Not osake o ireru: ireru is for making tea and coffee, while pouring into someone's glass is tsugu.
cuts.reason: Drinking-party etiquette; useful at work dinners but occasional.

cuts.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'sober up': being drunk 'wears off' (sameru), the same verb as me ga sameru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'expire': the date 'snaps' (kireru), as in gyuunyuu, shoumikigen kireteru. It's also used for passports and coupons.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but an occasional kitchen or paperwork remark.

cuts.trap: Not okane o kowasu: notes are 'crumbled' into change (kuzusu). Example: ichiman en kuzushite moraemasu ka.
cuts.reason: Only when breaking a note.

cuts.english: have time or money to spare; be relaxed about it
cuts.trap: English 'can afford' or 'have time to spare' has no single verb here; Japanese uses yoyuu ga aru / nai for time, money and calm.
cuts.reason: Yoyuu ga nai is kept; aru is just the positive form.

cuts.trap: Not just yotei ga ippai: a full schedule is 'stuffed' (tsumaru), like a blocked nose. Example: raishuu wa yotei ga tsumatteru.
cuts.reason: Natural, but yotei ga ippai is commoner and transparent.

cuts.english: can make it, can fit it in
cuts.trap: Not tsugou ga dekiru: an arrangement 'attaches' (tsuku). Example: tsugou tsuitara renraku shite.
cuts.reason: Tsugou ga ii already covers whether a time works for someone.

cuts.trap: Not jugyou o nuku or tobasu: skipping class or work is saboru (from 'sabotage'), while skipping a meal is nuku.
cuts.reason: Student slang, casual only.

cuts.trap: Not kopii o tsukuru: copies are 'taken' (toru), like shashin o toru; kopii suru also works.
cuts.reason: Office-only; kopii suru also works.

cuts.trap: Keep it apart from shigoto o sagasu (look for one) and shigoto ga mitsukaru (one turns up): mitsukeru is the transitive 'find'.
cuts.reason: Less natural than shigoto ga mitsukaru, which was also cut.

cuts.trap: Not tomodachi o tsukuru: 'make friends with X' is X to tomodachi ni naru, while tomodachi ga dekiru means gaining friends in general.
cuts.reason: Tomodachi ga dekiru is kept; ni naru can go in its notes.

cuts.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'dump': you get 'shaken off' (furu, passive furareru), as in kanojo ni furareta. Don't confuse it with ame ni furareru.
cuts.reason: Common gossip ('furareta'), but a narrow topic.

cuts.trap: Not uso ga mitsukaru: lies and secrets 'come out' with bareru (casual), as in uso bareta.
cuts.reason: Casual and natural, but less frequent than uso o tsuku.

cuts.trap: Not kodomo o motsu or morau: a child 'comes into being' (dekiru), while kodomo ga iru means you already have kids.
cuts.reason: Natural, but a life-event topic; akachan ga dekita is the more common wording.

cuts.english: the conversation gets lively, have a great chat
cuts.trap: No English verb fits: talk and parties 'swell up' (moriagaru), as in sugoi moriagatta ne.
cuts.reason: Natural (moriagatta ne), but an occasional comment.

cuts.trap: Not takarakuji ni katsu: prizes and lotteries are 'hit' (ataru), while katsu is for games and matches.
cuts.reason: Lottery talk only; a duplicate of takarakuji ga ataru.

cuts.trap: 'Exercise' pushes learners to undou suru, but casual talk prefers karada o ugokasu ('move the body').
cuts.reason: 'Move the body' is literal, and undou suru is also fine.

cuts.trap: Japanese has no verb for 'look forward': you 'make it a pleasure', as in tanoshimi ni shiteru (ne).
cuts.reason: The versatility list already has tanoshimi ('looking forward to it'); tanoshimi ni shiteru is its verb form.

cuts.trap: Not oto o tsukuru: noise is 'raised' (tateru). Example: oto tatenaide, akachan neteru kara.
cuts.reason: Good trap, but heard mostly as 'oto tatenaide'.

cuts.trap: Not yume ga hontou ni naru: dreams and wishes are 'granted' (kanau), and yume o kanaeru means making one come true.
cuts.reason: Correct, but more for songs and speeches than daily talk.

cuts.english: embarrass oneself, be put to shame
cuts.trap: Not hazukashii ni naru: you 'scratch up' shame (haji o kaku), the same kaku as ase o kaku and ibiki o kaku.
cuts.reason: Correct, but hazukashikatta is what people usually say.

cuts.trap: Like kami o kiru, you say you dyed your hair even when the salon did it. kinpatsu ni someru = go blond.
cuts.reason: Correct, but an occasional topic.

cuts.trap: Not hige o sodateru or nobasu: facial hair is 'made to sprout' (hayasu), the transitive of haeru. hige haeteru hito = a man with a beard.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.english: be a good person, have a nice personality
cuts.trap: 'He's nice' is usually seikaku ga ii or yasashii; seikaku ga warui means mean or nasty.
cuts.reason: 'Personality is good' is a literal guess, and it's right.

cuts.trap: Not mimi ga kikoenai: the plain, polite way is 'far ears' (mimi ga tooi), the mirror of me ga warui.
cuts.reason: Correct and polite, but rarely needed.

cuts.trap: Not juutai de tomaru: you 'fall into' traffic (hamaru), the same verb as geemu ni hamaru (get hooked).
cuts.reason: Natural, but mainly for drivers.

cuts.english: get hit / run over by a car
cuts.trap: Not kuruma ni utareru: being run over is hikareru, the passive of hiku, which sounds the same as the hiku in kaze o hiku.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare (and mostly heard as a warning).

cuts.trap: Not gasorin o kau or morau: fuel is 'put in' (ireru), as in gasorin irete kara iku.
cuts.reason: Drivers only.

cuts.trap: Not seki o tamotsu or sukuu: 'save me a seat' is seki totte oite, and seki o yoyaku suru means booking one.
cuts.reason: Good trap ('seki totte oite'), but occasional.

cuts.english: the call drops, get cut off
cuts.trap: Not denwa ga ochiru: a call 'snaps' (kireru). It's the intransitive of denwa o kiru (hang up).
cuts.reason: Denwa o kiru is kept; kireru fits in its notes as the intransitive partner.

cuts.trap: Not just yoku kikoenai: the set phrase is 'the phone is far', as in chotto denwa ga tooi n desu ga.
cuts.reason: A set phone phrase, but rare and a little formal.

cuts.english: be in a photo, appear in a picture
cuts.trap: Not shashin ni iru or haitte iru: appearing in a photo is utsuru, as in kono shashin ni utsutteru no dare?
cuts.reason: Correct, but mostly heard as a question about a photo.

cuts.trap: 'Silent mode' is the made-in-Japan manaa moodo ('manner mode') with ni suru, not sairento ni oku.

cuts.english: sleep lightly, be a light sleeper

cuts.trap: Not kibun ga warui, which means feeling sick: a bad mood is kigen ga warui. A good mood is kigen ga ii or gokigen.
