cuts.trap: Nothing in 'I don't feel like it' leads to noru (ride). The plain way to say it is ki ga noranai.
cuts.reason: Natural, but less frequent than the kept ki phrases; yaruki ga denai is close.

cuts.english: feel heavy and run-down, feel sluggish
cuts.trap: Not just tsukareta: the heavy, achy feeling of a cold coming on is karada ga darui.
cuts.reason: People mostly say just darui; guai ga warui covers the rest.

cuts.trap: Not suibun o nomu: you 'take in' fluids, suibun o toru, just as you say eiyou o toru for nutrition.
cuts.reason: Mostly heard as advice in summer; you rarely say it.

cuts.trap: 'Sigh' is a verb in English. Japanese uses a noun with tsuku, the same verb as uso o tsuku.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rarely said.

cuts.english: work a shift, be on the rota
cuts.trap: Not shifuto o suru: you 'enter' a shift, shifuto ni hairu (ashita shifuto haitteru).
cuts.reason: Shift work only.

cuts.english: get the hang of it, get the knack
cuts.trap: The set phrase is kotsu o tsukamu ('grab the knack'). Kotsu ga wakaru is also heard, but kotsu o toru is not.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: work up the courage, be brave
cuts.trap: Not yuuki o motsu or mitsukeru: you 'put out' courage, yuuki o dasu (yuuki dashite itta), as in genki o dasu.
cuts.reason: Same dasu as genki o dasu.

cuts.english: be perceptive, quick to catch on, have good instincts
cuts.trap: English 'sharp' leads to atama ga ii, which means clever. Picking up on things is kan ga ii.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: be compatible, go well together (people, also food pairings)
cuts.trap: 'We're compatible' has no Japanese verb to copy. You say the match is good, aishou ga ii (also wain to chiizu wa aishou ga ii).
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: have things to talk about, click in conversation
cuts.trap: Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'. People whose conversation fits are hanashi ga au; ki ga au is the separate idiom.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not demae o chuumon suru or kau: you 'take' delivery, demae o toru. Younger people also say uubaa tanomu.
cuts.reason: A bit dated; younger people say uubaa tanomu.

cuts.english: a queue forms, there's a line
cuts.trap: Not gyouretsu ga aru: a queue 'comes into being', gyouretsu ga dekiteru. Joining it is narabu.
cuts.reason: Correct, but narabu covers most queue talk.

cuts.english: put something off, deal with it later
cuts.trap: 'Put off' has no Japanese verb to copy. You turn the task into 'later', atomawashi ni suru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.english: a bug turns up (in the house)
cuts.trap: Not mushi ga iru for the moment of seeing it: pests (and ghosts) 'come out', gokiburi ga deta!
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.english: be a small eater, not eat much
cuts.trap: Not taberu no ga sukunai or chiisai: a small eater's eating is 'thin', shoku ga hosoi.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.english: get tested, have a (medical) check or test
cuts.trap: Not kensa o suru, which is what the doctor does: the patient 'receives' a test, kensa o ukeru, as in shujutsu o ukeru.
cuts.reason: Same ukeru as shiken o ukeru.

cuts.trap: Not kaze ga mawaru / hiromaru: a bug going around is hayaru, the same verb used for trends (infuru ga hayatteru).
cuts.reason: Natural, but mainly in winter.

cuts.english: get over a cold (make it better)
cuts.trap: Learners use intransitive naoru for everything. Telling someone to get well uses transitive naosu: hayaku kaze naoshite ne.
cuts.reason: Less common than kaze ga naoru; it fits that card's notes if you re-add it.

cuts.trap: English 'my legs are sore' leads to ashi ga itai. Next-day exercise ache is one noun, kinnikutsuu, with ni naru.
cuts.reason: Natural, but gym talk.

cuts.trap: Not netchuushou o toru / morau: you 'become' heatstroke, ni naru, usually in the warning netchuushou ni naranai you ni.
cuts.reason: Mostly heard as a summer warning.

cuts.english: be wide awake (and can't get to sleep)
cuts.trap: Not me ga sameru, which means waking up. Lying in bed wide awake is me ga saeru (koohii nonda kara me ga saete nerarenai).
cuts.reason: The me ga sameru card already covers feeling wide awake.

cuts.english: appear in a dream; dream about (someone)
cuts.trap: English 'I dreamt about you' leads to translating 'about'. Japanese says the person came out in the dream: yume ni kimi ga dete kita.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: make a dream come true, achieve one's dream
cuts.trap: English 'achieve / realise a dream' gives tassei suru or jitsugen suru. The everyday verb is kanaeru, the transitive half of yume ga kanau.
cuts.reason: More for speeches and songs than daily talk.

cuts.trap: English 'is it cooked / done?' leads to yaketa? or ryouri sareta. Asking whether meat is cooked through is mou hi tootteru?
cuts.reason: A cooking detail.

cuts.english: (a dish) makes you eat more rice; goes great with rice
cuts.trap: English has no matching phrase. Praising a dish as moreish with rice is gohan ga susumu, 'the rice moves forward', also sake ga susumu.
cuts.reason: A nice food compliment, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not gohan o ireru / dasu: dishing rice or soup into a bowl is yosou (gohan yosotte kureru?).
cuts.reason: Correct, but a home-kitchen detail.

cuts.english: the flavour has soaked in (simmered food)
cuts.trap: Not aji ga hairu: flavour soaking into simmered food is shimiru (kono daikon, aji ga shimite oishii).
cuts.reason: Simmered dishes only.

cuts.english: the alcohol kicks in; start to feel drunk
cuts.trap: English 'it's hitting me' has no verb a learner could map. Feeling the drink kick in is yoi ga mawaru, also osake ga mawaru.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: black out; one's memory goes blank (from drinking)
cuts.trap: Not kioku o nakusu (amnesia, formal): blacking out from drink is kioku ga tobu (nomisugite kioku tonda).
cuts.reason: Casual and occasional.

cuts.english: get caught at a red light
cuts.trap: Not shingou de tomaru / matsu alone: getting stopped by lights is hikkakaru, 'get snagged' (shingou zenbu hikkakatta).
cuts.reason: Natural, but a narrow remark.

cuts.trap: Not pakku suru or nimotsu o ireru: packing a bag is tsumeru, 'cram in' (mou nimotsu tsumeta?). nimotsu o matomeru means 'get your stuff together'.
cuts.reason: Mainly before trips.

cuts.trap: Not himo ga hazureru / aku: a knot coming loose is hodokeru (himo hodoketeru yo). Tying it is himo o musubu.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.english: be offended, take it the wrong way
cuts.trap: Not okoru or kizutsuku: 'don't take this the wrong way / no offence' is ki o waruku shinaide (ne).
cuts.reason: Natural ('ki o waruku shinaide'), but occasional.

cuts.trap: English 'make an excuse' leads to tsukuru. Everyday Japanese uses suru: iiwake suru na.
cuts.reason: A plain noun + suru verb; the lesson is the noun iiwake.

cuts.trap: Not iyahon o kiru / ireru: worn accessories take suru (or tsukeru), like masuku o suru and tokei o suru (iyahon shiteta kara kikoenakatta).
cuts.reason: Same 'accessory + suru' frame as masuku o suru.

cuts.trap: English 'get a perm' leads to morau. A perm is 'put on' with kakeru, like airon o kakeru (paama kaketa no?).
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.english: look up (a word) in the dictionary
cuts.trap: Not jisho o miru / sagasu: consulting a dictionary is hiku, 'pull' (jisho de hiite mita).
cuts.reason: Dated now that people search on their phones.

cuts.english: make fun of, look down on
cuts.trap: Not warau or anything with tsukuru: 'make fun of' is baka ni suru, literally 'treat as a fool'.
cuts.reason: Common ('baka ni shinaide'), and English 'make fun of' gives no hint to ni suru.

cuts.english: blame (someone else), pin it on someone
cuts.trap: Not semeru, which means 'criticise, attack'. To pin the blame on someone is X no sei ni suru.
cuts.reason: '~ no sei ni shinaide' is a common line, and English 'blame' pushes you to semeru, which is wrong.

cuts.trap: Not 'asa no hito ja nai': Japanese says you are weak at mornings, asa ga yowai. The opposite is asa ga tsuyoi.
cuts.reason: Same 'X ga yowai' idea as osake ga yowai; a fun one for that card's notes.

cuts.english: be treated (to a meal or drinks), let someone pay
cuts.trap: Not a passive of a 'treat' verb: the person treated says gochisou ni naru, and the payer says gochisou suru or ogoru.
cuts.reason: Polite and occasional; gochisousama covers the usual moment.

cuts.trap: Not chigai o iu or oshieru: here 'tell' is wakaru, and the difference is the subject. It is usually heard as chigai ga wakaranai.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.trap: There is no single verb for 'waste': Japanese says muda ni suru ('make it useless'), and 'a waste of time' is jikan no muda.
cuts.reason: Jikan no muda is the commoner way to say it.

cuts.trap: Not inu o aruku, because aruku can't take the dog as its object. You go on the dog's walk: inu no sanpo ni iku, or inu o sanpo ni tsureteku.
cuts.reason: Only for dog owners.

cuts.english: invite someone over (to your place), have people over
cuts.trap: Not shoutai suru, which is for formal invitations such as weddings. Having friends over uses yobu, 'call': tomodachi o uchi ni yobu.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.english: be reliable, dependable (someone you can count on)
cuts.trap: There is no plain adjective for 'reliable': a dependable person 'becomes a support', tayori ni naru. Tayori ni suru means 'rely on someone'.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not taijuu o tsukeru or eru: weight is the subject and it increases, taijuu ga fueru. To lose weight is taijuu ga heru, or simply yaseru.
cuts.reason: People mostly say futotta.

cuts.trap: Not nikki o motsu or tamotsu: keeping a diary or any record is tsukeru, as in kakeibo o tsukeru (keep household accounts).
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.english: run a fever, come down with a fever (of a person, often a child)
cuts.trap: Not netsu o morau: with the person as subject it is netsu o dashita (musuko ga netsu dashite). Netsu ga deta is the same event from the fever's side.
cuts.reason: Netsu ga deru is kept; netsu o dasu fits in its notes.

cuts.trap: Not pointo o morau as the default: points build up, so tamaru. Pointo o tameru is collecting them and pointo o tsukau is spending them.
cuts.reason: Same tameru/tamaru as okane o tameru.

cuts.english: music is playing (in a shop, at a party, on the radio)
cuts.trap: Not ongaku ga hiku or ongaku ga suru: a song that's on is kakatteru (or nagareteru), the intransitive of ongaku o kakeru.
cuts.reason: Ongaku o kakeru is kept; kakaru is its intransitive partner for the notes.

cuts.english: stick in one's mind, be memorable
cuts.trap: Not oboeyasui or kioku suru: 'the most memorable part was…' is ichiban inshou ni nokotta no wa…
cuts.reason: A bit bookish for casual talk.

cuts.trap: Not ruuru ni tsuite iku: following rules is mamoru ('protect'), like promises and time. Ruuru ni shitagau is stiffer.
cuts.reason: Natural, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not koe ga fukai: a deep voice is low, hikui. A high-pitched one is koe ga takai.
cuts.reason: Correct, but less often said than koe ga ookii.

cuts.trap: Not kami ga ochiru: hair coming out (in the shower, from stress, with age) is nukeru. Ochiteru is only for a hair lying on the floor.
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.english: come with a drink (a set includes it)
cuts.trap: Not dorinku to kuru: 'comes with' is tsuku (kore, saarada tsuku?). Tsuku 'arrive' is a different verb.
cuts.reason: Handy at restaurants, but mostly heard from staff.

cuts.english: be shocked, be hurt (by news, a remark)
cuts.trap: Not shokku suru: you receive a shock, so shokku uketa. Shokku datta is the other natural way.
cuts.reason: Shokku datta is the commoner way to say it.

cuts.trap: Not kyuuryou o morau, which is just 'get paid': a raise is the salary going up, kyuuryou agatta.
cuts.reason: 'Pay goes up' maps straight onto agaru.

cuts.trap: Not mushiba o motsu: cavities, like pimples and bruises, 'come into being', so dekiru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not deeta o nakusu: files and photos disappear, kieru (shashin zenbu kiechatta). Kesu is deleting them yourself.
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.trap: Not kaminari ga utsu: lightning falls (ochita). Kaminari ga naru is the thunder you hear.
cuts.reason: Correct, but rare.

cuts.trap: Not shio o kakeru: salt is shaken on, furu (same sound as ame ga furu). Kakeru is for liquids like shouyu.
cuts.reason: A cooking detail.

cuts.english: hot water comes out / runs (tap, shower)
cuts.trap: 'There's no hot water' is oyu ga denai, not oyu ga nai. This is the intransitive of mizu o dasu / oyu o dasu.
cuts.reason: 'Hot water comes out' maps straight onto deru.

cuts.trap: English 'call' pushes to denwa o kakeru; you yobu (summon) an ambulance, as in the shout kyuukyuusha yonde!
cuts.reason: 'Call an ambulance' maps onto yobu (call, summon).

cuts.trap: No English pairing to copy. 'Do you like the food here?' is asked as nihon no tabemono, kuchi ni au? Here au means 'fit', not 'meet'.
cuts.reason: Japanese people often ask foreigners 'kuchi ni au?' about the food, so you need to hear and answer it.

cuts.trap: Not waruguchi o hanasu. Badmouthing takes iu, like monku o iu and joudan o iu.
cuts.reason: Correct, but occasional.

cuts.english: skin gets rough or irritated, break out
cuts.trap: English 'my skin is dry / bad' pushes to hada ga kawaku or warui. Skin that flares up from stress, cold or lack of sleep areru (hada areta).
cuts.reason: Correct, but a narrow topic.

cuts.trap: Not himitsu o motsu or tamotsu. You keep a secret with mamoru (protect), the same verb as yakusoku o mamoru.
cuts.reason: Naisho ni suru is kept and is the casual way to say it.

cuts.trap: English 'rest up / recover' has no noun. Japanese 'takes off' the tiredness: onsen de tsukare o toru, yukkuri yasunde tsukare totte ne.
cuts.reason: Less common than tsukare ga toreru.

cuts.trap: Not kinniku o tsukuru. Muscle is 'attached' with tsukeru, the transitive half of kinniku ga tsuku.
cuts.reason: Gym talk.

cuts.english: a typhoon is coming, a typhoon hits
cuts.trap: English 'a typhoon hits' pushes to ataru or utsu. Japanese says the typhoon comes: ashita taifuu kuru rashii yo.
cuts.reason: 'A typhoon comes' maps straight onto kuru.

cuts.english: join a company, start working at a company
cuts.trap: English 'join a company' pushes to sanka suru (take part). Joining a firm, school or club is hairu: kaisha ni haitte sannen.
cuts.reason: Natural, but kaisha ni tsutomeru covers work; hairu = join is in the versatility list.

cuts.english: have a wedding, hold the ceremony
cuts.trap: English 'have a wedding' pushes to motsu or aru. A ceremony is held with ageru (shiki o ageru). Casual speech also says kekkonshiki yaru.
cuts.reason: Correct, but a life-event topic.

cuts.trap: Not futsukayoi ga aru. You become hungover (futsukayoi ni natta), or simply say futsukayoi da.
cuts.reason: People mostly say futsukayoi da.

cuts.english: have a meal now, make it mealtime
cuts.trap: English 'let's eat' pushes to gohan o tabeyou. At home people say sorosoro gohan ni shiyou (let's switch to the meal), and ofuro ni suru? gohan ni suru? asks which comes first.
cuts.reason: Natural at home, but versatility's -ni suru pattern already gives you the frame.

cuts.trap: Easy to guess once fuku is known. The risk is the homophones: kaze means wind or a cold, and fuku means blow or wipe. Keep it apart from kaze o hiku (catch a cold).
cuts.reviewReason: Two reviewers want it out of this domain. The traps review cuts it as fully guessable ('the wind blows' maps straight onto fuku; the draft itself says 'no verb trap'; lowest score in the domain at 3/2/2). The nuance review says to move it beside kaze o hiku in the body domain, or cut it, and this weather pass can't place items in another domain. Its content moved into kaze-ga-tsuyoi's notes (ii kaze fuiteru, kaze ga dete kita, kaze ga fuku vs kaze o hiku). The body domain can bring it back as a contrast partner if it wants one.
cuts.reason: 'The wind blows' maps straight onto fuku; its content lives in kaze ga tsuyoi's notes.

cuts.trap: 'Cough' is a verb in English; in Japanese the cough comes out, seki ga deru (seki ga tomaranai).
cuts.reviewReason: Cut by two reviewers (traps, nuance): same symptom + ga deru frame as netsu-ga-deru, which already lists seki as a partner, and a weak trap since seki (o) suru / seki shiteru are also fine. seki ga deru and seki shiteru are folded into netsu-ga-deru's use and notes.
cuts.reason: Same 'symptom ga deru' frame as netsu ga deru, which lists seki as a partner.

cuts.trap: Not densha o misu shita or densha o nakushita: missing a train is ni okureru (casually also nogashita or noriokureta).
cuts.reviewReason: Two reviewers wanted it gone: the nuance review cut it and the naturalness review retargeted it to a different collocation. Before the fact it says the same thing as densha ni maniawanai (the block used one sentence for both), after the fact natives say nogashita or noriokureta, and by ear it is easily confused with densha ga okureru. Its content now lives in other cards: the ga/ni contrast in densha-ga-okureru's use, and nogashita / noriokureta / misu shita in densha-ni-maniau's use and trap. Both reviewers proposed a replacement card, densha o nogasu or shuuden o nogasu (nogasu #2510, shuuden #8326, verified). It was not added because this pass adds no items and keeps slugs unchanged. It is recommended for the next additions pass.
cuts.reason: Says the same as densha ni maniawanai and is easily confused with densha ga okureru.
